name: Burkitts Reef ("Greg's Reef")
year: Construction Feb 1997 (2 days on-reef excavator work); first council application 1982 [R4][R8][R1][R6]
type: Existing natural basalt boulder headland reef, reshaped in place — boulders broken down/relocated with a rented excavator, not a new engineered structure [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]
purpose: Surfing only — remove/relocate hazardous boulders and old rail-track debris that made the point break dangerous and largely unsurfable [R1][R3][R6]
size: ~300 m3 of rock moved; at least 12 large basalt boulders relocated/broken down; ~2.5 m local tide swing exploited to work at low tide [R4][R8] Shape model (07_scale/shapes/burkitts-reef-bargara/HANDOFF.md section 3; LOW confidence): the traced outline is the whole visible basalt rock platform on the Esri image of 2025-09-05 (registry img-08): area 31,485 m2, 321 m E-W x 377 m N-S (minimum values; the image frame cuts the polygon at the south). It is NOT the reshaped boulder zone, whose location is not defined in any source; the card's ~300 m3 and ~12 boulders are text values only and cannot be checked against the outline. Tide swing ~2.5 m [R4] has no datum.
cost_usd_approx: ~USD $6,500-7,500 (rough 1997 FX estimate, not sourced from an FX reference) ASSUMPTION A1: the 1997 AUD/USD rate (about 0.65-0.75) is the agent's recollection, no exchange-rate source consulted; effect about +-10 %. The AUD 10,000 itself is reported identically by R1, R4, R6, R8 but all trace back to Redgard's account (no invoice seen).
financed_by: Greg Redgard personally, who mortgaged his house; approvals only (no funding) from the Beach Protection Authority of Queensland and Burnett Shire Council [R1][R6]
motivation: One local surfer's grassroots push, not a council/tourism/erosion program: Greg Redgard, a Bargara Boardriders Association member, first applied in 1982 and spent over a decade lobbying before approval landed in 1997 [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]
designer: Greg Redgard, a local sugarcane cutter with no engineering background or formal reef modelling/scale testing [R1][R4][R6]
contractor: None named as a firm — Redgard and his mates did the work themselves using a rented Kobelco hydraulic excavator [R1][R4][R6]
status_now: Still standing and still surfed as of the most recent (2024) coverage, known locally as "Greg's Reef"; no reported repair, damage, or removal in nearly three decades [R1][R5] Decision: verdict 'worked' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source, because every source found calls it a success; the evidence base is media and anecdotal (Redgard's own account, a researcher's before/after estimate relayed by R4, forum comments) with no monitoring data, so the verdict is of moderate reliability.
hover_text: A Bargara sugarcane cutter spent AUD $10,000 of his own money (mortgaging his house) to have an excavator reshape a natural basalt reef in 1997, after a 15-year fight for approval — surfable days rose from a handful a year to about 30, and the reef still works, unrepaired, almost three decades later [R1][R4][R6][R8].
design_as_planned: No formal engineering design, wave model, or scale test — Redgard designed and built it by instinct, telling ABC "Not rocket science, really, when you think about it" [R1]. The plan was simply to break down/relocate the boulders and discarded railway-track debris blocking the takeoff zone so a wave could "break over it," turning a hazard-strewn stretch into a rideable right-hand point break [R1][R6]. No modelled promises about wave height, beach width, or ecological effect were made [R1][R5][R6][R8].
as_built_vs_design: Because there was no formal design, sources report little planned-vs-built gap: construction (completed February 1997) matched Redgard's simple intent [R4] (February 1997 completion: R4; 'matched his intent' is the card author's reading of the absence of any reported gap). A Kobelco hydraulic excavator worked at low tide (using the ~2.5 m local tide range) to break down and reposition at least 12 large boulders, clearing a deep gutter that had split the wave into two disconnected sections, with gaps filled partly by hand — reportedly including carrying bricks out on a surfboard [R4][R6]. The Kobelco make and the 12 boulders are R4; the bricks on the surfboard are R6; the 'deep gutter that split the wave' detail is not isolated to one of R1/R4/R5/R6/R8 (paragraph-level attribution, the pages cannot be re-read here). Construction duration is reported two ways: [R4][R8] describe the on-reef excavator work as "two days (~8 hours)," while ABC News [R1] describes the whole job as completed "within weeks" of approval — a genuine, unresolved cross-source discrepancy the dossier flags rather than silently resolving. Some of the large rocks removed from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline rather than discarded, where locals still use them for fishing [R1][R4][R5][R6][R8].
outcome: Surfable days rose from "a handful" per year before the works to roughly 30 days a year afterward, with overhead (4+ ft) conditions on the order of 4 days a year, per researcher Andrew Pitt (SurfingRamps.com.au), cited independently via Raised Water Research and a Swellnet forum comment [R4][R8]. Wave face height is reported at 2-6 ft (0.5-2 m), period 7-10 seconds, described as a consistent peeling face that occasionally barrels [R4] (wave face and period; the 'consistent peeling' wording is paragraph-level, R3/R4/R8). Best swell window is November-April. The modification has held for nearly three decades with no reported maintenance, storm damage, or re-work [R1] (status as of January 2024; 'no reported' is a negative finding of this card). No coastal-protection outcome or ecological impact study was found (not a stated goal) [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8].
why_worked_or_failed: By the consensus of the sources listed in References (the card author's synthesis [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]; points (1)-(4) are inferences, not source statements), this is treated as a rare unambiguous success among artificial/enhanced surf reefs: (1) it reshaped an existing natural reef rather than importing new structure, unlike sandbag/geotextile reefs that must create a wholly new bathymetric feature; (2) it was a simple, low-risk intervention — removing hazards and gap-filling rather than engineering a specific wave shape, so there was little to go wrong structurally, unlike geotextile-bag reefs whose fabric tore, shifted, or sank; (3) a large natural tide range (~2.5 m) made the boulders workable at low tide with ordinary excavation equipment, without marine plant or diving contractors; (4) rock/boulder material is inherently more durable than sand-filled geotextile bags (general engineering judgement of the card author, unsourced here). No source reports a failure mode for this reef [R3][R4].
unexpected_results: Boulders cleared from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline, where locals now use them as a fishing spot [R5] — an unplanned secondary benefit. The project was picked up by TIME magazine (per ABC) as the "world's first surf enhancement project" [R1] and resurfaced in Australian national media in January 2024 as a good-news/DIY-hero story [R1][R7]. A marine-park dive site with the same name ("Burkitts Reef Dive Site", scuba/snorkel) is marketed separately [R10][R15]; it is NOT established that it is the same reef as the reshaped surf break: the image registry rejected the dive video as showing the natural marine-park reef, not the rock-reshaped surf break (03_images/reefs/burkitts-reef-bargara/images.json img-06, img-07; Lior 2026-09-25), so the 'two recreational audiences' reading and the dive site's ~9 m depth [R10] are not used for the surf reef. Redgard's daughter Tahlija, who grew up surfing the reef, became a professional surfer and credits it directly [R1]. No litigation, safety incident, localism/crowding conflict, or negative unexpected consequence was found in any source [R1][R5][R6][R10].
could_be_better: None of the sources reviewed (a negative finding of this card; including comparison pages that do critique other reefs' bag sizes, crest depths, and funding models) offer a specific critique of Burkitts Reef's execution — it is consistently used as the positive contrast case rather than a subject of critique. No critical surfer commentary was found. Sources suggest very little "could have been done better": if anything, some note it did not create "a world-class surf spot," only a modest, locally valued improvement — offered as a realistic-expectations lesson rather than a criticism [R3][R4][R8].
relevance_to_israel: Bargara's ~2.5 m tide swing [R4] is far larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast's tide range (well under 0.5 m, micro-tidal [R18], a web tide table) — Burkitts' construction method assumed tidal exposure that a Haifa-area site would not get, so similar reshaping there would likely need different plant (barge/crane, diver-assisted work) rather than simple low-tide excavator access (inference of the card author, unsourced). Bargara's 2-6 ft, 7-10 s point-break wave [R4] comes from a defined Coral Sea/Pacific swell season (Nov-Apr; the season is stated without a located source in this card, (unsourced)); Israeli Mediterranean wave climate is generally smaller and more wind-swell dominated with shorter period (general statement of the card author, (unsourced) here; Lior's Shikmona buoy readings are cited in the Albany card). The core transferable lesson is procedural/economic rather than technical: a modest, self-funded, reshape-what's-already-there approach (relocating existing boulders rather than importing new engineered material) achieved a multi-decade, apparently maintenance-free improvement for roughly AUD $10,000 [R1][R4][R6], in contrast to far more expensive professionally engineered geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere that have frequently failed or required costly renewal (comparison is the card author's, based on the other reef cards of this project). For any Haifa/Israel natural reef or rock outcrop with existing hazards, a similarly minimal clear/reshape approach is the direct analogy worth testing, if geology and permitting allow [R4][R1].

reviews.quote_or_summary: You really couldn't surf it, because you'd take off, go for about 2 or 3 metres and you would just run into rocks.
The wave could break over it. Not rocket science, really, when you think about it.
He took Burkitts Reef, redefined what was possible and made what was once unrideable an absolute playground.

Assessed the reef's before/after performance: surfable days rose from "a handful... every year" to about 30/year, with the wave changing from a hazard-split break into a smooth peeling lip with some barrel action.

reviews.quote_or_summary: Prior wave broke a few days/yr, now 30 days/yr plus overhead 4 days/yr — explicitly contrasted with failed professionally-designed reefs.

The surf break of Burkitts Reef at Bargara, in Queensland's Bundaberg region, was previously obstructed by large rocks. Then Greg Redgard and his mates turned the 'unrideable' beach into a surfers' playground.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Surfable days rose from "a handful" per year before the works to roughly 30 days a year afterward, with overhead (4+ ft) conditions on the order of 4 days a year, per researcher Andrew Pitt (SurfingRamps.com.au), cited independently via Raised Water Research and a Swellnet forum comment [R4][R8]. Wave face height is reported at 2-6 ft (0.5-2 m), period 7-10 seconds, described as a consistent peeling face that occasionally barrels [R4] (wave face and period; the 'consistent peeling' wording is paragraph-level, R3/R4/R8). Best swell window is November-April. The modification has held for nearly three decades with no reported maintenance, storm damage, or re-work [R1] (status as of January 2024; 'no reported' is a negative finding of this card). No coastal-protection outcome or ecological impact study was found (not a stated goal) [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: By the consensus of the sources listed in References (the card author's synthesis [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]; points (1)-(4) are inferences, not source statements), this is treated as a rare unambiguous success among artificial/enhanced surf reefs: (1) it reshaped an existing natural reef rather than importing new structure, unlike sandbag/geotextile reefs that must create a wholly new bathymetric feature; (2) it was a simple, low-risk intervention — removing hazards and gap-filling rather than engineering a specific wave shape, so there was little to go wrong structurally, unlike geotextile-bag reefs whose fabric tore, shifted, or sank; (3) a large natural tide range (~2.5 m) made the boulders workable at low tide with ordinary excavation equipment, without marine plant or diving contractors; (4) rock/boulder material is inherently more durable than sand-filled geotextile bags (general engineering judgement of the card author, unsourced here). No source reports a failure mode for this reef [R3][R4].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Boulders cleared from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline, where locals now use them as a fishing spot [R5] — an unplanned secondary benefit. The project was picked up by TIME magazine (per ABC) as the "world's first surf enhancement project" [R1] and resurfaced in Australian national media in January 2024 as a good-news/DIY-hero story [R1][R7]. A marine-park dive site with the same name ("Burkitts Reef Dive Site", scuba/snorkel) is marketed separately [R10][R15]; it is NOT established that it is the same reef as the reshaped surf break: the image registry rejected the dive video as showing the natural marine-park reef, not the rock-reshaped surf break (03_images/reefs/burkitts-reef-bargara/images.json img-06, img-07; Lior 2026-09-25), so the 'two recreational audiences' reading and the dive site's ~9 m depth [R10] are not used for the surf reef. Redgard's daughter Tahlija, who grew up surfing the reef, became a professional surfer and credits it directly [R1]. No litigation, safety incident, localism/crowding conflict, or negative unexpected consequence was found in any source [R1][R5][R6][R10].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: None of the sources reviewed (a negative finding of this card; including comparison pages that do critique other reefs' bag sizes, crest depths, and funding models) offer a specific critique of Burkitts Reef's execution — it is consistently used as the positive contrast case rather than a subject of critique. No critical surfer commentary was found. Sources suggest very little "could have been done better": if anything, some note it did not create "a world-class surf spot," only a modest, locally valued improvement — offered as a realistic-expectations lesson rather than a criticism [R3][R4][R8].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Bargara's ~2.5 m tide swing [R4] is far larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast's tide range (well under 0.5 m, micro-tidal [R18], a web tide table) — Burkitts' construction method assumed tidal exposure that a Haifa-area site would not get, so similar reshaping there would likely need different plant (barge/crane, diver-assisted work) rather than simple low-tide excavator access (inference of the card author, unsourced). Bargara's 2-6 ft, 7-10 s point-break wave [R4] comes from a defined Coral Sea/Pacific swell season (Nov-Apr; the season is stated without a located source in this card, (unsourced)); Israeli Mediterranean wave climate is generally smaller and more wind-swell dominated with shorter period (general statement of the card author, (unsourced) here; Lior's Shikmona buoy readings are cited in the Albany card). The core transferable lesson is procedural/economic rather than technical: a modest, self-funded, reshape-what's-already-there approach (relocating existing boulders rather than importing new engineered material) achieved a multi-decade, apparently maintenance-free improvement for roughly AUD $10,000 [R1][R4][R6], in contrast to far more expensive professionally engineered geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere that have frequently failed or required costly renewal (comparison is the card author's, based on the other reef cards of this project). For any Haifa/Israel natural reef or rock outcrop with existing hazards, a similarly minimal clear/reshape approach is the direct analogy worth testing, if geology and permitting allow [R4][R1].

name: Cable Station Reef (Cables Reef)
year: 1999 (construction Feb-Dec 1999; site studies from 1988; design/feasibility report to WA govt 1994) [R2] Sources disagree on the year: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.1-2, section 3.1.1) state the reef was constructed in 1998 ('world's first artificial surfing reef built in Perth in 1998'); the card keeps 1999 until Lior decides [R17]. Decision (agent default, 2026-09-24; re-checked 2026-10-10): 1999 kept because construction start in February 1999 is announced in a contemporary WA Government media statement of 7 Feb 1999 [R20] and in R2; the 1998 of [R17] is a single later secondary statement. Lior may overrule.
type: Granite boulders (over 10,000 tons, boulders up to 3 m) placed on existing natural limestone reef/bedrock; one source (ICM) and another (The Inertia, quoting the Committee) instead describe the placed rock as limestone rather than granite — sources disagree [R1][R2][R4][R6]
purpose: Surf-only enhancement: create a more consistent, higher-quality surfing spot with left- and right-hand waves and a 'gently barreling' face for intermediate surfers, for swells 0.5-3.5 m at a peel angle of ~45°; not designed as a coastal-protection structure [R1][R2]
size: Length ~140 m (north-south), max width ~70 m, ~275 m offshore, water depth 3-6 m, reef crest 1-3 m below average tide (~1.5 m below lowest tide per a 2009 review); volume of rock ~3,500 m3 per Wikipedia vs ~5,000 m3 per Coastal Management (ICM) - sources disagree [R1][R2][R4] Added 2026-10-10: Blacka et al. (2013, Appendix A.1 p.92-93; Table 4.2 p.65): V-shape rock, 140 m longshore x 70 m cross-shore (max dims), 275 m offshore, depth 3.0-6.0 m, crest submergence 1.0-2.5 m below MSL, 5,500 m3 of 1.5 t (body) and 3.0 t (keyed perimeter) granite boulders placed by excavator from a barge [R18]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2) give 5,000 m3 of limestone rock placed from a barge, designed as a 50 m long right-hand breaker (Lyons 1992 UWA BEng thesis) [R17]. Sources disagree: volume 3,500 [R1] / 5,000 [R4][R17] / 5,500 m3 [R18] (Wikipedia / ICM and Mead & Borrero / Blacka); crest 1-3 m (card) [R2] vs 1.0-2.5 m (Blacka) [R18] below mean level, and Pitt 2009 ~1.5 m below the lowest tide (relayed by [R2]; original not seen); material granite (Blacka [R18], card [R2]) vs limestone (Mead & Borrero [R17]); Blacka gives mass classes 1.5 t / 3.0 t [R18], not 'up to 3 m across' [R2]. The design plan traced for the 3D model (Lyons 1992, reproduced in Blacka 2013 Fig. A.2) has an RL datum ambiguity of 0.78 m (chart datum vs 'below MSL'): the 0.78 m is the 'MTL 0.78 m above datum' of Pattiaratchi 1999 p.3 [R21] and the 'below MSL' wording is Blacka's [R18]; DERIVED comparison of the two, this project, 07_scale/shapes/cables-reef-wa/HANDOFF.md section 3 and discrepancy 1. Shape/3D model (07_scale/shapes/cables-reef-wa/HANDOFF.md section 3; traced from the design plan Blacka 2013 Fig. A.2, scale from its printed dimensions, +-3 %): footprint 121 x 76 m (4,049 m2; 4,355 m2 with the drawn southern extension), the 3D model measures 254-263 m from the reef centre to the 0 m AHD line (DERIVED from the DoT WA soundings [R22]; stated: about 250 m [R21], about 275 m [R18]). The model's default rock volume is the surface surveyed by the WA Department of Transport in Nov 1999 on this footprint, 4,671 m3 +-1,000, and 5,219 m3 in Feb 2002 (surveyed single-beam surfaces over the measured 1998 seabed [R22]); the idealised design surface on the measured bed gives 3,920 m3 (4,249 m3 with the drawn extension). The model volume is no longer calibrated to any stated volume (DERIVED, this project: 07_scale/shapes/cables-reef-wa/3d/METHODS_3D.md sections 3.4 and 4). The traced 121 x 76 m differs from the 140 x 70 m of the text sources [R2][R18] by -13 % / +9 % (DERIVED: (121-140)/140 and (76-70)/70, this project, 07_scale/shapes/cables-reef-wa/HANDOFF.md discrepancy 2); the card keeps the published text values and the model keeps its own traced values.
cost: Approximately AUD $2 million for study, design and construction combined [R2] Added 2026-10-10: Blacka et al. (2013, p.94, Table 4.4 p.69): documented total cost A$1.51 M (Ranasinghe 2001) to A$1.8 M (Jackson & Corbett 2007); about A$2.5 M in 2013 AUD (0.5 feasibility + 2.0 construction), A$457 per m3 [R18].

ASSUMPTION A1: AUD/USD 0.63-0.67 for 1999 is the agent's recollection, no exchange-rate source was consulted (replace with the RBA historical series); effect: US figure uncertain by about +-10 % and ignores inflation. A$2 M is [R2]; Blacka (2013) [R18] gives A$1.51-1.8 M nominal
financed_by: Western Australia Department of Sport and Recreation [R2]
motivation: The site was a natural point break, Cable Station reef, surfed since the late 1940s and regarded highly through the 1950s-1980s, which local surfers (per Len Dibben) believed had been degraded by nearby coastal engineering works (Cottesloe Groyne, Dutch Inn Groyne and others) [R3]. This fed the WA Surf Rider Association's 1975 'Build a Reef' campaign (surfers John Balgarnie and Geoff Berry), carried through to the 1999 build by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell working with the Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee [R3][R6], with site-selection (M. Crawford, 1988) and a 1994 engineering feasibility report to the WA government preceding construction [R2]
designer: Client/advocacy body: Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee, driven by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell [R3][R6]. Site selection: M. Crawford (1988) [R2]. Design sketches enabling funding: Andrew Pitt, founder of SurfingRamps.com.au [R2]. Engineering studies: WA Department of Marine and Harbours and the University of Western Australia, reporting to the WA government in 1994 [R2]. Physical-model design work (random-wave flume, 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin, optimum bed slope 1:20, final 'boomerang-shaped' reef) documented in Hutt et al., 'Design Studies for an Artificial Surfing Reef: Cable Station, Western Australia' [R8]
contractor: WA Limestone, using a barge-based cycle of transporting and placing the granite boulders onto the limestone bedrock [R2]
status_now: No removal or dismantling reported in any source found; the granite/limestone construction is repeatedly described as structurally durable ('stood the test of time,' better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere) as of the most recent sources reviewed (2023-2024) [R2][R3]. Wave-frequency consistency remains disputed among surfers [R1][R2][R6]
hover_text: A 140 m x 70 m granite-boulder reef built in 1999 for about AUD $2 million (state-government funded) to improve surfing off Cottesloe/Leighton, Perth; it proved structurally durable (unlike sand-filled geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere) but its wave frequency remains disputed, with a 2009 assessment finding only a handful of good surf days per month against the original design target [R1][R2].
design_as_planned: The Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee's design goal was a reef generating consistent left- and right-hand waves with a 'gently barreling' face, working across a 0.5-3.5 m swell range at a ~45° peel angle suited to intermediate surfers [R1][R2]. Physical-model testing (random-wave flume; 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin) found an optimum bottom slope of 1:20 (matching the site's natural bed slope and slopes recorded at many surf breaks worldwide); several reef shapes were tested and a 'boomerang-shaped' form that minimised fill volume and merged with the existing natural reef was selected as final [R8]. Placing rock directly on the existing limestone bedrock (rather than a sand-filled geotextile-bag structure on sand) was explicitly meant to avoid sinking and remove the need for sand cover [R2] Added 2026-10-10: designed by UWA and the WA Department of Marine and Harbours using 2D and 3D physical models and numerical studies (Ranasinghe et al. 2001); design plan Lyons (1992), reproduced as Blacka et al. (2013) Fig. A.2 (Appendix A.1, p.92-94) [R18][R17].
as_built_vs_design: Construction began February 1999, reached ~90% completion by May 1999, but was not fully finished until December 1999 [R2]. WA Limestone used a cyclical barge-transport-and-placement process, placing over 10,000 tons of quarried granite boulders (up to 3 m across) on the limestone bedrock [R2]. One documented mid-project change: once it became clear the rock-on-bedrock method needed no sand cover and prevented sinking, that realisation 'led to an extension of the reef's southern end' beyond the original footprint [R2] — a design-to-built change, though no source gives a size or cost figure for the extension. No cost-overrun figure was found in any source listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement)
outcome: Early academic monitoring was positive: Stacey Bancroft's 1999 study found peel angles closely matched the ~45° design target and surfable days exceeded predicted values across three measurement methods [R2][R9]; Charitha Pattiaratchi's 1999-2001 monitoring concluded the reef was 'performing according to its design and... as well or better than predicted,' citing roughly four to six months of good conditions in 2000-2001, though the paper itself notes this 'has been disputed by some members of the local surfing population' [R9][R2]. A 2009 assessment by Andrew Pitt found the reef 'only provides a "few surfable days per month"' and does not reliably break chest-high waves, attributing this to the crest depth (~1.5 m below lowest tide) and the site's position in the swell shadow of Rottnest Island and other outer reefs, which block a significant share of incoming wave energy [R2]. Wikipedia similarly notes performance is 'hampered by the presence of offshore islands and reefs which block a significant fraction of the wave energy' [R1]. Two conflicting headline frequency figures exist across sources: some describe ~150 rideable days per year, others (Pitt, 2009) describe only a handful of good days per month — this dossier could not resolve which is more current [R2][R6]. Structurally the reef has proven durable, with better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs built elsewhere in the same era [R2]. No coastal-protection outcome (beach widening/salient formation) was reported, consistent with the reef never being designed for that purpose [R2] Added 2026-10-10: Pattiaratchi (2007), cited by Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2): surfable days rose from 5-7 per year before to 142 after construction; the site was 'almost' a break, sheltered by Rottnest Island and fringing reefs, small wave climate, narrow swell window; public reaction was generally negative ('not producing good waves'); the authors argue success should be judged before vs after, not against the 'perfect wave' promise (interested party: the designers) [R17]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.93): Pattiaratchi's (2003) video study found surfable days as predicted or better, but surfers report good quality only in big swells, that modelling over-predicted wave height, and few good days per year; no information on long-term stability or durability; settlement/scour 'not reported'; rated 'partially' successful for surfing and 'not designed at all for coastal protection' (p.92); site tide range 0.8 m, Hs 1-2 m summer and 1.5-2.5 m winter, longshore transport negligible (Table 4.3 p.67) [R18].
why_worked_or_failed: Cable Station Reef is repeatedly cited (with Burkitts Reef and Palm Beach Reef) as one of the few artificial surf reefs built from solid rock rather than sand-filled geotextile bags, and one of the few that did not structurally fail [R6][R7]. Surf scientist Shaw Mead told Newsroom (NZ) that 'while the structures have failed (except for Cable Station (limestone), Borth (rock), Palm Beach (rock) and Narrowneck (sandbags maintained)), all have created surfing waves that have replicated the designs' [R7]. The engineering logic: geotextile sand-filled containers fail because losing sand from even one bag changes the whole structure's shape, whereas rock placed directly on hard limestone bedrock does not sink, needs no sand cover, and keeps its shape under wave attack [R2][R6]. It under-delivers on wave frequency because (1) the reef crest sits too deep for smaller/moderate swells to break reliably, against a 0.5 m minimum-swell design target [R2]; and (2) the site lies in the lee of Rottnest Island and other offshore reefs which absorb/block a meaningful share of incoming swell energy [R1][R2]. Verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source: the rock structure is durable and reproduces its design [R6][R7][R18], but wave frequency is disputed and Blacka et al. rate it only 'partially' successful for surfing [R18] (p.92-93)
unexpected_results: Access to the site has caused dune erosion, as surfers cross the cliff face on foot to reach the break [R2]. Positively, Bancroft's monitoring found significant biological recolonisation of the placed rock surfaces, an ecological benefit not central to the original surf-only design brief [R2]. No reports of increased fishing pressure, dangerous rips, drowning incidents, or litigation tied specifically to Cable Station Reef were found in the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement)
could_be_better: Andrew Pitt's 2009 assessment recommended making the reef shallower and extending its seaward 'nose' further offshore, to intercept more swell before it is blocked by Rottnest Island and the outer reefs, and to allow smaller swells to break as originally designed [R2]. Surfers' recurring complaint across sources is consistency, not quality — they 'appreciate the quality of the wave when it breaks' but see 'lack of frequency as the biggest problem' [R1][R2][R6]
relevance_to_israel: Cable Station's core engineering lesson — build in solid rock placed directly on hard substrate rather than sand-filled geotextile bags on a sandy bed — removes tide-driven sand-burial risk as a failure mode, directly relevant to any Israeli reef design [R2][R6]. Its real-world problem was insufficient swell energy reaching too-deep a crest, not excess swell [R1][R2]; Lior's own field measurements at the Shikmona buoy off Haifa define the 'minimum surfable wave' window there as 0.45-0.6 m significant wave height (0.6-0.8 m maximum), with swell approach ~284-294 deg (WNW) and peak periods ~5.7-6.2 s — a substantially smaller, more marginal wave climate than Cable Station's 0.5-3.5 m design range [R15]. The transferable lesson is that a low-energy site like Haifa/Shikmona faces exactly Cable Station's failure mode (crest set too deep to reliably break the smaller end of the local swell range) if the crest is not kept shallow — the same design lever Pitt recommended for Cable Station, and the same one Lior's own 'Light Construction' concept sketch addresses by placing its crest near the natural Wave Breaking Depth line [R15]. A government/community-driven, surfer-advocated funding model (WA Dept of Sport and Recreation, after a 24-year advocacy campaign from 1975-1999) is also a plausible funding-model precedent for an Israeli project pursued via local surfer/NGO advocacy [R2][R3]

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameCable Station Reef (Cables Reef)
PlaceLeighton / Cottesloe, Perth, Western Australia
CountryAustralia
Year1999 (construction Feb-Dec 1999; site studies from 1988; design/feasibility report to WA govt 1994) [R2] Sources disagree on the year: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.1-2, section 3.1.1) state the reef was constructed in 1998 ('world's first artificial surfing reef built in Perth in 1998'); the card keeps 1999 until Lior decides [R17]. Decision (agent default, 2026-09-24; re-checked 2026-10-10): 1999 kept because construction start in February 1999 is announced in a contemporary WA Government media statement of 7 Feb 1999 [R20] and in R2; the 1998 of [R17] is a single later secondary statement. Lior may overrule.
TypeGranite boulders (over 10,000 tons, boulders up to 3 m) placed on existing natural limestone reef/bedrock; one source (ICM) and another (The Inertia, quoting the Committee) instead describe the placed rock as limestone rather than granite — sources disagree [R1][R2][R4][R6]
PurposeSurf-only enhancement: create a more consistent, higher-quality surfing spot with left- and right-hand waves and a 'gently barreling' face for intermediate surfers, for swells 0.5-3.5 m at a peel angle of ~45°; not designed as a coastal-protection structure [R1][R2]
SizeLength ~140 m (north-south), max width ~70 m, ~275 m offshore, water depth 3-6 m, reef crest 1-3 m below average tide (~1.5 m below lowest tide per a 2009 review); volume of rock ~3,500 m3 per Wikipedia vs ~5,000 m3 per Coastal Management (ICM) - sources disagree [R1][R2][R4] Added 2026-10-10: Blacka et al. (2013, Appendix A.1 p.92-93; Table 4.2 p.65): V-shape rock, 140 m longshore x 70 m cross-shore (max dims), 275 m offshore, depth 3.0-6.0 m, crest submergence 1.0-2.5 m below MSL, 5,500 m3 of 1.5 t (body) and 3.0 t (keyed perimeter) granite boulders placed by excavator from a barge [R18]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2) give 5,000 m3 of limestone rock placed from a barge, designed as a 50 m long right-hand breaker (Lyons 1992 UWA BEng thesis) [R17]. Sources disagree: volume 3,500 [R1] / 5,000 [R4][R17] / 5,500 m3 [R18] (Wikipedia / ICM and Mead & Borrero / Blacka); crest 1-3 m (card) [R2] vs 1.0-2.5 m (Blacka) [R18] below mean level, and Pitt 2009 ~1.5 m below the lowest tide (relayed by [R2]; original not seen); material granite (Blacka [R18], card [R2]) vs limestone (Mead & Borrero [R17]); Blacka gives mass classes 1.5 t / 3.0 t [R18], not 'up to 3 m across' [R2]. The design plan traced for the 3D model (Lyons 1992, reproduced in Blacka 2013 Fig. A.2) has an RL datum ambiguity of 0.78 m (chart datum vs 'below MSL'): the 0.78 m is the 'MTL 0.78 m above datum' of Pattiaratchi 1999 p.3 [R21] and the 'below MSL' wording is Blacka's [R18]; DERIVED comparison of the two, this project, 07_scale/shapes/cables-reef-wa/HANDOFF.md section 3 and discrepancy 1. Shape/3D model (07_scale/shapes/cables-reef-wa/HANDOFF.md section 3; traced from the design plan Blacka 2013 Fig. A.2, scale from its printed dimensions, +-3 %): footprint 121 x 76 m (4,049 m2; 4,355 m2 with the drawn southern extension), the 3D model measures 254-263 m from the reef centre to the 0 m AHD line (DERIVED from the DoT WA soundings [R22]; stated: about 250 m [R21], about 275 m [R18]). sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: The site was a natural point break, Cable Station reef, surfed since the late 1940s and regarded highly through the 1950s-1980s, which local surfers (per Len Dibben) believed had been degraded by nearby coastal engineering works (Cottesloe Groyne, Dutch Inn Groyne and others) [R3]. This fed the WA Surf Rider Association's 1975 'Build a Reef' campaign (surfers John Balgarnie and Geoff Berry), carried through to the 1999 build by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell working with the Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee [R3][R6], with site-selection (M. Crawford, 1988) and a 1994 engineering feasibility report to the WA government preceding construction [R2]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee's design goal was a reef generating consistent left- and right-hand waves with a 'gently barreling' face, working across a 0.5-3.5 m swell range at a ~45° peel angle suited to intermediate surfers [R1][R2]. Physical-model testing (random-wave flume; 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin) found an optimum bottom slope of 1:20 (matching the site's natural bed slope and slopes recorded at many surf breaks worldwide); several reef shapes were tested and a 'boomerang-shaped' form that minimised fill volume and merged with the existing natural reef was selected as final [R8]. Placing rock directly on the existing limestone bedrock (rather than a sand-filled geotextile-bag structure on sand) was explicitly meant to avoid sinking and remove the need for sand cover [R2] Added 2026-10-10: designed by UWA and the WA Department of Marine and Harbours using 2D and 3D physical models and numerical studies (Ranasinghe et al. 2001); design plan Lyons (1992), reproduced as Blacka et al. (2013) Fig. A.2 (Appendix A.1, p.92-94) [R18][R17].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction began February 1999, reached ~90% completion by May 1999, but was not fully finished until December 1999 [R2]. WA Limestone used a cyclical barge-transport-and-placement process, placing over 10,000 tons of quarried granite boulders (up to 3 m across) on the limestone bedrock [R2]. One documented mid-project change: once it became clear the rock-on-bedrock method needed no sand cover and prevented sinking, that realisation 'led to an extension of the reef's southern end' beyond the original footprint [R2] — a design-to-built change, though no source gives a size or cost figure for the extension. No cost-overrun figure was found in any source listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement)

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Early academic monitoring was positive: Stacey Bancroft's 1999 study found peel angles closely matched the ~45° design target and surfable days exceeded predicted values across three measurement methods [R2][R9]; Charitha Pattiaratchi's 1999-2001 monitoring concluded the reef was 'performing according to its design and... as well or better than predicted,' citing roughly four to six months of good conditions in 2000-2001, though the paper itself notes this 'has been disputed by some members of the local surfing population' [R9][R2]. A 2009 assessment by Andrew Pitt found the reef 'only provides a "few surfable days per month"' and does not reliably break chest-high waves, attributing this to the crest depth (~1.5 m below lowest tide) and the site's position in the swell shadow of Rottnest Island and other outer reefs, which block a significant share of incoming wave energy [R2]. Wikipedia similarly notes performance is 'hampered by the presence of offshore islands and reefs which block a significant fraction of the wave energy' [R1]. Two conflicting headline frequency figures exist across sources: some describe ~150 rideable days per year, others (Pitt, 2009) describe only a handful of good days per month — this dossier could not resolve which is more current [R2][R6]. Structurally the reef has proven durable, with better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs built elsewhere in the same era [R2]. No coastal-protection outcome (beach widening/salient formation) was reported, consistent with the reef never being designed for that purpose [R2] Added 2026-10-10: Pattiaratchi (2007), cited by Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2): surfable days rose from 5-7 per year before to 142 after construction; the site was 'almost' a break, sheltered by Rottnest Island and fringing reefs, small wave climate, narrow swell window; public reaction was generally negative ('not producing good waves'); the authors argue success should be judged before vs after, not against the 'perfect wave' promise (interested party: the designers) [R17]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.93): Pattiaratchi's (2003) video study found surfable days as predicted or better, but surfers report good quality only in big swells, that modelling over-predicted wave height, and few good days per year; no information on long-term stability or durability; settlement/scour 'not reported'; rated 'partially' successful for surfing and 'not designed at all for coastal protection' (p.92); site tide range 0.8 m, Hs 1-2 m summer and 1.5-2.5 m winter, longshore transport negligible (Table 4.3 p.67) [R18].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Cable Station Reef is repeatedly cited (with Burkitts Reef and Palm Beach Reef) as one of the few artificial surf reefs built from solid rock rather than sand-filled geotextile bags, and one of the few that did not structurally fail [R6][R7]. Surf scientist Shaw Mead told Newsroom (NZ) that 'while the structures have failed (except for Cable Station (limestone), Borth (rock), Palm Beach (rock) and Narrowneck (sandbags maintained)), all have created surfing waves that have replicated the designs' [R7]. The engineering logic: geotextile sand-filled containers fail because losing sand from even one bag changes the whole structure's shape, whereas rock placed directly on hard limestone bedrock does not sink, needs no sand cover, and keeps its shape under wave attack [R2][R6]. It under-delivers on wave frequency because (1) the reef crest sits too deep for smaller/moderate swells to break reliably, against a 0.5 m minimum-swell design target [R2]; and (2) the site lies in the lee of Rottnest Island and other offshore reefs which absorb/block a meaningful share of incoming swell energy [R1][R2]. Verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source: the rock structure is durable and reproduces its design [R6][R7][R18], but wave frequency is disputed and Blacka et al. rate it only 'partially' successful for surfing [R18] (p.92-93)

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Access to the site has caused dune erosion, as surfers cross the cliff face on foot to reach the break [R2]. Positively, Bancroft's monitoring found significant biological recolonisation of the placed rock surfaces, an ecological benefit not central to the original surf-only design brief [R2]. No reports of increased fishing pressure, dangerous rips, drowning incidents, or litigation tied specifically to Cable Station Reef were found in the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement)

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Andrew Pitt's 2009 assessment recommended making the reef shallower and extending its seaward 'nose' further offshore, to intercept more swell before it is blocked by Rottnest Island and the outer reefs, and to allow smaller swells to break as originally designed [R2]. Surfers' recurring complaint across sources is consistency, not quality — they 'appreciate the quality of the wave when it breaks' but see 'lack of frequency as the biggest problem' [R1][R2][R6]

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Cable Station's core engineering lesson — build in solid rock placed directly on hard substrate rather than sand-filled geotextile bags on a sandy bed — removes tide-driven sand-burial risk as a failure mode, directly relevant to any Israeli reef design [R2][R6]. Its real-world problem was insufficient swell energy reaching too-deep a crest, not excess swell [R1][R2]; Lior's own field measurements at the Shikmona buoy off Haifa define the 'minimum surfable wave' window there as 0.45-0.6 m significant wave height (0.6-0.8 m maximum), with swell approach ~284-294 deg (WNW) and peak periods ~5.7-6.2 s — a substantially smaller, more marginal wave climate than Cable Station's 0.5-3.5 m design range [R15]. The transferable lesson is that a low-energy site like Haifa/Shikmona faces exactly Cable Station's failure mode (crest set too deep to reliably break the smaller end of the local swell range) if the crest is not kept shallow — the same design lever Pitt recommended for Cable Station, and the same one Lior's own 'Light Construction' concept sketch addresses by placing its crest near the natural Wave Breaking Depth line [R15]. A government/community-driven, surfer-advocated funding model (WA Dept of Sport and Recreation, after a 24-year advocacy campaign from 1975-1999) is also a plausible funding-model precedent for an Israeli project pursued via local surfer/NGO advocacy [R2][R3]

name: Narrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
year: Construction began August 1999, completed by December 2000 [R2][R8]; renewed/topped up with 84 more containers June 2018 [R2][R9][R14]. [Added 2026-10-10] Blacka et al. (2013, p.94) also give construction from August 1999, main phase complete December 2000, with crest raise/trim work in 2001, 2002, 2004 and 2006 and about 50 further containers 2001-2007 (p.97) [R23].
type: Submerged multi-purpose artificial reef (MPR) built from sand-filled geotextile containers ("mega sandbags"), placed on the seabed by split-hull barge with GPS positioning [R1][R2][R3][R9].
purpose: Primary: coastal/erosion protection for the Narrowneck isthmus, where only ~100 m of land separates the Nerang River from the ocean [R2][R14]. Secondary ("multi-purpose"): surfing amenity, folded in partly for public-relations value in a surf-centric region [R2]. A tertiary, unplanned outcome was ecological habitat creation [R1][R3][R8][R9].
size: Volume approx. 70,000 m3 of sand (the largest multi-purpose reef ever built at the time), from approx. 400 geotextile containers each approx. 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter [R1][R9][R3]. Footprint reported as 350 m x 600 m, split "V" shape, 200 m offshore, bags 1-10 m below sea level [R9]; a second source directly states the reef "measures 450 meters long by 250 meters wide" [R8] -- the two footprint figures disagree and both are given per the reference rule. Crest lowered 1 m before construction, landing about 1.5 m below the low-tide waterline [R2][R3]; by 2017 low-tide depth over the reef measured 2.5-2.6 m, i.e. the crest had sunk/settled deeper than designed [R2]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on footprint: Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.65) give a V-shape of 170 m longshore x 280 m cross-shore (maximum dimensions), water depth 2-10 m, offshore 100-600 m, min. submergence 1.0 m [R23] - a third figure beside 350 x 600 m [R9] and 450 x 250 m [R8]; all three kept, unresolved. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2) also quote about 70,000 m3 (Jackson 2007) [R22]. For comparison the 3D model work (2026-10-10) counts 534 containers x 147 m3 = 78,500 m3 placed, of which only 17-27 % remains as an exposed mound [R24]. SOURCES DISAGREE on crest lowering: the card's '1 m' [R2][R3] vs Blacka (p.94) design -1.0 m AHD to built -1.5 m AHD, i.e. 0.5 m [R23]; the 3D work measures the present crest at -2.2 m AHD [R24] (see as_built_vs_design). Container counts and volume in the primary monitoring papers (2026-10-10 audit): 408 containers, 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter, placed August 1999 - December 2000 (Jackson et al. 2007, printed p.4); about 450 by 2006 (+10 in 2002-03, +15 in 2004, +17 in 2006; Jackson et al. 2012, p.3 and Fig 4 table p.4); +84 in the 2017-18 renewal [R26][R27][R25]; about 534 placed in total. The project's 147 m3 per container is DERIVED: 60,000 m3 (Jackson et al. 2007, Table 2, printed p.13, Narrowneck column [R26]) / 408 containers (same paper, p.4), this project, 07_scale/shapes/narrowneck-gold-coast/HANDOFF.md section 3c and 3d/METHODS_3D.md assumption A12 (the same 147 m3 is assumed for the later containers). So the 70,000 m3 quoted by the card's sources and the 60,000 m3 behind it are not reconciled here. Project-traced footprint (not a source statement): the visible container field on the Esri image of 8 Aug 2020 covers 6,239 m2 (arms 5,948 m2; bounding box 113.3 x 157.4 m; a lower bound, the deeper toe is not visible); the council asset polygon (OBJECTID 4637) is 171 x 262 m, 34,565 m2, which agrees with Blacka's 170 x 280 m [R23][R28]; the card's 350 x 600 m [R9] and 450 x 250 m [R8] are not supported by either.
cost: Original 1999 build: AUD $2.3 million (approx. AUD $30/m3) per one source [R3], and separately "roughly $2.1 million AUD... over the first 10 years" per another [R5] -- both given since they disagree on scope (one-off build vs. 10-year total). Lior's own notes and a Hebrew-language source both give "$2.5 million," currency unspecified [R19][R20] -- not reconciled with the figures above. 2017-2018 renewal: approx. AUD $2 million per Mayor Tom Tate, as reported by the Gold Coast Bulletin via The Inertia [R10]. [Added 2026-10-10] Blacka et al. (2013, A.2.7 p.101, Table 4.4 p.69): total A$2.8 M including top-ups and maintenance (Jackson & Corbett 2007) = about A$3.9 M in 2013 AUD, A$56 per m3 (not comparable with the card's A$30/m3, a different basis and year); about two thirds construction, one third studies (Ranasinghe 2001); A$9,800 minimum per metre of beach protected [R23]. Economic context (p.100): a 25-year ARI erosion event about A$305 M (1996 AUD), 5-year ARI about A$47 M, Gold Coast surf industry about A$160 M per year [R23].
cost_usd_approx: Very rough conversions by this report (not sourced): original build AUD $2.3M (1999 AUD~USD 0.65) approx. USD $1.5M; 2017-2018 renewal AUD $2M (2018 AUD~USD 0.75) approx. USD $1.5M. ASSUMPTION: the exchange rates (AUD/USD 0.65 for 1999, 0.75 for 2018) are unsourced estimates of this project; order of magnitude only.
financed_by: Gold Coast City Council, as part of its Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R1][R2][R9][R13]. No private or state/federal co-funding was found in any of the sources listed in References (a negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement).
motivation: Erosion problem predates the reef by decades: a 1971 Delft University of Technology report, commissioned by the Queensland Government, recommended a groyne at Narrowneck [R9][R13]. Training walls built at the Spit in 1985 helped erosion further north but not at Narrowneck itself, and Cyclone Nancy (1990) eroded the beach back to the boulder wall protecting the Nerang River [R2]. Gold Coast City Council chose an artificial reef instead of the recommended groyne, branding it a "Multi-Purpose Reef" so that surfing amenity could be folded into the PR case in a surf-centric city [R2][R9][R13]. No evidence found of state/federal political involvement or a single named political champion for the original 1999 project; Mayor Tom Tate became the public face of the 2017-2018 renewal [R10]. [Added 2026-10-10] Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): the decision to build was driven by a cost-benefit analysis (Raybould and Mules 1998), as part of the Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy (Queensland Environment Award 2000); the first MPR designed primarily for coastal protection with surfing secondary (p.2) [R22].
designer: Original 1999 design: Prof. Kerry Black and Shaw Mead (University of Waikato, NZ; later founders of coastal-engineering firm ASR) [R11]. ICM (International Coastal Management, Gold Coast) separately credits its founder Angus Jackson with leading the project as part of the wider Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R3] -- the two attributions disagree on lead designer; both given. The 2017-2018 renewal's coastal-engineering consultant was reported by Swellnet as ICM [R2].
contractor: Not named for the 1999 build beyond "Gold Coast City Council" as project owner [R2][R9]. For the 2017-2018 renewal, the placement barge was the split-hull dredger Faucon, whose skipper gave on-record comments to Swellnet [R2].
status_now: Still in place and monitored by Gold Coast City Council as of the most recent sources found (2019 monitoring, 2026 commentary) [R12][R14]. As of January 2026, the Gold Coast mayor announced plans to "fast-track" a separate, new rockwall/groyne structure immediately south of Narrowneck -- not a rebuild of the existing reef -- contested by local surfer/environmental group Save Our Spit Alliance; a live, unresolved controversy, not a completed project [R12].
hover_text: A 70,000 m3 sand-filled geotextile reef built 1999-2000 for about AUD $2.3M to protect Narrowneck's isthmus; it worked well for coastal protection but a last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision left the promised surf underperforming, while the reef became an unplanned ecological hotspot whose fishing traffic then tore the bags with boat anchors, forcing a 2017-2018 renewal [R1][R2][R3][R9][R11].
design_as_planned: Designed by Kerry Black (University of Waikato) and Shaw Mead, using refraction-diffraction (WBEND) and Boussinesq wave modelling, checked against a 1:50-scale physical model at the UNSW Water Research Laboratory [R5][R11]. Stated targets: widen the beach 20-30 m in the reef's lee and produce surfable waves under defined conditions [R5]. A 2007 performance report (cited by Swellnet) noted the reef needed "long period, clean swell" to replicate the modelled wave shape, and that "larger swells, lower tides, and offshore winds have the potential to produce hollow, plunging breakers" [R2] -- the promised surf was explicitly conditional. The original design was a split "V" shape for both left- and right-hand rides with a paddling channel between the arms [R3][R9]. [Added 2026-10-10] Design criteria (Blacka et al. 2013, A.2.1-A.2.4 p.94-96): the aim was for over 80% (about 420,000 of 500,000 m3/yr) of the northward longshore drift to bypass; the empirical method predicted an 80 m salient, GENESIS needed a 30% wave-height reduction for a 50 m shoreline shift, and the WRL physical model gave wave transmission 0.5 over the crest and 0.9 at the shoreline, i.e. a 30-40 m salient at most; all design studies used the original -1.0 m AHD crest [R23]. Site: Hs about 1.0 m, tide range 2 m, beach slope 1:50 [R23]. Surf design basis: Burleigh Heads and Kirra surfing parameters (Mead 2000); headlands of several million m3 cannot be replicated (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.2-3) [R22].
as_built_vs_design: The most consequential change was a late, last-minute council decision to lower the reef's crest by 1 metre before construction -- "the change would have no effect on sand accretion but was terminal to Narrowneck becoming a good surfing reef," per Swellnet [R2]. Otherwise the built reef followed the approx. 400-container, approx. 70,000 m3 design, placed via split-hull barge with GPS [R1][R3][R9]. By approx. 2011 an underwater survey found several containers missing or damaged and seaward containers buried by sand [R4]. By 2017 the bags had "settled further into the sand" over 17 years, deeper than as-built [R2]. Designer Shaw Mead later attributed geotextile-bag failures across his firm's projects worldwide to specific causes per site, identifying boat anchors as the Gold Coast failure mechanism: "The containers failed due to a number of reasons including anchors (Gold Coast), debris strikes (Kovalam), during construction with over-filling (Mount Reef), propellor strike (Boscombe)" [R11]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on the crest lowering: Blacka et al. (2013, A.2.1 p.94) state the original design crest was -1.0 m AHD and that Gold Coast City Council and ICM adopted a lower -1.5 m AHD crest for safety, with possible top-up, i.e. a 0.5 m lowering; all design modelling used -1.0 m (A.2.2 p.95) [R23]. The card's Swellnet figure of 1 m [R2] is kept as the conflicting source. The crest was later not topped up after settling, to keep user risk manageable, which Blacka thinks contributed to the poor protection performance (Section 5.2 p.77-78; Fig 5.1 shows the reef 'sucking dry' in a wave trough) [R23]. Crest raised or trimmed in 2001, 2002, 2004 and 2006, about 50 more containers placed 2001-2007, peak placement 90-100 containers per month (p.94, 97) [R23]. Containers stable in 8-10 m maximum waves; nine storms with H>5 m by 2002; a composite geotextile was added to later bags after damage by anchors, spears, knives and boards (p.98) [R23]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3): the split-hull dredge could not position the filled containers exactly, so the structure is non-uniform, which reduced surfability [R22]. 3D work 2026-10-10: measured present crest -2.2 m AHD (Vieira da Silva 2021), 0.7 m deeper than the -1.5 m built crest; 17-27 % of the 78,500 m3 placed stands as an exposed mound, the rest buried, stacked, displaced or lost [R24]. Crest levels by source (all are statements, not agreed): design -0.67 m AHD (Black & Mead 2001, as quoted by Vieira da Silva et al. 2021 [R29]; the 2001 paper itself was not opened) and Waikato model -1.0 m AHD (Jackson et al. 2007); adopted for the 1999 contract -1.5 m AHD (-0.5 m LAT); target crest -1.5 m LAT = RL -2.5 m AHD ('compromise between safety and surfing') (Jackson et al. 2007, printed pp.4, 7) [R26]; measured after the 2018 top-up -2.2 m AHD (Vieira da Silva et al. 2021, accepted manuscript p.5) [R29]. AHD = LAT + 0.760 m at the Gold Coast Seaway (MSQ 2014), so -2.2 m AHD = 1.44 m below LAT [R25]. The card's '1.5 m below the low-tide waterline' matches the -1.5 m LAT target only (DERIVED: comparison of the Swellnet/ICM wording [R2][R3] with the target level in Jackson et al. 2007 p.7 [R26]).
outcome: Coastal protection: judged successful by the council and most independent sources; an 11-year monitoring study (Jackson et al., ICCE proceedings) found 2009 storm erosion "was accommodated within the wider beach created in 1999," with gradual post-storm recovery producing a mild groyne effect [R4]. A 2019 City statement described continued sand-volume increases, but specifically in offshore sandbars rather than the upper beach -- contradicting earlier (2010-era) reports of a 30-50 m salient, which Google Earth historical imagery does not corroborate [R14]. Wikipedia (citing Turner 2006) gives an independently monitored beach-widening figure of approx. 20 m, lower than the 30-50 m figure elsewhere [R1][R14]; both given per the reference rule. Surfing: consistently underperforming versus expectations -- "disappointing in its secondary objective to improve surfing" [R9]; surfers "seldom surf the reef," persisting after the 2017-2018 renewal [R14]. An earlier study (via ecoshape.org) reported the reef broke waves "roughly 50% of the time," faces 0.7-2.0 m, average ride 150-200 m / 30 s, "fun, but not hollow, in average conditions" [R5]. Ecology: widely reported as an unplanned success -- popular fishing/diving/snorkelling site with macro-algae, fish and reported turtle activity on the geotextile substrate [R1][R3][R8][R9]; the 2011 survey found "high abundance and biodiversity" despite sand-burial and container damage [R4]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on the salient: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4, Fig. 5 p.5) report ARGUS monitoring (Blacka et al. 2008) with beach widening of 30-50 m in the lee over about 2 km after 12 years, the chart annotated 'salient widths 50-100 m' [R22]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.98-100) argue the published 20-50 m salient is a likely misreading: WRL beach widths were measured against an arbitrary dune reference line that dips away from the coast near the reef (p.98) [R23]. Turner (2005) found about 20 m accretion within 1000 m of the reef in 2001-2003; Blacka et al. (2008) found over 8 years the shoreline receded 2.8 m/yr north and south and 4.3 m/yr in the lee, ending about 15 m further back than its neighbours by mid-2008 (planform perturbation only about 10 m by eye; Figs A.7, A.8); a 1.5 million m3 nourishment south of the reef earlier complicates the analysis [R23]. Surfing: rides up to 60 s from the reef onto adjacent sandbars (Corbett 2010a, via Mead & Borrero p.3), below expectations [R22]. Blacka rates both coastal protection and surfing 'Minor' (Table 4.1 p.63), and notes the design models over-predicted the salient (Black & Andrews 2001, p.25) [R23].
why_worked_or_failed: Coastal protection worked primarily because the reef's core hydraulic function -- dissipating wave energy offshore and trapping sediment in the nearshore sandbar system -- does not depend on precise crest depth or bag integrity to the same degree surf-wave shaping does; even a degraded, buried or partially damaged reef still perturbs the sand-transport regime [R4][R14]. Surfing underperformed for a documented, specific reason: the council's last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision, made for reasons unrelated to surf quality, put the structure too deep for consistent wave-breaking under normal swell/tide/wind combinations [R2]. Compounding this, geotextile bags are inherently fragile: Shaw Mead stated that losing even a single sand-filled container changes the seabed shape and degrades wave quality, and that Gold Coast's containers specifically failed due to boat anchors [R11]. Mead's broader verdict: he "no longer believes in the viability of geotextile bags for artificial reef construction," having led a critical industry review approximately a decade after Narrowneck "which led to the change to traditional rock construction methods of the most recent MPRs built" [R11]. [Added 2026-10-10] The modelled long-period clean swell needed to reproduce the predicted salient is unlike typical, shorter-period Gold Coast waves (Blacka et al. 2013, p.96, 100); the crest was not topped up after settling (p.77-78) [R23]. The reef cannot reproduce headland sheltering, and its non-uniform container placement reduced surfability (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.2-3) [R22].
unexpected_results: Ecological colonisation and the resulting fishing/anchor-damage cycle: the reef's unplanned success as a fish habitat drew recreational fishing traffic, whose boat anchors are identified as the specific mechanism that tore the geotextile containers [R11] -- an ecological win directly causing the structural failure that required the 2017-2018 renewal. "Moving the goalposts" on beach-widening claims: early (2010-era) monitoring described a clear 30-50 m salient; by 2019 the City's official position shifted to say a salient was "never expected" and sand build-up was always meant to be offshore -- flagged by multiple Swellnet commenters as inconsistent with what residents were originally told [R14]. A 2026 political sequel: 27 years after Narrowneck was built to avoid a conventional groyne, the Gold Coast mayor proposed fast-tracking a new rockwall/groyne immediately adjacent to it, prompting the same updrift/downdrift erosion-displacement objections coastal engineers raise about hard groynes generally [R12]. Depth-measurement uncertainty: the City's post-renewal survey data claims no settlement of the new containers, directly contradicting anecdotal local reports that the new bags were already breaking less often and appeared to be settling [R14].
could_be_better: Experts'/engineers' view: Shaw Mead, the reef's original designer, has publicly stated (in a critical review conducted roughly a decade after Narrowneck was built) that sand-filled geotextile containers should not be used for multi-purpose reef construction at all, and that the industry has since moved to rock construction [R11]. Swellnet's 2017 reporting singles out the crest-lowering decision as the single design change most responsible for the surf underperformance, implying a purely surf-focused crest depth would have produced a better wave without necessarily compromising protection [R2]. Surfers'/locals' view: commenters were blunter -- one ("warddy," 2019) called it an "absolute waste of money" and suggested rock construction instead; another ("the-spleen_2") noted "beach widening" had originally been "the core of the project" as pitched by Griffith University, and found it "funny to see how the idea has changed over time" toward the offshore-sandbar framing [R14].
relevance_to_israel: Narrowneck's central lesson for a Haifa or other Israeli Mediterranean project is the crest-depth-versus-tide-range trade-off: the reef's surf underperformance is traced by an independent source specifically to a council decision to change crest depth relative to the tide datum, made for reasons unrelated to surfing, which then dominated wave-breaking outcomes [R2]. The Gold Coast has a meaningful astronomical tide range (crest explicitly set "1.5 m below the low tide waterline") [R2][R3] -- a variable a designer must actively engineer around, since a fixed crest depth performs differently at high versus low tide. Lior's own draft outreach material argues the Mediterranean's smaller tidal range at Haifa is an advantage for reef stability and maintenance ("the tide conditions here allow high stability and natural long-term maintenance") [R18] -- this is Lior's own hypothesis, not an independently sourced engineering conclusion, and no numeric Haifa/Mediterranean tide-range figure was found in the sources fetched for this dossier. If correct (INFERENCE of this card's author from Lior's hypothesis [R18]; no Haifa tide-range figure is sourced here, so this is unsourced), a Haifa reef would face a smaller version of Narrowneck's tide-datum problem, making crest-depth choice a one-time design decision rather than a chronic multi-condition compromise. Separately, Narrowneck's identified failure mechanism -- boat anchors tearing geotextile bags that had become a popular fishing spot [R11] -- is directly transferable: any Israeli geotextile-based reef that succeeds ecologically should expect the same anchor-damage risk and may want to restrict anchoring or use more anchor-resistant materials such as rock, per Mead's own post-Narrowneck design shift [R11]. Gold Coast tide planes for comparison (Seaway, MSQ 2026, above LAT): MHWS 1.53, MLWS 0.22, HAT 2.03 m, so a spring range of 1.31 m [R25]. A Haifa figure is still not sourced in this card.

videos.title: NARROWNECK REEF
videos.what_it_shows: Interview-style documentary with the reef's design engineer explaining why Narrowneck Reef was built (Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy, 1999), how the geotextile sandbags were placed by split-hull dredge, why a submerged reef beat groynes/beach dewatering, and the marine growth/monitoring outcomes over approx. 10 years.
key_quotes: [00:00:19] "The [Narrowneck] Reef is a geotextile bag reef and its primary objective was Coastal protection."

[00:01:00] "...what we wanted was another control point just this side of Surfers Paradise we looked at groins we looked at beach dewatering... and the one that came out best was a submerged artificial Reef without the added bonuses of Surfing and Diving it was clearly the best solution."
[00:01:33] "We've constructed a structure that you can't see but it's constantly reducing the sand transport and the storm cut so we have a wider Beach a more stable Beach."

[00:02:52] "The difference between a geotextile structure and a concrete or rock structure is the type of growth we get... 10 m of water we're getting Kelps we're getting Turtles and I've dive with dolphins."
