hover.outcome: A 70,000 m3 sand-filled geotextile reef built 1999-2000 for about AUD $2.3M to protect Narrowneck's isthmus; it worked well for coastal protection but a last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision left the promised surf underperforming, while the reef became an unplanned ecological hotspot whose fishing traffic then tore the bags with boat anchors, forcing a 2017-2018 renewal [R1][R2][R3][R9][R11].

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameNarrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
PlaceNarrowneck, Gold Coast, Queensland
CountryAustralia
YearConstruction began August 1999, completed by December 2000 [R2][R8]; renewed/topped up with 84 more containers June 2018 [R2][R9][R14]. [Added 2026-10-10] Blacka et al. (2013, p.94) also give construction from August 1999, main phase complete December 2000, with crest raise/trim work in 2001, 2002, 2004 and 2006 and about 50 further containers 2001-2007 (p.97) [R23].
TypeSubmerged multi-purpose artificial reef (MPR) built from sand-filled geotextile containers ("mega sandbags"), placed on the seabed by split-hull barge with GPS positioning [R1][R2][R3][R9].
PurposePrimary: coastal/erosion protection for the Narrowneck isthmus, where only ~100 m of land separates the Nerang River from the ocean [R2][R14]. Secondary ("multi-purpose"): surfing amenity, folded in partly for public-relations value in a surf-centric region [R2]. A tertiary, unplanned outcome was ecological habitat creation [R1][R3][R8][R9].
SizeVolume approx. 70,000 m3 of sand (the largest multi-purpose reef ever built at the time), from approx. 400 geotextile containers each approx. 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter [R1][R9][R3]. Footprint reported as 350 m x 600 m, split "V" shape, 200 m offshore, bags 1-10 m below sea level [R9]; a second source directly states the reef "measures 450 meters long by 250 meters wide" [R8] -- the two footprint figures disagree and both are given per the reference rule. Crest lowered 1 m before construction, landing about 1.5 m below the low-tide waterline [R2][R3]; by 2017 low-tide depth over the reef measured 2.5-2.6 m, i.e. the crest had sunk/settled deeper than designed [R2]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on footprint: Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.65) give a V-shape of 170 m longshore x 280 m cross-shore (maximum dimensions), water depth 2-10 m, offshore 100-600 m, min. submergence 1.0 m [R23] - a third figure beside 350 x 600 m [R9] and 450 x 250 m [R8]; all three kept, unresolved. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2) also quote about 70,000 m3 (Jackson 2007) [R22]. For comparison the 3D model work (2026-10-10) counts 534 containers x 147 m3 = 78,500 m3 placed, of which only 17-27 % remains as an exposed mound [R24]. SOURCES DISAGREE on crest lowering: the card's '1 m' [R2][R3] vs Blacka (p.94) design -1.0 m AHD to built -1.5 m AHD, i.e. 0.5 m [R23]; the 3D work measures the present crest at -2.2 m AHD [R24] (see as_built_vs_design). Container counts and volume in the primary monitoring papers (2026-10-10 audit): 408 containers, 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter, placed August 1999 - December 2000 (Jackson et al. 2007, printed p.4); about 450 by 2006 (+10 in 2002-03, +15 in 2004, +17 in 2006; Jackson et al. 2012, p.3 and Fig 4 table p.4); +84 in the 2017-18 renewal [R26][R27][R25]; about 534 placed in total. The project's 147 m3 per container is DERIVED: 60,000 m3 (Jackson et al. 2007, Table 2, printed p.13, Narrowneck column [R26]) / 408 containers (same paper, p.4), this project, 07_scale/shapes/narrowneck-gold-coast/HANDOFF.md section 3c and 3d/METHODS_3D.md assumption A12 (the same 147 m3 is assumed for the later containers). So the 70,000 m3 quoted by the card's sources and the 60,000 m3 behind it are not reconciled here. Project-traced footprint (not a source statement): the visible container field on the Esri image of 8 Aug 2020 covers 6,239 m2 (arms 5,948 m2; bounding box 113.3 x 157.4 m; a lower bound, the deeper toe is not visible); the council asset polygon (OBJECTID 4637) is 171 x 262 m, 34,565 m2, which agrees with Blacka's 170 x 280 m [R23][R28]; the card's 350 x 600 m [R9] and 450 x 250 m [R8] are not supported by either.
CostOriginal 1999 build: AUD $2.3 million (approx. AUD $30/m3) per one source [R3], and separately "roughly $2.1 million AUD... over the first 10 years" per another [R5] -- both given since they disagree on scope (one-off build vs. 10-year total). Lior's own notes and a Hebrew-language source both give "$2.5 million," currency unspecified [R19][R20] -- not reconciled with the figures above. 2017-2018 renewal: approx. AUD $2 million per Mayor Tom Tate, as reported by the Gold Coast Bulletin via The Inertia [R10]. [Added 2026-10-10] Blacka et al. (2013, A.2.7 p.101, Table 4.4 p.69): total A$2.8 M including top-ups and maintenance (Jackson & Corbett 2007) = about A$3.9 M in 2013 AUD, A$56 per m3 (not comparable with the card's A$30/m3, a different basis and year); about two thirds construction, one third studies (Ranasinghe 2001); A$9,800 minimum per metre of beach protected [R23]. Economic context (p.100): a 25-year ARI erosion event about A$305 M (1996 AUD), 5-year ARI about A$47 M, Gold Coast surf industry about A$160 M per year [R23].
Cost (approx. USD)Very rough conversions by this report (not sourced): original build AUD $2.3M (1999 AUD~USD 0.65) approx. USD $1.5M; 2017-2018 renewal AUD $2M (2018 AUD~USD 0.75) approx. USD $1.5M. ASSUMPTION: the exchange rates (AUD/USD 0.65 for 1999, 0.75 for 2018) are unsourced estimates of this project; order of magnitude only.
Financed byGold Coast City Council, as part of its Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R1][R2][R9][R13]. No private or state/federal co-funding was found in any of the sources listed in References (a negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement).
DesignerOriginal 1999 design: Prof. Kerry Black and Shaw Mead (University of Waikato, NZ; later founders of coastal-engineering firm ASR) [R11]. ICM (International Coastal Management, Gold Coast) separately credits its founder Angus Jackson with leading the project as part of the wider Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R3] -- the two attributions disagree on lead designer; both given. The 2017-2018 renewal's coastal-engineering consultant was reported by Swellnet as ICM [R2].
ContractorNot named for the 1999 build beyond "Gold Coast City Council" as project owner [R2][R9]. For the 2017-2018 renewal, the placement barge was the split-hull dredger Faucon, whose skipper gave on-record comments to Swellnet [R2].
Status nowStill in place and monitored by Gold Coast City Council as of the most recent sources found (2019 monitoring, 2026 commentary) [R12][R14]. As of January 2026, the Gold Coast mayor announced plans to "fast-track" a separate, new rockwall/groyne structure immediately south of Narrowneck -- not a rebuild of the existing reef -- contested by local surfer/environmental group Save Our Spit Alliance; a live, unresolved controversy, not a completed project [R12].
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Erosion problem predates the reef by decades: a 1971 Delft University of Technology report, commissioned by the Queensland Government, recommended a groyne at Narrowneck [R9][R13]. Training walls built at the Spit in 1985 helped erosion further north but not at Narrowneck itself, and Cyclone Nancy (1990) eroded the beach back to the boulder wall protecting the Nerang River [R2]. Gold Coast City Council chose an artificial reef instead of the recommended groyne, branding it a "Multi-Purpose Reef" so that surfing amenity could be folded into the PR case in a surf-centric city [R2][R9][R13]. No evidence found of state/federal political involvement or a single named political champion for the original 1999 project; Mayor Tom Tate became the public face of the 2017-2018 renewal [R10]. [Added 2026-10-10] Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): the decision to build was driven by a cost-benefit analysis (Raybould and Mules 1998), as part of the Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy (Queensland Environment Award 2000); the first MPR designed primarily for coastal protection with surfing secondary (p.2) [R22].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: Designed by Kerry Black (University of Waikato) and Shaw Mead, using refraction-diffraction (WBEND) and Boussinesq wave modelling, checked against a 1:50-scale physical model at the UNSW Water Research Laboratory [R5][R11]. Stated targets: widen the beach 20-30 m in the reef's lee and produce surfable waves under defined conditions [R5]. A 2007 performance report (cited by Swellnet) noted the reef needed "long period, clean swell" to replicate the modelled wave shape, and that "larger swells, lower tides, and offshore winds have the potential to produce hollow, plunging breakers" [R2] -- the promised surf was explicitly conditional. The original design was a split "V" shape for both left- and right-hand rides with a paddling channel between the arms [R3][R9]. [Added 2026-10-10] Design criteria (Blacka et al. 2013, A.2.1-A.2.4 p.94-96): the aim was for over 80% (about 420,000 of 500,000 m3/yr) of the northward longshore drift to bypass; the empirical method predicted an 80 m salient, GENESIS needed a 30% wave-height reduction for a 50 m shoreline shift, and the WRL physical model gave wave transmission 0.5 over the crest and 0.9 at the shoreline, i.e. a 30-40 m salient at most; all design studies used the original -1.0 m AHD crest [R23]. Site: Hs about 1.0 m, tide range 2 m, beach slope 1:50 [R23]. Surf design basis: Burleigh Heads and Kirra surfing parameters (Mead 2000); headlands of several million m3 cannot be replicated (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.2-3) [R22].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The most consequential change was a late, last-minute council decision to lower the reef's crest by 1 metre before construction -- "the change would have no effect on sand accretion but was terminal to Narrowneck becoming a good surfing reef," per Swellnet [R2]. Otherwise the built reef followed the approx. 400-container, approx. 70,000 m3 design, placed via split-hull barge with GPS [R1][R3][R9]. By approx. 2011 an underwater survey found several containers missing or damaged and seaward containers buried by sand [R4]. By 2017 the bags had "settled further into the sand" over 17 years, deeper than as-built [R2]. Designer Shaw Mead later attributed geotextile-bag failures across his firm's projects worldwide to specific causes per site, identifying boat anchors as the Gold Coast failure mechanism: "The containers failed due to a number of reasons including anchors (Gold Coast), debris strikes (Kovalam), during construction with over-filling (Mount Reef), propellor strike (Boscombe)" [R11]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on the crest lowering: Blacka et al. (2013, A.2.1 p.94) state the original design crest was -1.0 m AHD and that Gold Coast City Council and ICM adopted a lower -1.5 m AHD crest for safety, with possible top-up, i.e. a 0.5 m lowering; all design modelling used -1.0 m (A.2.2 p.95) [R23]. The card's Swellnet figure of 1 m [R2] is kept as the conflicting source. The crest was later not topped up after settling, to keep user risk manageable, which Blacka thinks contributed to the poor protection performance (Section 5.2 p.77-78; Fig 5.1 shows the reef 'sucking dry' in a wave trough) [R23]. Crest raised or trimmed in 2001, 2002, 2004 and 2006, about 50 more containers placed 2001-2007, peak placement 90-100 containers per month (p.94, 97) [R23]. Containers stable in 8-10 m maximum waves; nine storms with H>5 m by 2002; a composite geotextile was added to later bags after damage by anchors, spears, knives and boards (p.98) [R23]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3): the split-hull dredge could not position the filled containers exactly, so the structure is non-uniform, which reduced surfability [R22]. 3D work 2026-10-10: measured present crest -2.2 m AHD (Vieira da Silva 2021), 0.7 m deeper than the -1.5 m built crest; 17-27 % of the 78,500 m3 placed stands as an exposed mound, the rest buried, stacked, displaced or lost [R24]. Crest levels by source (all are statements, not agreed): design -0.67 m AHD (Black & Mead 2001, as quoted by Vieira da Silva et al. 2021 [R29]; the 2001 paper itself was not opened) and Waikato model -1.0 m AHD (Jackson et al. 2007); adopted for the 1999 contract -1.5 m AHD (-0.5 m LAT); target crest -1.5 m LAT = RL -2.5 m AHD ('compromise between safety and surfing') (Jackson et al. 2007, printed pp.4, 7) [R26]; measured after the 2018 top-up -2.2 m AHD (Vieira da Silva et al. 2021, accepted manuscript p.5) [R29]. AHD = LAT + 0.760 m at the Gold Coast Seaway (MSQ 2014), so -2.2 m AHD = 1.44 m below LAT [R25]. The card's '1.5 m below the low-tide waterline' matches the -1.5 m LAT target only (DERIVED: comparison of the Swellnet/ICM wording [R2][R3] with the target level in Jackson et al. 2007 p.7 [R26]).

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Coastal protection: judged successful by the council and most independent sources; an 11-year monitoring study (Jackson et al., ICCE proceedings) found 2009 storm erosion "was accommodated within the wider beach created in 1999," with gradual post-storm recovery producing a mild groyne effect [R4]. A 2019 City statement described continued sand-volume increases, but specifically in offshore sandbars rather than the upper beach -- contradicting earlier (2010-era) reports of a 30-50 m salient, which Google Earth historical imagery does not corroborate [R14]. Wikipedia (citing Turner 2006) gives an independently monitored beach-widening figure of approx. 20 m, lower than the 30-50 m figure elsewhere [R1][R14]; both given per the reference rule. Surfing: consistently underperforming versus expectations -- "disappointing in its secondary objective to improve surfing" [R9]; surfers "seldom surf the reef," persisting after the 2017-2018 renewal [R14]. An earlier study (via ecoshape.org) reported the reef broke waves "roughly 50% of the time," faces 0.7-2.0 m, average ride 150-200 m / 30 s, "fun, but not hollow, in average conditions" [R5]. Ecology: widely reported as an unplanned success -- popular fishing/diving/snorkelling site with macro-algae, fish and reported turtle activity on the geotextile substrate [R1][R3][R8][R9]; the 2011 survey found "high abundance and biodiversity" despite sand-burial and container damage [R4]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on the salient: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4, Fig. 5 p.5) report ARGUS monitoring (Blacka et al. 2008) with beach widening of 30-50 m in the lee over about 2 km after 12 years, the chart annotated 'salient widths 50-100 m' [R22]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.98-100) argue the published 20-50 m salient is a likely misreading: WRL beach widths were measured against an arbitrary dune reference line that dips away from the coast near the reef (p.98) [R23]. Turner (2005) found about 20 m accretion within 1000 m of the reef in 2001-2003; Blacka et al. (2008) found over 8 years the shoreline receded 2.8 m/yr north and south and 4.3 m/yr in the lee, ending about 15 m further back than its neighbours by mid-2008 (planform perturbation only about 10 m by eye; Figs A.7, A.8); a 1.5 million m3 nourishment south of the reef earlier complicates the analysis [R23]. Surfing: rides up to 60 s from the reef onto adjacent sandbars (Corbett 2010a, via Mead & Borrero p.3), below expectations [R22]. Blacka rates both coastal protection and surfing 'Minor' (Table 4.1 p.63), and notes the design models over-predicted the salient (Black & Andrews 2001, p.25) [R23].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Coastal protection worked primarily because the reef's core hydraulic function -- dissipating wave energy offshore and trapping sediment in the nearshore sandbar system -- does not depend on precise crest depth or bag integrity to the same degree surf-wave shaping does; even a degraded, buried or partially damaged reef still perturbs the sand-transport regime [R4][R14]. Surfing underperformed for a documented, specific reason: the council's last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision, made for reasons unrelated to surf quality, put the structure too deep for consistent wave-breaking under normal swell/tide/wind combinations [R2]. Compounding this, geotextile bags are inherently fragile: Shaw Mead stated that losing even a single sand-filled container changes the seabed shape and degrades wave quality, and that Gold Coast's containers specifically failed due to boat anchors [R11]. Mead's broader verdict: he "no longer believes in the viability of geotextile bags for artificial reef construction," having led a critical industry review approximately a decade after Narrowneck "which led to the change to traditional rock construction methods of the most recent MPRs built" [R11]. [Added 2026-10-10] The modelled long-period clean swell needed to reproduce the predicted salient is unlike typical, shorter-period Gold Coast waves (Blacka et al. 2013, p.96, 100); the crest was not topped up after settling (p.77-78) [R23]. The reef cannot reproduce headland sheltering, and its non-uniform container placement reduced surfability (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.2-3) [R22].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Ecological colonisation and the resulting fishing/anchor-damage cycle: the reef's unplanned success as a fish habitat drew recreational fishing traffic, whose boat anchors are identified as the specific mechanism that tore the geotextile containers [R11] -- an ecological win directly causing the structural failure that required the 2017-2018 renewal. "Moving the goalposts" on beach-widening claims: early (2010-era) monitoring described a clear 30-50 m salient; by 2019 the City's official position shifted to say a salient was "never expected" and sand build-up was always meant to be offshore -- flagged by multiple Swellnet commenters as inconsistent with what residents were originally told [R14]. A 2026 political sequel: 27 years after Narrowneck was built to avoid a conventional groyne, the Gold Coast mayor proposed fast-tracking a new rockwall/groyne immediately adjacent to it, prompting the same updrift/downdrift erosion-displacement objections coastal engineers raise about hard groynes generally [R12]. Depth-measurement uncertainty: the City's post-renewal survey data claims no settlement of the new containers, directly contradicting anecdotal local reports that the new bags were already breaking less often and appeared to be settling [R14].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Experts'/engineers' view: Shaw Mead, the reef's original designer, has publicly stated (in a critical review conducted roughly a decade after Narrowneck was built) that sand-filled geotextile containers should not be used for multi-purpose reef construction at all, and that the industry has since moved to rock construction [R11]. Swellnet's 2017 reporting singles out the crest-lowering decision as the single design change most responsible for the surf underperformance, implying a purely surf-focused crest depth would have produced a better wave without necessarily compromising protection [R2]. Surfers'/locals' view: commenters were blunter -- one ("warddy," 2019) called it an "absolute waste of money" and suggested rock construction instead; another ("the-spleen_2") noted "beach widening" had originally been "the core of the project" as pitched by Griffith University, and found it "funny to see how the idea has changed over time" toward the offshore-sandbar framing [R14].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Narrowneck's central lesson for a Haifa or other Israeli Mediterranean project is the crest-depth-versus-tide-range trade-off: the reef's surf underperformance is traced by an independent source specifically to a council decision to change crest depth relative to the tide datum, made for reasons unrelated to surfing, which then dominated wave-breaking outcomes [R2]. The Gold Coast has a meaningful astronomical tide range (crest explicitly set "1.5 m below the low tide waterline") [R2][R3] -- a variable a designer must actively engineer around, since a fixed crest depth performs differently at high versus low tide. Lior's own draft outreach material argues the Mediterranean's smaller tidal range at Haifa is an advantage for reef stability and maintenance ("the tide conditions here allow high stability and natural long-term maintenance") [R18] -- this is Lior's own hypothesis, not an independently sourced engineering conclusion, and no numeric Haifa/Mediterranean tide-range figure was found in the sources fetched for this dossier. If correct (INFERENCE of this card's author from Lior's hypothesis [R18]; no Haifa tide-range figure is sourced here, so this is unsourced), a Haifa reef would face a smaller version of Narrowneck's tide-datum problem, making crest-depth choice a one-time design decision rather than a chronic multi-condition compromise. Separately, Narrowneck's identified failure mechanism -- boat anchors tearing geotextile bags that had become a popular fishing spot [R11] -- is directly transferable: any Israeli geotextile-based reef that succeeds ecologically should expect the same anchor-damage risk and may want to restrict anchoring or use more anchor-resistant materials such as rock, per Mead's own post-Narrowneck design shift [R11]. Gold Coast tide planes for comparison (Seaway, MSQ 2026, above LAT): MHWS 1.53, MLWS 0.22, HAT 2.03 m, so a spring range of 1.31 m [R25]. A Haifa figure is still not sourced in this card.

footprint.name: Narrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
footprint.shape_type_notes: Dual-arm split-V / chevron: two separate wishbone-shaped reef units ('north arm' and 'south arm' in this report's own labelling) set side by side alongshore, joined by a narrow central channel across which a small submerged weir (two containers) was added in 2004. Confirmed by text and four plan-view figures in the primary monitoring paper (Jackson et al. 2012, [R4]). This is NOT an inshore/offshore concentric-lobe arrangement (see gemini_comparison).
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward north -- the Narrowneck isthmus trends roughly N-S per general regional geography, no source gives an exact shoreline azimuth); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0.

footprint.orientation_notes: Two arms (north/south) run alongshore either side of a central channel/weir, matching the card's pre-existing 'split V shape... paddling channel between the arms' language [R3][R9]. Alongshore axis 'north' is this report's own convention, not a sourced compass bearing.

disagree.gemini: Inshore Lobe + Offshore Lobe stacked cross-shore (same alongshore position, different offshore distances)
disagree.ours: North arm + South arm split alongshore (same offshore-distance range, different alongshore positions), joined by a central channel/weir
disagree.why_ours: The primary monitoring paper (Jackson et al. 2012, [R4]) explicitly states a weir was built 'between the two arms of the reef' and shows this in 4 separate plan-view figures (Figs. 2,4,5,7), consistently depicting two side-by-side wishbone lobes joined by a narrow waist -- not a near-shore ring and a further-offshore ring. This directly matches the card's own pre-existing 'split V shape... paddling channel between the arms' language [R3][R9]. Gemini's own audit already senses something is off (it flags the '180m offshore' label as ambiguous) but never revisits the underlying inshore/offshore-lobe topology itself, which this report identifies as the actual root issue.

disagree.why_ours: Gemini's clean 400x220 matches neither of our two sourced figures and no citation ties it to a specific page in Gemini's own 3 listed sources; this report could not find '400' or '220' stated anywhere in the primary paper obtained, nor on the ICM webpage (re-checked, no plan dimensions present).

disagree.ours: 1.0-1.5 (2012 design value, R4) or 2.5-2.6 (2017 settled value, R2) depending on date

The primary paper states 1.0-1.5m as of 2012 [R4 p.13]; [R2] separately gives 2.5-2.6m for the settled, pre-2018-renewal (2017) state. 2.2 sits between these but is not derivable from either without an unstated averaging assumption; Gemini's own audit note cites three different numbers (-1.0m design, -2.5m settled, -1.5m post-2018-refurbishment), none of which is 2.2m either.

disagree.gemini: 180 (inshore lobe) / ~300 (offshore ridge) / 380 (outer toe) -- tiered framing
disagree.ours: 200 (single figure, treated as the shoreward edge of the whole two-arm structure)
disagree.why_ours: Gemini's tiered offshore-distance framing is a direct consequence of the rejected inshore/offshore-lobe topology. With the alongshore-split topology used here, there is no separate 'outer ridge' 300-380m out; the reef's full cross-shore extent (200-550m in this report's schematic) comes from each arm's own outer horn, not a second, more-offshore reef ring.

footprint.confidence: Photo outline (default): the visible container field is well measured (edges ~1 m, frame/scale confirmed, second tile set 0.2 m), but it is a lower bound (deeper toe to ~10 m invisible, detector-limited seaward edge, 24 faint patches excluded). Design outlines (Option 2 built 2018 but south reef/bridge only partly; 2004 design; 2011 relief zone) are placed to +-15 m and are envelopes. No post-renewal survey or as-built plan exists. Scale conflict resolved.
open_issues: No plan-view figure with a legible printed scale bar was found for this reef in any source consulted (primary paper, ICM webpage, or the card's image list); the polygon vertices in this file are a documented schematic, not a survey-grade digitization.
The card's own pre-existing footprint disagreement (350x600m [R9] vs. 450x250m [R8]) remains unreconciled; no third, tie-breaking source was found.

This report assumes north/south mirror symmetry between the two arms for the schematic polygon; Jackson et al. 2012 Fig. 4 suggests the two arms may not be perfectly identical, but source resolution does not support characterizing the actual asymmetry.

The exact shoreline azimuth at Narrowneck (to convert 'alongshore = positive north' into a true compass bearing) was not found in any source consulted; the isthmus's roughly N-S trend is inferred from general regional geography, not a stated figure.

Crest depth is genuinely time-varying (~1.0-1.5m as designed/2012 -> ~2.5-2.6m by 2017 settled -> an unstated, presumably shallower figure after the 2018 renewal); any single crest-depth number used elsewhere for this reef should specify which date/state it refers to.
The central channel's width (~100m, used to space the two arms in the schematic polygon) is this report's own unsourced assumption, not a published figure.

- channel containers (3, two faint) have an unresolved identity (the 2004 weir containers are N-S oriented and not visible in 2020)
- published envelope sizes (350 x 600, 450 x 250, 256 x 151 m) describe the design footprint or an asset envelope, not the container field
+ Corbett 2023 confirms Option 2 was built; the Option 2 -6 m envelope contains 97 % of the traced arms
+ Corbett Fig 2 and Jackson Fig 2 are the same CAD design on one scale (no scale conflict)

name: Pratte's Reef (permit name: Chevron Reef)
place: Dockweiler State Beach / El Segundo, California
year: 2000-2001 built (Phase I fall 2000, 110 bags; Phase II spring 2001, +90 bags); removed 2008-2010 Phase 2 dated 2000 in Blacka et al. (2013, p.117) [R19] vs spring 2001 above: sources disagree. RESOLVED 2026-10-10: the monitoring paper by the reef's monitors gives the second installation as 23-24 April 2001 (90 new bags, +80 % volume, crest widened and made shallower, placed over the Phase I bags) [R28, p.3]; Blacka's 'Phase 2 in 2000' is not supported by that primary text.
type: Submerged artificial surf reef (ASR), sand-filled geotextile bags in a V/chevron layout [R4][R28]
purpose: Surfing — court/permit-mandated legal mitigation for a surf break lost to a 1984 Chevron rock groin [R1][R7]
size: ~200 geotextile bags total, ~1,400-1,600 m3 built volume (vs. ~3,800 m3 / 5,000 yd3 in the original 1997 proposal); crest ~0.9-2.4 m below low-tide sea level (sources disagree) Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3) give 1,350 m3, the smallest MPR ever built, placed very close to shore [R18] (card 1,400-1,600 m3: sources disagree slightly, both kept). Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2; A.11): 64 m x 29 m V, depth 3.0 m (MLLW), 50 m from the undisturbed shoreline; Phase 1 design 110 bags of 3.0 x 2.1 x 1.2 m (~12.7 t, 80-90% fill), crest 1.8 m below MLLW; after Phase 2 (+90 bags, +80% volume) apex 0.9 m below MLLW; crest then dropped 1.5 m in a year; seabed scoured to ~4 m depth [R19]. Primary-source values (Borrero & Nelsen 2003): initial installation 110 bags on 22 September 2000, each about 14 tons when filled, 4 x 7 x 10 ft, max 280 ft3 (7.9 m3), filled 80-90 %; depth at the outermost point after the initial installation about -6 ft MLLW (1.83 m below MLLW); after Phase II within 3 ft of MLLW (0.91 m); obtuse 'V' with apex offshore (p.2-3); 'Pratte's only extends 30' (unit not printed, metres by context; p.14); 'approximately 1600 cubic meters of sand contained in 200' bags (p.16) [R28]. 200 bags x 7.9 m3 x 80-90 % fill = 1,264-1,422 m3 (project arithmetic, not a source value). Project-traced Phase I design layout (not the as-built 200-bag reef): 110 bags, area 435.2 m2, bounding box 58.0 x 28.6 m (alongshore x cross-shore), arms 44.7 / 44.4 deg to the V axis, traced by hand on the Skelly design drawing (RWR copy) and cross-checked on Fig. 4 of [R28] [R4][R28][R29]. Blacka's 64 x 29 m [R19] is therefore 10 % longer than this traced outline (58.0 m); its basis is not stated.
cost: $300,000 Chevron construction payment + $200,000-250,000 California Coastal Conservancy grant + $50,000 Surfrider add-on + ~$300,000 anonymous donation for removal; Surfline's cumulative headline figure is $850,000 over 2000-2008 [R1][R4][R7]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3): US$300,000 to build (Phase 1 budget only) and removal in 2010 cost more than twice that [R18]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.117-119): build US$550,000 ($300,000 + $250,000); removal US$551,000 (stage 1 budget $285,000; stage 2 $266,000 two years later); 142.5 containers removed, 1 left visible, 42.5 torn or buried [R19]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the build total (US$300,000 Phase 1 only [R18] vs US$550,000 total [R19]) and the removal total (more than US$600,000 [R18] vs US$551,000 [R19]); all kept.
financed_by: Chevron Corporation (construction, as legal mitigation), California Coastal Conservancy (construction top-up), Surfrider Foundation (added funds + anonymous-donor-funded removal) [R1][R4][R7]
motivation: Court/permit-mandated mitigation for loss of the surfable Grand Avenue break, caused by Chevron's 1984 rock groin built to stop beach erosion threatening its El Segundo refinery's offshore oil-pipeline terminal [R1][R7]
contractor: Placed by barge-mounted crane (builder not separately named in sources); removal directed by Coastal Frontiers Corporation, with American Marine Corporation (dive crew) and Morrissey Construction Company (onshore handling/disposal) [R3][R6][R10]
status_now: Removed. Phase I removal fall 2008 (Sept 30-Oct 17, 2008); Phase II removal fall 2010, coinciding with expiry of the original 10-year experimental permit [R1][R3][R6][R9][R10]. First-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R9][R10]
hover_text: ~200 sand-filled geotextile bags (~1,400-1,600 m3) built 2000-2001 for roughly $550,000-$850,000, funded by Chevron as legal mitigation for a lost surf break; never produced a consistently surfable wave in 8 years and was removed in 2008-2010, the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R1][R7][R6].
design_as_planned: The original 1997 CEQA filing by Surfrider Foundation (via the LA Dept. of Parks & Recreation) described '10-20 large geo-textile fabric bags containing approx. 5,000 cubic yards of sand' [R8]. As engineered by Skelly Engineering, the built design called for a V-shaped (delta/chevron) reef with arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves like a natural point break, cresting close to the low-tide waterline for consistent breaking [R4]. The goal was purely restoring a lost surfing amenity at the Grand Avenue break, not beach nourishment or ecological habitat creation [R4][R1].
as_built_vs_design: Construction proceeded in two funded phases instead of one: 110 bags in fall 2000 (using the initial $300,000 Chevron payment), then ~90 more bags in spring 2001 once the Coastal Conservancy added $200,000-250,000, for roughly 200 bags total [R1][R7]. Even after that expansion, the built reef was far smaller than the 1997 proposal's ~5,000 yd3 (~3,800 m3) target: built volume is reported at only ~1,400-1,600 m3 [R2][R4] — under half the size first proposed, and by Surfrider's own later accounting roughly one-seventh the volume of Mount Maunganui and one-tenth to one-thirtieth the volume of Narrowneck [R7]. Individual bags were also markedly smaller (~8 m3 each) than Narrowneck's containers (140-320 m3 each) [R2]. Chad Nelsen (Surfrider): 'we probably should have said $300,000 is not enough' [R7]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the Phase 2 date: Blacka et al. (2013, p.117) date the 90-bag extension in 2000 [R19]; the card has spring 2001 [R1][R7]. RESOLVED 2026-10-10 for 2001: Borrero & Nelsen (2003) p.3 give the second installation on 23-24 April 2001, 90 bags [R28]. Blacka Table A.11 also: after Phase 2 apex 0.9 m below MLLW and the crest then dropped 1.5 m in a year [R19].
outcome: Wikipedia states the reef 'had very little effect on the surfing conditions at Dockweiler Beach and ... no measurable effect on the shoreline morphology' [R1][R2]. Surfline's 2008 feature: over 'eight plus years, Pratte's Reef was as useless as useless gets' and 'it never produced a consistently surfable wave' [R7]. Diver surveys found bags had moved, sunk, and been buried by sand, with the black polypropylene material visibly deteriorating — 'largely disintegrated' within about two years [R4][R2]. No coastal-protection or ecological benefit is reported in any of the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement). The reef was removed over two phases (fall 2008, fall 2010), the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R7][R9][R10].
why_worked_or_failed: Undersized for its budget and site: a $300,000-$550,000 construction budget bought a reef roughly 1/7 the size of Mount Maunganui's and 1/10-1/30 the size of Narrowneck's [R7]. Crest-depth mismatch: on big swells the crest was too deep to trigger breaking, so waves broke outside the reef [R1][R7]. Pre-existing degraded beach: the Chevron groin had already straightened/steepened the beach and buried the original Grand Avenue break in trapped sand, conditions a small mitigation reef could not reverse [R7]. Material/structural failure: sand-filled fabric bags resting on a sandy, mobile seabed with no rigid foundation settled, sank, and were buried, and the polypropylene fabric deteriorated within roughly two years [R4][R2]. Insufficient pre-construction monitoring: Nelsen said more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions beforehand 'would have told us the reef was too small before we even put it in' [R7]. Surfer and local comments on a YouTube video (2026, evidence grade D, anecdotal) agree that it rarely or never produced a rideable wave: too small, a steep approach that gave swells no time to build, swell shadow from Catalina Island and the land mass, and a V instead of a triangle [R33].
unexpected_results: No fishing-pressure or ecological side effects are reported for Pratte's Reef in any source found, unlike Narrowneck (Gold Coast), whose geotextile containers were colonized by macro-algae, benthos and pelagic fish and became popular for local (spear-)fishing, diving and snorkeling, though also flagged as vulnerable to vessel/anchor damage as a design risk [R17]. The project's most consequential outcome may have been legal/political: the 1984 mitigation condition Tom Pratte secured is credited by Surfrider as the first case in which the California Coastal Commission formally recognized a surf break as a protectable coastal recreational resource, a precedent Surfrider says later helped protect Trestles from development [R7]. Surfrider itself updated its institutional policy on artificial reefs after this project, moving toward protecting existing surf breaks rather than promising to recreate lost ones: 'I don't think we should ever trade a surf spot for the promise of building something else' (Chad Nelsen) [R7]. No litigation was found in any source listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement).
could_be_better: Surfrider's Chad Nelsen (2008 Surfline retrospective): should have told Chevron up front that $300,000 was not enough to build a working reef; more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions before construction would have revealed the reef was undersized before it was built; more broadly, mitigation itself is often 'a false promise', and protecting existing surf breaks is preferable to engineering replacements after the fact [R7]. Named Surfline commenters (2008): depth/tide design was wrong ('Andrew': should have been 'nearly dry on a negative tide to be legit', not 8 feet deep at zero tide); distance from shore was wrong, though commenters disagreed on direction ('Randy Wright': 'simply too far away from the shore'; Dr. Jose Borrero, quoted elsewhere: 'too small and too close to shore'); cruder/cheaper materials might have worked as well ('prattes is a joke': rocks or 'smashed up cars'); lack of surfer input in the engineering process ('evan') [R7][R4].
relevance_to_israel: Tidal range is the single most transferable engineering lesson: Pratte's Reef's crest depth was wrong for the local tide swing (too deep to break big swells; ~8 ft/2.4 m deep even at zero/low tide per a Surfrider-sourced figure) [R7]. Santa Monica Bay has a mean tidal range of ~1.4-1.7 m [R12], versus Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m [R13], consistent with the Mediterranean's generally small tides [R11] — a crest depth calibrated for Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m swing is a much smaller, more predictable engineering target than one spanning ~1.5 m, supporting Lior's thesis that Israel's small tidal range is a structural advantage for reef stability [R15]. Budget-driven undersizing (Nelsen: '$300,000 is not enough' [R7]) is, in this card author's INFERENCE (not a sourced statement), a transferable governance/funding risk, not a site-specific one, relevant to any small pilot reef Israel might build on a limited budget. Material degradation (UV/wave abrasion of polypropylene bags within ~2 years; the 'largely disintegrated within about two years' finding is the diver-survey report in the outcome field [R4][R2]) is a warning for any low-cost geotextile design proposed for the Israeli coast, including Lior's own 'cheap & light materials... for fast deployment and removal' sketch [R15]. Israel has no directly comparable built ASR yet — its only confirmed built geotextile project is the Ashkelon Geotube, a shore-protection structure, not a surf reef [R14]. Tide levels (NOAA CO-OPS Santa Monica 9410840, epoch 1983-2001, relative to MSL): MHHW +0.804, MLLW -0.849, HAT +1.382, LAT -1.469 m, i.e. MHHW - MLLW = 1.653 m [R30]; this is the sourced replacement for the live tide-forecast figure [R12]. Haifa's 0.3-0.4 m [R13] is a web tide-table figure, not a primary source.

videos.title: Pratte's Reef
videos.relevance_evidence: Title is the reef's name and the description names Chevron USA, Surfrider and Tom Pratte. About 13 of the 30 minutes (roughly 14:00-27:00) are the reef itself: its purpose, designer Dave Skelly explaining the planned geotextile-bag chevron layout, and a Tom Pratte tribute. It is a PRE-construction documentary (closing line says the wave 'remains to be seen'); the spoken track contains nothing about the built reef. Earlier frame checks (2026-09-24) found no footage of the actual reef; whether the picture shows plans/animation is not verifiable from the transcript.

segments.what: [this reef] Narrator intro: Surfrider South Bay chapter + Chevron USA, aim of the El Segundo reef (to restore lost surf). Spoken only, no site footage described.
segments.quote: the designers of the El Segundo reef hoped to restore some portion of what has been lost

segments.what: [context, not the reef] 1983 El Nino erosion; Chevron proposes the 900 ft rock groin (jetty) plus about 620,000 cubic ft of sand. This is the structure whose surf damage led to the reef.
segments.quote: chevron proposed installing a 900 foot rock jetty with a renourishment project

segments.what: [context, not the reef] Groin construction recalled by a surf photographer and local surfers; the groin wave breaks only 3-5 times a year, surfable by experts only.
segments.quote: the new wave broke three to five times a year and only the most experienced surfers could ride it

segments.what: [context] Surfrider South Bay chapter, Tom Pratte's surf-impact survey, the Coastal Commission mitigation condition, Chevron versus Surfrider positions on what counts as mitigation.
segments.quote: the only true mitigation is restoration of the surf

segments.what: [this reef] Tom Pratte introduced as the key negotiator and original Surfrider founder; Chevron forced to fund mitigation.
segments.quote: Tom was the original founder of the Surfrider Foundation

segments.what: [this reef] Reef chosen as the mitigation: an underwater breakwater that could create waves and protect the beach.
segments.quote: we can create waves and protect the beach

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly Engineering selected to design, engineer and permit the first artificial surfing reef; designer Dave Skelly (from about 15:06) calls it a submerged breakwater, a simple design to prove the concept.
segments.quote: it's actually a submerged breakwater this project is kind of the dream of every surfer

segments.what: [context, NOT this reef] Archival film of Hoppy Schwartz's 1971 sandbag reef near the Redondo breakwater, which settled into the sand and vanished.
segments.quote: although no waves ever broke on Hoppy's reef the original concept was ahead of its time

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly: engineering is simple, the hard part is permitting (city, state, federal agencies).
segments.quote: the biggest hurdle for this project is actually getting permission to do it

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly explains the design: giant geotextile sand bags, 12-14 tons each, borrowed from river bank-erosion use, life of at least two decades.
segments.quote: my concept is to put out gigantic sand bags a nice bag weighs about 12 to 14 tons

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly on site conditions (10 ft tide range, mobile bottom, waves from different directions), the chevron/V-shaped bag layout for a right and a left, reef set in deeper water, 6-8 ft waves on the reef, sandbar and smaller waves in its lee.
segments.quote: the formation that we're placing these bags in is a chevron shape formation or v-shaped

segments.what: [this reef] Skelly on consulting El Segundo locals; the reef's effect expected to reach only about 100-200 ft either side.
segments.quote: limited to maybe 100 to 200 feet on either side of it in the max

segments.what: [this reef] Interviewees on aims and the future of surf reefs: prove the concept, not a world-class wave; first of its kind.
segments.quote: basically prove the concept that we can go out there and create a surfable wave

segments.what: [this reef] Tribute to Tom Pratte (died of cancer shortly before the agreement); the reef is named for him.
segments.quote: it's Tom's reef period

segments.what: [this reef] Closing: credit to Chevron, the Coastal Commission treats surf breaks as a protected resource; narrator says it remains to be seen whether the reef will make a perfect wave (reef not yet built).

videos.date: 2016-04-18 (upload date; content/interviews are contemporaneous with the 1998-2000 project run-up, before construction)
videos.what_it_shows: A ~30-minute documentary about the origin of Pratte's Reef: the 1983-84 El Nino storm damage and Chevron groin construction, Tom Pratte's Coastal Commission mitigation condition, the earlier failed 'Hoppy's Reef' attempt near Redondo Beach, and on-camera interviews with reef designer Dave Skelly (Skelly Engineering) explaining the planned V/chevron-shaped geotextile-bag design, plus commentary from Surfrider/local surfers and a tribute to Tom Pratte (d. 1994). Confirmed to be specifically about this site via its title, description, and content (references the El Segundo/Chevron groin, Dave Skelly, and the Surfrider/Chevron agreement).
key_quotes: [00:14:30] "We settled on Dave Skelly engineering... he was very enthusiastic about the project... would building this reef destroy something the locals value?"
[00:15:21] Dave Skelly: "It's actually a submerged breakwater... this project is kind of the dream of every surfer."

[00:18:36] Dave Skelly, describing the design: "My concept is to put out gigantic sand bags — a nice bag weighs about 12 to 14 tons, that's a rather large bag. Geotextile fabrics... have been used on the Mississippi River to control bank erosion... these bags will last probably at least two decades and possibly longer."

[00:19:04] Dave Skelly: "Construction in the surf zone is really difficult, and out here at El Segundo we have a 10-foot tide range, a mobile bottom, and waves that come from different directions. The formation that we're placing these bags in is a chevron shape formation, or v-shaped, and hopefully that will create a good right break and a good left break."

[00:23:56] Unnamed interviewee, on Tom Pratte: "Tom basically held a big company accountable for the destruction of a wave. The man was definitely ahead of his time, was a visionary — the whole project really is because of his foresight... it's Tom's reef, period."
[00:26:03] Narrator (closing): "An object lesson to see what happens... whether the crest of the perfect wave will ever rise from the waters off El Segundo remains to be seen."

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NamePratte's Reef (permit name: Chevron Reef)
PlaceDockweiler State Beach / El Segundo, California
CountryUSA
Year2000-2001 built (Phase I fall 2000, 110 bags; Phase II spring 2001, +90 bags); removed 2008-2010 Phase 2 dated 2000 in Blacka et al. (2013, p.117) [R19] vs spring 2001 above: sources disagree. RESOLVED 2026-10-10: the monitoring paper by the reef's monitors gives the second installation as 23-24 April 2001 (90 new bags, +80 % volume, crest widened and made shallower, placed over the Phase I bags) [R28, p.3]; Blacka's 'Phase 2 in 2000' is not supported by that primary text.
TypeSubmerged artificial surf reef (ASR), sand-filled geotextile bags in a V/chevron layout [R4][R28]
PurposeSurfing — court/permit-mandated legal mitigation for a surf break lost to a 1984 Chevron rock groin [R1][R7]
Size~200 geotextile bags total, ~1,400-1,600 m3 built volume (vs. ~3,800 m3 / 5,000 yd3 in the original 1997 proposal); crest ~0.9-2.4 m below low-tide sea level (sources disagree) Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3) give 1,350 m3, the smallest MPR ever built, placed very close to shore [R18] (card 1,400-1,600 m3: sources disagree slightly, both kept). Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2; A.11): 64 m x 29 m V, depth 3.0 m (MLLW), 50 m from the undisturbed shoreline; Phase 1 design 110 bags of 3.0 x 2.1 x 1.2 m (~12.7 t, 80-90% fill), crest 1.8 m below MLLW; after Phase 2 (+90 bags, +80% volume) apex 0.9 m below MLLW; crest then dropped 1.5 m in a year; seabed scoured to ~4 m depth [R19]. Primary-source values (Borrero & Nelsen 2003): initial installation 110 bags on 22 September 2000, each about 14 tons when filled, 4 x 7 x 10 ft, max 280 ft3 (7.9 m3), filled 80-90 %; depth at the outermost point after the initial installation about -6 ft MLLW (1.83 m below MLLW); after Phase II within 3 ft of MLLW (0.91 m); obtuse 'V' with apex offshore (p.2-3); 'Pratte's only extends 30' (unit not printed, metres by context; p.14); 'approximately 1600 cubic meters of sand contained in 200' bags (p.16) [R28]. 200 bags x 7.9 m3 x 80-90 % fill = 1,264-1,422 m3 (project arithmetic, not a source value). Project-traced Phase I design layout (not the as-built 200-bag reef): 110 bags, area 435.2 m2, bounding box 58.0 x 28.6 m (alongshore x cross-shore), arms 44.7 / 44.4 deg to the V axis, traced by hand on the Skelly design drawing (RWR copy) and cross-checked on Fig. 4 of [R28] [R4][R28][R29]. Blacka's 64 x 29 m [R19] is therefore 10 % longer than this traced outline (58.0 m); its basis is not stated.
Cost$300,000 Chevron construction payment + $200,000-250,000 California Coastal Conservancy grant + $50,000 Surfrider add-on + ~$300,000 anonymous donation for removal; Surfline's cumulative headline figure is $850,000 over 2000-2008 [R1][R4][R7]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3): US$300,000 to build (Phase 1 budget only) and removal in 2010 cost more than twice that [R18]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.117-119): build US$550,000 ($300,000 + $250,000); removal US$551,000 (stage 1 budget $285,000; stage 2 $266,000 two years later); 142.5 containers removed, 1 left visible, 42.5 torn or buried [R19]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the build total (US$300,000 Phase 1 only [R18] vs US$550,000 total [R19]) and the removal total (more than US$600,000 [R18] vs US$551,000 [R19]); all kept.
Cost (approx. USD)850000
Financed byChevron Corporation (construction, as legal mitigation), California Coastal Conservancy (construction top-up), Surfrider Foundation (added funds + anonymous-donor-funded removal) [R1][R4][R7]
DesignerSkelly Engineering (David W. Skelly, PE)
ContractorPlaced by barge-mounted crane (builder not separately named in sources); removal directed by Coastal Frontiers Corporation, with American Marine Corporation (dive crew) and Morrissey Construction Company (onshore handling/disposal) [R3][R6][R10]
Status nowRemoved. Phase I removal fall 2008 (Sept 30-Oct 17, 2008); Phase II removal fall 2010, coinciding with expiry of the original 10-year experimental permit [R1][R3][R6][R9][R10]. First-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R9][R10]

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Court/permit-mandated mitigation for loss of the surfable Grand Avenue break, caused by Chevron's 1984 rock groin built to stop beach erosion threatening its El Segundo refinery's offshore oil-pipeline terminal [R1][R7]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The original 1997 CEQA filing by Surfrider Foundation (via the LA Dept. of Parks & Recreation) described '10-20 large geo-textile fabric bags containing approx. 5,000 cubic yards of sand' [R8]. As engineered by Skelly Engineering, the built design called for a V-shaped (delta/chevron) reef with arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves like a natural point break, cresting close to the low-tide waterline for consistent breaking [R4]. The goal was purely restoring a lost surfing amenity at the Grand Avenue break, not beach nourishment or ecological habitat creation [R4][R1].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction proceeded in two funded phases instead of one: 110 bags in fall 2000 (using the initial $300,000 Chevron payment), then ~90 more bags in spring 2001 once the Coastal Conservancy added $200,000-250,000, for roughly 200 bags total [R1][R7]. Even after that expansion, the built reef was far smaller than the 1997 proposal's ~5,000 yd3 (~3,800 m3) target: built volume is reported at only ~1,400-1,600 m3 [R2][R4] — under half the size first proposed, and by Surfrider's own later accounting roughly one-seventh the volume of Mount Maunganui and one-tenth to one-thirtieth the volume of Narrowneck [R7]. Individual bags were also markedly smaller (~8 m3 each) than Narrowneck's containers (140-320 m3 each) [R2]. Chad Nelsen (Surfrider): 'we probably should have said $300,000 is not enough' [R7]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the Phase 2 date: Blacka et al. (2013, p.117) date the 90-bag extension in 2000 [R19]; the card has spring 2001 [R1][R7]. RESOLVED 2026-10-10 for 2001: Borrero & Nelsen (2003) p.3 give the second installation on 23-24 April 2001, 90 bags [R28]. Blacka Table A.11 also: after Phase 2 apex 0.9 m below MLLW and the crest then dropped 1.5 m in a year [R19].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Wikipedia states the reef 'had very little effect on the surfing conditions at Dockweiler Beach and ... no measurable effect on the shoreline morphology' [R1][R2]. Surfline's 2008 feature: over 'eight plus years, Pratte's Reef was as useless as useless gets' and 'it never produced a consistently surfable wave' [R7]. Diver surveys found bags had moved, sunk, and been buried by sand, with the black polypropylene material visibly deteriorating — 'largely disintegrated' within about two years [R4][R2]. No coastal-protection or ecological benefit is reported in any of the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement). The reef was removed over two phases (fall 2008, fall 2010), the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R7][R9][R10].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Undersized for its budget and site: a $300,000-$550,000 construction budget bought a reef roughly 1/7 the size of Mount Maunganui's and 1/10-1/30 the size of Narrowneck's [R7]. Crest-depth mismatch: on big swells the crest was too deep to trigger breaking, so waves broke outside the reef [R1][R7]. Pre-existing degraded beach: the Chevron groin had already straightened/steepened the beach and buried the original Grand Avenue break in trapped sand, conditions a small mitigation reef could not reverse [R7]. Material/structural failure: sand-filled fabric bags resting on a sandy, mobile seabed with no rigid foundation settled, sank, and were buried, and the polypropylene fabric deteriorated within roughly two years [R4][R2]. Insufficient pre-construction monitoring: Nelsen said more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions beforehand 'would have told us the reef was too small before we even put it in' [R7]. Surfer and local comments on a YouTube video (2026, evidence grade D, anecdotal) agree that it rarely or never produced a rideable wave: too small, a steep approach that gave swells no time to build, swell shadow from Catalina Island and the land mass, and a V instead of a triangle [R33].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: No fishing-pressure or ecological side effects are reported for Pratte's Reef in any source found, unlike Narrowneck (Gold Coast), whose geotextile containers were colonized by macro-algae, benthos and pelagic fish and became popular for local (spear-)fishing, diving and snorkeling, though also flagged as vulnerable to vessel/anchor damage as a design risk [R17]. The project's most consequential outcome may have been legal/political: the 1984 mitigation condition Tom Pratte secured is credited by Surfrider as the first case in which the California Coastal Commission formally recognized a surf break as a protectable coastal recreational resource, a precedent Surfrider says later helped protect Trestles from development [R7]. Surfrider itself updated its institutional policy on artificial reefs after this project, moving toward protecting existing surf breaks rather than promising to recreate lost ones: 'I don't think we should ever trade a surf spot for the promise of building something else' (Chad Nelsen) [R7]. No litigation was found in any source listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement).

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Surfrider's Chad Nelsen (2008 Surfline retrospective): should have told Chevron up front that $300,000 was not enough to build a working reef; more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions before construction would have revealed the reef was undersized before it was built; more broadly, mitigation itself is often 'a false promise', and protecting existing surf breaks is preferable to engineering replacements after the fact [R7]. Named Surfline commenters (2008): depth/tide design was wrong ('Andrew': should have been 'nearly dry on a negative tide to be legit', not 8 feet deep at zero tide); distance from shore was wrong, though commenters disagreed on direction ('Randy Wright': 'simply too far away from the shore'; Dr. Jose Borrero, quoted elsewhere: 'too small and too close to shore'); cruder/cheaper materials might have worked as well ('prattes is a joke': rocks or 'smashed up cars'); lack of surfer input in the engineering process ('evan') [R7][R4].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tidal range is the single most transferable engineering lesson: Pratte's Reef's crest depth was wrong for the local tide swing (too deep to break big swells; ~8 ft/2.4 m deep even at zero/low tide per a Surfrider-sourced figure) [R7]. Santa Monica Bay has a mean tidal range of ~1.4-1.7 m [R12], versus Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m [R13], consistent with the Mediterranean's generally small tides [R11] — a crest depth calibrated for Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m swing is a much smaller, more predictable engineering target than one spanning ~1.5 m, supporting Lior's thesis that Israel's small tidal range is a structural advantage for reef stability [R15]. Budget-driven undersizing (Nelsen: '$300,000 is not enough' [R7]) is, in this card author's INFERENCE (not a sourced statement), a transferable governance/funding risk, not a site-specific one, relevant to any small pilot reef Israel might build on a limited budget. Material degradation (UV/wave abrasion of polypropylene bags within ~2 years; the 'largely disintegrated within about two years' finding is the diver-survey report in the outcome field [R4][R2]) is a warning for any low-cost geotextile design proposed for the Israeli coast, including Lior's own 'cheap & light materials... for fast deployment and removal' sketch [R15]. Israel has no directly comparable built ASR yet — its only confirmed built geotextile project is the Ashkelon Geotube, a shore-protection structure, not a surf reef [R14]. Tide levels (NOAA CO-OPS Santa Monica 9410840, epoch 1983-2001, relative to MSL): MHHW +0.804, MLLW -0.849, HAT +1.382, LAT -1.469 m, i.e. MHHW - MLLW = 1.653 m [R30]; this is the sourced replacement for the live tide-forecast figure [R12]. Haifa's 0.3-0.4 m [R13] is a web tide-table figure, not a primary source.

footprint.orientation_notes: The reinforced central 'spine' block (where the two arms of bags converge) is the most-offshore point of the structure and faces the 'WAVE DIRECTION' arrow drawn on the Skelly Engineering plan view, i.e. the apex points seaward into the incident swell, consistent with the card's design narrative ('arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves'). The drawing's own 45-degree angle annotation (measured from a vertical reference line to one arm) and this file's pixel-geometry check (~92 degrees between the two arms, i.e. ~46 degrees each side of the wave-direction axis) agree closely. The two arms are markedly ASYMMETRIC: ~44 m from spine to one tip, ~33 m to the other (a ~25% difference) - a refinement on Gemini's near-symmetric 9-vertex polygon. No compass bearing for the wave-direction axis, and no indication of which arm points which alongshore (e.g. north vs south) direction, could be determined from the design drawing itself (no north arrow). Gemini's specific '260-280 deg, W-WNW' bearing is plausible for a Santa Monica Bay/El Segundo south-/west-facing beach but is not confirmed in any source in our card or found in this pass.
footprint.materials: ~200 sand-filled geotextile (described as polyester/black polypropylene) bags total, built in two phases: 110 bags fall 2000 (this drawing's exact bag count) + ~90 more bags spring 2001; individual bags ~14 tons (R4) or ~14,000 lb (R7) - sources disagree ~2x; bag footprint 3 m x 1.2 m per the Raised Water Research bag-size diagram (R4) [R1][R2][R4][R7].

footprint.confidence: The outline is traced on the reef designer's own scaled plan drawing (Skelly Engineering design layout, 110 bags + 30 optional, also published as the 'design layout' in Borrero & Nelsen 2003), using only the solid-outline bags; the printed scale bar agrees with the known bag size (4 x 7 x 10 ft = 7.9 m3) within about 3-6% and two reproductions of the drawing agree to about 1% in area. It is a design drawing, not a survey or photo: nothing of the structure is visible on any image (removed 2008-2010), the April 2001 second phase (90 more bags, crest widened) is not drawn, the built bags moved and sank, and the map position cannot be fixed.
open_issues: This file's Skelly-drawing-based measurements (R4) describe the Phase I design only (110 bags + up to 30 'optional' bags = up to 140), matching the fall-2000 as-built count exactly. No plan-view drawing was found anywhere in our references for the spring-2001 Phase II addition (~90 more bags, bringing the total to ~200 built) - the FINAL as-built footprint (2001-2008) may have been somewhat larger than reported here, by an unknown amount.

The arm cross-section width (4 m) and spine-block size (8x6 m) used to turn the drawing's bag-chain centrelines into a closed polygon are this file's own estimate (from the bag-size diagram and visual inspection), not a published figure - area_m2 (324.1) should be read as order-of-magnitude only, not a precise footprint.

No compass bearing or north arrow appears on the Skelly drawing; this file's alongshore (x) axis direction is an arbitrary, stated-but-unverified convention (same limitation flagged in the parallel cables-reef-wa.md file for that reef).

The card's own two pre-existing crest-depth figures (-0.9 m MLLW per R4's text vs ~2.4 m/8 ft at zero tide per R7) remain unresolved; this file's new '-6 ft MSL' (1.83 m) reading from the drawing itself is a third data point, close to but not identical to either, plausibly a datum (MSL vs MLLW vs 'zero tide') difference rather than a genuine conflict - not resolved here.

image26.png's single '200 m' scale bar was shown (via the Narrowneck cross-check) not to transfer reliably across the graphic's 4 photo panels; its Pratte's-specific reading (~68.5x34.3 m) is reported for completeness in the derivation table only and is excluded from this file's headline/confidence-bearing numbers.

All pixel measurements come from a low-resolution (308x385 px) scanned engineering drawing; scale-bar tick-mark reading, bag-corner anti-aliasing, and line thickness contribute an estimated +/-10% uncertainty to every length/width/area figure derived from it.

shape_conf_factors: + Scaled drawing from the designer of record (Skelly Engineering) with a printed scale bar (0-15-30-60-90 ft); the bar ticks fit a straight line to within 0.5 px in both reproductions (img1, img5) and the two reproductions are related by a near-uniform affine map (x scale 0.8763 vs 0.8783 expected from the bars, 0.2% apart; y scale 1.5% lower)

+ Independent scale check (verification 2026-10-05): ICCE-2010 gives the Pratte's bag as 7.9 m3 maximum volume; a secondary web summary (primary not located) gives the bag as 4 x 7 x 10 ft = 280 ft3 = 7.93 m3, which matches ICCE's figure by arithmetic. The drawing's bag grid, measured on both reproductions, has a column pitch of 6.8-6.9 ft (bag width 7 ft) and a row pitch of 9.4-9.6 ft (bag length 10 ft), i.e. 1-6% below nominal; spine block 10.6 m for 5 columns (2.12 m each) and 14.1 m for 5 rows (2.82 m each)

+ Solid-outline bags only: the drawing legend shows 110 solid + 30 dashed 'optional' bags; the 30 dashed bags are the outer two rows on each arm near the apex and the left column of the spine, and are excluded (this verification removed about 49 m2 of dashed-bag area that the first trace had wrongly included)

+ Arm angles 44.7 / 44.4 deg to the V axis (printed 45; re-measured on the canonical polygon: long edges at 43.7-46.5 deg), spine block 5 x 5 bag grid. NOTE the printed crest label '-6 ft MSL' (1.83 m below MSL = about 0.97 m below MLLW, using NOAA Los Angeles datums MSL = MLLW + 2.82 ft) does NOT match ICCE-2010's '1.8 m below MLLW at the outermost point after installation' (different datum and quantity); it is close to the post-Phase-II crest (-0.9 m MLLW, RWR). The crest depth therefore cannot identify which phase the drawing shows; the bag count (110) does

- Design drawing only (Phase I, 110 bags). Phase II (April 2001, +90 bags, volume +80%, crest widened and made shallower, bags placed directly over the Phase I bags - ICCE 2010 p.7) is NOT drawn: the final reef was higher and wider at the crest than this footprint, by an unknown amount, and it is unknown whether any of the 30 optional bags were built

- Bags were crane-placed, moved, sank and were buried (Borrero 2010; RWR), so the real footprint differed from the design by metres; no as-built survey, multibeam plot or aerial photo could be retrieved (Borrero & Nelsen 2003 figures and the CCRP aerials are blocked: HTTP 403)
- Drawing has no north arrow; orientation (+x toward SSE) is inferred from the 1996 concept plan (north arrow) and the present shoreline (155.5 deg, own fit)

- Published coordinates disagree by 100s of metres (card/Wikipedia is 288 m offshore of today's dry-sand edge; RWR and Gemini coordinates are 113-119 m), and all three lie SOUTH of the short rock groin at 33.91685,-118.43030 (taken to be the Grand Street jetty) whereas the CCC staff report (300 yd north of the Grand Avenue jetty) and Borrero & Nelsen 2003 (about 200 m south of the Hyperion 1-mile outfall, within 500 m of it and of the Grand Street jetty) put the reef NORTH of that jetty; so no lat/lon polygon is given (geo = null)

- Outline position depends on the stroke edge: +-1 px = +-0.2 m = about +-4% area; solid/dashed classification of the edge rows adds about +-10 m2; scale-bar anisotropy between reproductions about 1.5%

+ (re-verified 2026-10-10) the primary 2003 paper confirms the bag size (4 x 7 x 10 ft, 7.9 m3), the Phase I count (110) and a 30 m cross-shore extent (p.14; its Fig. 20 re-measured at 29.0 x 58.5 m on its own bar vs our 28.6 x 58.0 m); Fig. 4 is the same Skelly design drawing as img1 (and the same raster as img5, so those two are not independent of each other). It does NOT contain an as-built plan, so confidence stays medium; the datum of the crest label stays ambiguous (drawing '-6' MSL' vs paper '-6 ft MLLW': same number, 0.85 m apart) and is not resolvable from the paper
