sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Tourism and economic development for a declining South Taranaki town, via more frequent good surfing conditions; explicitly not a coastal-protection project [R2][R3]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: Two reefs were planned: a cheaper north reef (built first) costed at ~NZ$1.3 million [R3], designed (consent stage) as a 99 x 30 x 3.5 m reef of about 4,900 m3 [R18] (the 2004 concept was ~90 x 20 m with bags 1.5-2 m high [R19]) for a fast hollow right-hand wave 1.8-2.5 m high rideable for ~100 m [R2][R3][R18]; and a larger, never-built south reef meant to deliver a 200 m ride on waves up to 3.6 m high [R3]. ASR tested the design in a small-scale wave pool at its Raglan facility [R2]. Kerry Black publicly expected the north reef to be finished within about two months of construction starting [R2][R3]. Design history [R18, printed pp. 2-3]: the idea was first pursued in 1998 by Mr Eddie Klaassen and future Trust members; Dr Kerry Black did a site-selection study (sites within 10 km of the town; best sites in Opunake Bay); ASR Ltd's Phase I feasibility study (2001, computer modelling and data collection) found two satisfactory positions, north and south sides of the bay; after consultation the north side was chosen and ASR did the Phase II detailed design and environmental studies for the consents. The position was set from bathymetry, rock and sand cover, aerial photographs, video and visual observations, numerical modelling and wave-angle measurements. Built from large sand-filled geo-textile containers made to reproduce the designed profile, not fixed to the seabed (stability from weight and friction). Black and Mead (2006) 'Opunake Reef Construction Manual' (ASR) is cited by TRC (printed p.20), not found online.

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Only the cheaper north reef was ever attempted; the south reef was never built [R2][R13][R14]. Construction, planned for ~2 months, instead dragged on for years: by 2009 all 27 geotextile bags were reportedly in place but still needed "fine tuning" (more sand, closing gaps between bags), while spending had already passed NZ$1.7 million against the NZ$1.1 million council allocation [R1][R2]. A 2009-10 proposal to cap the geo-containers with rock (est. NZ$150,000) was pledged by ASR's new part-owner Sealutions LLC as part of a sale agreement but was never honoured [R2]. In 2010 seabed changes were reported to be causing uneven performance across the reef [R2]. By August 2011 the council, Trust and ASR relationship had broken down entirely, ending in litigation [R2]. TRC 2009 (read 2026-10-13) [R18]: construction began early 2006, was halted by weather and the equipment being needed at Mount Maunganui, resumed over the next two summers (site sign: works February 2007 to May 200?, read as 2008); as of April 2008 27 bags were in place with fine-tuning planned for 2009/2010; the council still rated the Trust's environmental performance 'good' and noted no adverse effects (baseline kaimoana and intertidal surveys 2006-07; post-construction surveys to follow); the as-built confirmation and the position survey (+-5 m) required by consent 6377-1 conditions 9 and 10 were not yet due ('reef not yet complete', Table 3); the required signs at Opunake Beach were missing and TRC called the nearly finished reef 'already a potential hazard' for boating (printed p.15); TRC recommended a dive survey of the structure in 2009-10 (printed p.18) - its result was not found.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: No source found gives a measured/instrumented surf-quality outcome for Opunake (no wave-height, peel-angle or ride-length monitoring data, unlike Narrowneck) — "not found" (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement). Qualitatively, every source agrees the reef never produced the promised rideable waves; a 2021 investigative piece states flatly the reef "didn't produce the expected waves" [R1]. The reef did attract fish and other sea-life, but the structure itself began to break apart, with pieces washing ashore [R1]. No coastal-protection outcome is reported because none was designed in [R3]. No removal/dismantling is documented in any source found [R1][R2]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3-4) note the inside (most complete) section gives good-quality waves but the reef is widely considered a failure; predominant NW winds are mostly offshore and waves are pre-conditioned in the bay [R13]. This differs in tone from [R1] (reef 'didn't produce the expected waves'): sources disagree, both kept. Blacka Table 4.1 rates surfing 'No (construction incomplete)' [R14].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: It failed. Contributing causes across sources: chronic under-budgeting and repeated funding shortfalls (the NZ$1.1-1.3M allocation proved far short of the NZ$1.7M+ actually spent, and later top-up requests of NZ$400,000, NZ$150,000 and NZ$133,000 were each unmet or only partly met) [R1][R2]; the intrinsic durability problem of sand-filled geotextile bags, which ASR co-founder Shaw Mead later called the technology's "fatal flaw" — a single torn bag loses sand and changes the whole structure's shape [R5]; seabed changes over time causing uneven performance across the reef by 2010 [R2]; and corporate instability at ASR (majority sale to Sealutions LLC, an unhonoured completion pledge, and ASR's own liquidation in 2012) that removed any prospect of finishing the fix [R1][R2]. Because the reef was designed purely for surfing with no coastal-protection goal, there was no secondary benefit to justify the sunk cost once the surf failed to materialise [R3].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The reef attracted fish and other sea-life even as it failed to produce surf [R1]. Pieces of the failed structure washed ashore over time [R1], a pattern echoed more dramatically at the related Mount Maunganui and Boscombe ASR reefs [R1]. The dispute escalated beyond an engineering failure into litigation: the Trust sued ASR in 2011, and the council wrote off first a NZ$400,000 loan and then its whole claim as unrecoverable [R1][R2]. No source found documents fishing pressure, swimmer-safety/rip-current incidents, or tourism data specific to Opunake — "not found" [R1][R5].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: ASR co-founder Shaw Mead concluded the geotextile-bag construction method itself was the core weakness and said it led him to shift subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to traditional rock construction [R5]; he separately called the sandbag approach "an evolutionary deadend" in an email to Newsroom [R1]. At Opunake specifically, ASR's own 2009-10 fix proposal was to cap the geo-containers with rock rather than keep tuning bags with sand, but the funding for that fix was never delivered [R2]. Surfrider Foundation CEO Jim Moriarty argued more broadly that ocean-based artificial-reef attempts as a class have "absolutely horrible" results and that effort should go into protecting natural breaks instead [R6]. NZ Surfing Magazine editor Cory Scott was blunter still: "not one artificial reef has created a wave of any quality, despite claims to the contrary" [R1]. Process-wise, the repeated pattern of underestimating both time (2 months expected; it ran years) and cost (three separate unmet top-up requests) suggests firmer contingency budgeting and a completion-guarantee contract with the builder would have been needed to finish the job at all [R1][R2].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tide range is the biggest physical contrast: Opunake's open New Zealand coast shows a sample tidal range on the order of ~2.5 m (high 2.94 m / low 0.47 m, one sample day, datum not stated) [R7] and more than 3.0 m according to Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.3) [R14], versus well under half a metre at Haifa on Israel's virtually tideless Mediterranean coast (~0.36-0.40 m high / ~0.00-0.07 m low) [R12]. A geotextile-bag reef at Opunake has to keep working across that ~2.5 m swing in water depth every tide cycle — a substantially harder crest-depth design problem than any Israeli Mediterranean site would present, which is a point in Israel's favour for a similar reef proposal (INFERENCE of this card's author; the ~2.5 m swing is DERIVED as 2.94 m - 0.47 m = 2.47 m from one sample day [R7], Blacka's spring range is >3.0 m [R14]). However, the dominant documented failure modes at Opunake — chronic under-budgeting, repeated shortfalls in "finishing" funding, corporate instability at the design/construction firm, and the durability problem of sand-filled geotextile bags (tear -> sand loss -> shape change -> wave-quality loss) [R1][R2][R5] — are not tide-dependent and would transfer directly to any Israeli geotextile-bag project, including the Ashkelon geotube project already logged in this project's master list, which itself suffered partial construction failure (15 of 48 geotubes destroyed before the layout was completed) and higher-than-expected maintenance costs (Bar, D. and Drimer, N. (2023), J. Mar. Sci. Eng. 11, 236, https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse11020236, as summarised in 01_source_notes/jmse2023_bar_drimer_paper.md and 02_research/00_master_list.md; paper's own figures not re-checked in this audit). The clearest transferable lesson is financial and material: secure full contingency funding and a completion-guarantee contract before committing to a geotextile-bag structure, and weigh rock-based construction (which ASR's own co-founder ultimately endorsed over bags) given the technology's poor track record on sand-bag durability [R1][R2][R5][R7][R12]. Design crest level [R18]: the shallowest contour was set at 0.0 m below chart datum (= lowest astronomical tide), i.e. as shallow as possible without emerging except at extreme low tide, in a 3 m or larger tidal range; for Haifa's small tide the equivalent crest depth would be set relative to local mean sea level, not chart datum (project reasoning, not a source statement).

name: Boscombe Surf Reef
year: Construction began June 2008; officially opened 19 November 2009 [R1][R4]. Primary-source timeline (Rendle 2016 p. 64): construction started 30 Aug 2008, suspended 13 Nov 2008, resumed 18 Apr 2009, official opening 2 Oct 2009 (the text on p. 65 says completion Nov 2009 after 18 months) [R17].
type: Submerged multi-purpose artificial surf reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers ("geobags"), not rock [R1][R4][R7].
purpose: Coastal-town regeneration and surf tourism: create a reliable, higher-quality wave to roughly double good surfing days (from ~77 to ~154/yr) and double annual surf-related beach visits (from ~5,000 to ~10,000); marketed as Europe's/the Northern Hemisphere's first artificial surf reef [R1][R3][R4].
size: ~55 geotextile containers, each ~2–3 m high and ~60 m long; total sand-fill volume ≈13,000 m³; footprint ≈1 hectare (2.5 acres); positioned 220 m from the seawall base, ~240 m east of the pier [R4][R7]. Rendle's thesis [R17] (primary): 32 containers built in two layers, placed by divers and filled in situ (p. 68); design drawing of Dec 2006 shows about 46 labelled bags, footprint 4,474 m2, bag volume 10,450 m3 + fill 1,750 m3 (Fig. 5.3, p. 95); Table 4.4 design: volume 11,900 m3, footprint 5,450 m2, length 120 m, height 2.8-4.1 m (p. 70); containers up to 67 m long, 100-800 m3 (p. 69); eight T4 containers about 4 m diameter, 65-70 m long, 746.7 m3 each (Table 5.3, p. 98; p. 121) [R17]. Counts differ between sources (32 / about 46 / 54-55) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) give 12,800 m3 [R18] (the designers' value; Blacka Table 4.4 cost/rate implies about 12,760 m3 [R19]); volume sources therefore disagree: about 13,000 [R4][R7] / 11,900 or 12,200 (Rendle design) / 12,800 [R18], all kept. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.66): footprint 80 m (longshore) x 90 m (cross-shore), depth 3-5 m, 225 m offshore, submergence 0.5 m, tide range 1.8 m, T~4 s, H~0.5 m (Table 4.3) [R19]; the card's 120 m length is Rendle's design figure, so footprint figures differ by source. Project-traced outline (not a source statement): reef plan area 4,042 m2, minimum rotated rectangle 121.1 x 45.0 m, about 220-225 m offshore, west edge 242 m east of the pier head, traced on the Esri Wayback image of 2011-09-28 and checked against the April 2011 survey figure [R22][R21]. The '1 hectare' of [R4]/Wikipedia is therefore not the plan area of the reef body (4,042 m2); the basis of the 1 ha figure is not stated by those sources (not reconciled).
cost: £3–3.2 million actually spent on the reef structure itself, against an original 1999–2003-era estimate of £1.4 million; the wider Boscombe seafront/pier regeneration scheme (reef + pier refurbishment + seafront) totalled ≈£11 million [R1][R2]. One New Zealand outlet states the cost as "more than NZD $6 million," over a year behind schedule — not corroborated by any UK source [R8]. Rendle (2016, p. 65-67): original GBP 600,000 (Black et al. 2000), GBP 1.1 m (ASR Ltd 2006, incl. 20 % contingency), final about GBP 3.2 m; repairs and marine-park works a further GBP 700,000 (funded partly by GBP 306,531 insurance and a GBP 254,000 Coastal Communities Fund grant, p. 64); Weight (2000) estimate GBP 618,000 for two reefs (Table 4.3, p. 66) [R17]. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.4): about A$4.9 M in 2013 dollars, A$384 per m3 [R19]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) note the contract was fixed-price, so claimed overruns concern delays rather than contract cost [R18]; this can sit beside the early-estimate comparison above.
cost_usd_approx: £3.2M ≈ US $5.1M at 2009 average GBP/USD rates (~1.59); NZD $6M ≈ US $4.2M at 2010 average NZD/USD rates (~0.70) — rough conversions, not sourced from any single article [R1][R2][R8]. ASSUMPTION: the exchange rates (GBP/USD ~1.59, NZD/USD ~0.70) are unsourced estimates of this project (not confirmed against a rate table); order of magnitude only.
financed_by: Bournemouth Borough Council, funded via sale of a car park (on which Barratt Developments built the Honeycombe Chine Flats) and sale of beach "pods" as part of the Overstrand seafront building [R1][R4].
motivation: Boscombe was a rundown 20th-century seaside suburb of Bournemouth in need of regeneration; the reef was one plank of a wider council-led seafront renewal that also refurbished Boscombe Pier and built new beachfront "pods" and flats [R1][R10]. A feasibility study was approved in 1999 and detailed plans approved in March 2003, with construction not starting until 2008 [R6][R1]. Financing was structured opportunistically around unrelated seafront property sales rather than a dedicated capital grant [R1][R4].
designer: Dr Kerry Black (oceanographer, ex-University of Waikato/NIWA, co-founder of ASR Ltd) did the wave-science/concept design; Shaw Mead (ASR co-founder) is credited as design/surf-science lead [R8][R7].
contractor: ASR Ltd (Artificial Surf Reefs Ltd), a New Zealand company; managing director Nick Behunin [R1][R4][R6].
status_now: Permanently closed to surfing since 31 March/April 2011 after storm and boat-propeller damage; ASR Ltd went into liquidation September 2012; rebranded and reopened in stages (2014, then 2017) as a "Coastal Activity Park" for diving, snorkelling, windsurfing/kitesurfing and other non-surf water activities; by 2018 described as largely forgotten/neglected; debris from the structure was still washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R1][R3][R4][R8].
hover_text: A ~1-hectare, 13,000 m³ sand-filled geotextile-bag surf reef opened November 2009 for £3–3.2M (Bournemouth Borough Council, funded via land/beach-pod sales); a boat-propeller strike and storm damage forced permanent closure to surfing by 2011, ASR Ltd liquidated in 2012, and the site was rebranded a non-surf "Coastal Activity Park" from 2014 [R1][R2][R4][R8].
design_as_planned: The reef was designed as a submerged, angled ramp of stacked geotextile sand containers that would intercept the dominant swell direction and reshape it into rideable peeling waves, rather than "creating" waves from nothing [R10]. ASR director Shaw Mead described the mechanism directly: "The reef doesn't actually create waves. It's angled to catch the mean wave direction, and it acts as a ramp which changes the way the waves break" [R10]. The design target was a "Grade 5" wave under good swell conditions, producing rides of roughly 75 m to the right and 35 m to the left, suited to bodyboarders and surfers [R10]. Eleven specific design/performance objectives were set, including materially increasing surf-day frequency (from ~77 to ~154 good surf days/yr) and beach-visit numbers (from ~5,000 to ~10,000/yr) [R1][R2].
as_built_vs_design: The structure eventually installed — 55 sand-filled geotextile bags forming a ~1-hectare submerged mound ~13,000 m³ in volume — matched the general geotube concept, but construction ran roughly a decade behind the original 1999–2003 planning timeline and cost more than double the original £1.4 million estimate, landing at £3–3.2 million for the reef alone [R1][R2][R6]. Construction was repeatedly delayed and beset by "setbacks during building works" before the reef finally opened in November 2009 [R1]. Shaw Mead later blamed the outcome on "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions," distancing his own design/surf-science role from those problems [R8]. Rendle (2016): built crest about +0.5 m chart datum against a design crest of 0 m CD (Table 4.4; 0.3 m CD on the Dec 2006 drawing), so the crest is higher than planned (p. 70); not all containers were filled to capacity and some bags of the plan were missing in the final construction (p. 98, p. 122) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): the reef was built to design under a fixed-price contract and completed in late September 2009 [R18] (designers' view; the card's headline opening date is November 2009 and Rendle 2016 documents shortfalls [R17], so sources disagree). AUDIT NOTE 2026-10-10: 'submerged' holds at high water only; the built crest (+0.5 m CD, about -0.9 m MSL using the project's conversion MSL = CD - 1.40 m, NTSLF offset; Rendle uses 1.66 m, unresolved) is exposed at low tide (Rendle p.70-71) [R17][R20].
outcome: A University of Plymouth interim evaluation (Dr Mark Davidson, published May 2010) found the reef met only 4 of its 11 original design objectives, stating: "The wave length is rather too intense and challenging [and it] is not quite as consistent as it should be" [R1][R2]. This evaluation is credited solely to Dr Mark Davidson in every source found; a claim (raised during a Gemini-survey cross-check) that the evaluation was co-authored by "Reeve" and "Medina" is not confirmed anywhere and is rejected — the only genuine Davidson co-authored paper found online is the separate, later Rendle & Davidson (2012, ICCE Proceedings) study on structural degradation, with a different co-author [R1]. In practice the reef worked best around low tide, with rides largely limited to steep, short sections, mainly ridden by bodyboarders rather than the standup surfers it was marketed to [R1]. A routine inspection in March 2011 found "substantial changes" to the reef's profile; it was closed for safety on 31 March 2011 [R1]. In April 2011 further damage was found, with one geo-container removed and another repaired, apparently after an unidentified boat's propeller struck the reef [R1][R9]. Repairs begun in August 2011 were suspended for winter and never satisfactorily completed [R1][R7]. ASR Ltd went into liquidation in September 2012 (one source: November 2012), owing the council roughly £14,800–£15,000; the council obtained a £306,531 insurance settlement in 2013 [R1][R4][R6]. A 2012 plan to repurpose the site as a dive/snorkel trail was itself abandoned [R5]. The site was rebranded in 2014 and again in 2017 as a "Coastal Activity Park," with surfing dropped as a priority [R1][R6]. Debris from the decaying structure was reported washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Rendle (2016, p. 70-71): Davidson 2010 found 4 of 11 criteria met and 2 partly; rides about 20 m left / 40 m right against 20 m / 65 m designed; surfable only 1-2 h around mid-tide because the crest is exposed at low tide and too deep at high tide; the wave model shows attenuation in the lee (p. 143-144) and the shoreline did not respond, no salient (p. 102) [R17]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the Plymouth evaluation score: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4), reporting the Plymouth University monitoring of May 2010, say the reef met 7 of 11 criteria (7 of the 9 agreed by Council and builders) and that media mis-reported '4 out of 10' [R18]; Rendle (2016, p.70-71) gives 4 of 11 met and 2 partly [R17]. The authors of [R18] designed the reef (interested party); Davidson (2010) must be checked directly. Both kept. Shoreline: Blacka et al. (2013, p.70) report no noticeable long-term change of the 0 m shoreline (Rendle & Davidson 2012); design accretion was predicted mostly near the -1 m contour (K. Black pers. comm.), which Rendle & Davidson did not report; inshore scour and steepening were well predicted; rated surfing 'partially', protection 'minor' [R19].
why_worked_or_failed: Shaw Mead's own later analysis concluded sand-filled geotextile bags were a structural dead end: "the sandbags were an evolutionary dead-end," and "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" — a design fundamentally vulnerable to point-impact damage [R8][R9]. The proximate damage cause was a boat-propeller strike, a mechanism Geosynthetics Magazine groups with damage at other ASR reefs elsewhere (anchor damage at Gold Coast, debris strikes at Kovalam, over-filling at Mount Maunganui) as evidence of a general geotextile-reef vulnerability pattern [R9]. Even before the propeller strike, the University of Plymouth's Davidson evaluation had already found the reef meeting only 4 of 11 design objectives, indicating the wave-shaping design itself, not only later physical damage, fell short [R1][R2]. Shaw Mead's own explanation for the broader project's failure also emphasises non-engineering causes — "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions" during a near-decade gap between 2003 planning approval and 2008 construction start [R8][R6][R1]. Rendle (2016): after winter 2009-10 sand moved inside the bags (seaward to landward, p. 94); a T4 container (746.7 m3) lost its sand in 2011 (cause contested: weak container, propeller strike or vandalism) and a second in 2012, together 1,493.4 m3 = 12.5 % of 11,900 m3 (Table 5.3, p. 98), gaps of 5 m then 8-10 m, 2 m crest dip; construction shortcuts (wrong grain size supplied, weather, end-of-summer deadline, p. 98); first inspection found poorly repaired tears (p. 120) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4-5): 17 bathymetry surveys and 3 beach-profile surveys; beach accreted up to 60 m over >500 m within 6 months; about 60 hardwood groynes in Poole Bay (roughly every 180 m) and renourishment every 10-12 years, so the beach response sits within a managed shoreline [R18].
unexpected_results: The project drew media coverage in an estimated 60 countries around its 2009 opening, and local Boscombe hospitality businesses reported a real economic uplift regardless of the reef's technical shortcomings [R2]. Some media coverage carried headlines setting expectations the reef's actual short, steep, low-tide-only wave could not meet [R9]. The site was closed in 2011 over safety concerns involving hazardous undercurrents and gaps in the deteriorating structure, serious enough that local surfer/photographer Chris Skone-Roberts warned "it is just a question of time before someone dies" [R2]. Loose material and debris from the decaying geotextile bags continued washing ashore for years after closure, documented as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Dolphins were reported investigating the new structure shortly after construction, an unplanned/unmeasured ecological footnote [R10].
could_be_better: Shaw Mead (ASR co-designer) concluded the material choice itself was wrong — sand-filled geotextile bags are "an evolutionary dead-end" for a structure that must survive years of surf-zone wave energy and occasional impacts — and moved ASR's subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to rock construction instead [R8]. Geosynthetics Magazine's review implies the fix is structural redundancy: a single ruptured bag should not be able to reshape the whole reef, pointing toward either more failure-tolerant bag engineering or abandoning fabric containers for point-impact-prone sites like a boat channel [R9]. The University of Plymouth's own evaluation implies the wave-shaping geometry needed further hydrodynamic refinement even independent of material failure, since only 4 of 11 objectives were met while the structure was still intact [R1][R2]. Local critics, including councillor Ben Grower, framed the entire project as a governance and money failure rather than a fixable engineering detail [R2][R5]. Rendle's lessons (p. 121-122): compare real seabed level with the design before building, no bags missing from the final build, seal the fill ports, the +0.5 m higher crest added stress, avoid geotextile in an exposed shallow surf zone [R17].
relevance_to_israel: Boscombe's tidal range is modest by UK Atlantic-coast standards (same-day check showed roughly 0.9–1.1 m high-to-low, illustrative only) [R12]; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is effectively micro-tidal, though no sourced numeric tidal-range figure for Haifa was found in this research [R14]. What transfers directly: Boscombe's central lesson is that geotextile-sandbag construction is vulnerable to point-impact damage (boat strikes, anchors, debris) and to cascading shape-change once any single bag ruptures, regardless of tidal regime [R8][R9]. Haifa's proposed reef site is assessed against real Shikmona-buoy wave data (significant wave height 0.45–0.8 m in the surfable window, occasional peaks to ~1.2 m), a much gentler wave-energy environment than the UK Channel/Atlantic-influenced south coast that shaped Boscombe's design — meaning less storm-wave loading, but underscoring that any Israeli project should still plan explicitly for boat-strike/anchor exposure in a working coastal-shipping and fishing environment [R14]. Tide levels from the design paper (Mead et al. 2010, Table 1): MHWS +0.81 m and MLWS -0.95 m relative to MSL, i.e. a spring range of 1.76 m [R20] (project conversion from chart datum; the same-day 0.9-1.1 m above is one day only). Haifa wave figures [R14] are Lior's own readings of the IsraMar Shikmona buoy, not a published source.

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameBoscombe Surf Reef
PlaceBoscombe, Bournemouth, Dorset
CountryUnited Kingdom
YearConstruction began June 2008; officially opened 19 November 2009 [R1][R4]. Primary-source timeline (Rendle 2016 p. 64): construction started 30 Aug 2008, suspended 13 Nov 2008, resumed 18 Apr 2009, official opening 2 Oct 2009 (the text on p. 65 says completion Nov 2009 after 18 months) [R17].
TypeSubmerged multi-purpose artificial surf reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers ("geobags"), not rock [R1][R4][R7].
PurposeCoastal-town regeneration and surf tourism: create a reliable, higher-quality wave to roughly double good surfing days (from ~77 to ~154/yr) and double annual surf-related beach visits (from ~5,000 to ~10,000); marketed as Europe's/the Northern Hemisphere's first artificial surf reef [R1][R3][R4].
Size~55 geotextile containers, each ~2–3 m high and ~60 m long; total sand-fill volume ≈13,000 m³; footprint ≈1 hectare (2.5 acres); positioned 220 m from the seawall base, ~240 m east of the pier [R4][R7]. Rendle's thesis [R17] (primary): 32 containers built in two layers, placed by divers and filled in situ (p. 68); design drawing of Dec 2006 shows about 46 labelled bags, footprint 4,474 m2, bag volume 10,450 m3 + fill 1,750 m3 (Fig. 5.3, p. 95); Table 4.4 design: volume 11,900 m3, footprint 5,450 m2, length 120 m, height 2.8-4.1 m (p. 70); containers up to 67 m long, 100-800 m3 (p. 69); eight T4 containers about 4 m diameter, 65-70 m long, 746.7 m3 each (Table 5.3, p. 98; p. 121) [R17]. Counts differ between sources (32 / about 46 / 54-55) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) give 12,800 m3 [R18] (the designers' value; Blacka Table 4.4 cost/rate implies about 12,760 m3 [R19]); volume sources therefore disagree: about 13,000 [R4][R7] / 11,900 or 12,200 (Rendle design) / 12,800 [R18], all kept. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.66): footprint 80 m (longshore) x 90 m (cross-shore), depth 3-5 m, 225 m offshore, submergence 0.5 m, tide range 1.8 m, T~4 s, H~0.5 m (Table 4.3) [R19]; the card's 120 m length is Rendle's design figure, so footprint figures differ by source. Project-traced outline (not a source statement): reef plan area 4,042 m2, minimum rotated rectangle 121.1 x 45.0 m, about 220-225 m offshore, west edge 242 m east of the pier head, traced on the Esri Wayback image of 2011-09-28 and checked against the April 2011 survey figure [R22][R21]. The '1 hectare' of [R4]/Wikipedia is therefore not the plan area of the reef body (4,042 m2); the basis of the 1 ha figure is not stated by those sources (not reconciled).
Cost£3–3.2 million actually spent on the reef structure itself, against an original 1999–2003-era estimate of £1.4 million; the wider Boscombe seafront/pier regeneration scheme (reef + pier refurbishment + seafront) totalled ≈£11 million [R1][R2]. One New Zealand outlet states the cost as "more than NZD $6 million," over a year behind schedule — not corroborated by any UK source [R8]. Rendle (2016, p. 65-67): original GBP 600,000 (Black et al. 2000), GBP 1.1 m (ASR Ltd 2006, incl. 20 % contingency), final about GBP 3.2 m; repairs and marine-park works a further GBP 700,000 (funded partly by GBP 306,531 insurance and a GBP 254,000 Coastal Communities Fund grant, p. 64); Weight (2000) estimate GBP 618,000 for two reefs (Table 4.3, p. 66) [R17]. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.4): about A$4.9 M in 2013 dollars, A$384 per m3 [R19]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) note the contract was fixed-price, so claimed overruns concern delays rather than contract cost [R18]; this can sit beside the early-estimate comparison above.
Cost (approx. USD)£3.2M ≈ US $5.1M at 2009 average GBP/USD rates (~1.59); NZD $6M ≈ US $4.2M at 2010 average NZD/USD rates (~0.70) — rough conversions, not sourced from any single article [R1][R2][R8]. ASSUMPTION: the exchange rates (GBP/USD ~1.59, NZD/USD ~0.70) are unsourced estimates of this project (not confirmed against a rate table); order of magnitude only.
Financed byBournemouth Borough Council, funded via sale of a car park (on which Barratt Developments built the Honeycombe Chine Flats) and sale of beach "pods" as part of the Overstrand seafront building [R1][R4].
DesignerDr Kerry Black (oceanographer, ex-University of Waikato/NIWA, co-founder of ASR Ltd) did the wave-science/concept design; Shaw Mead (ASR co-founder) is credited as design/surf-science lead [R8][R7].
ContractorASR Ltd (Artificial Surf Reefs Ltd), a New Zealand company; managing director Nick Behunin [R1][R4][R6].
Status nowPermanently closed to surfing since 31 March/April 2011 after storm and boat-propeller damage; ASR Ltd went into liquidation September 2012; rebranded and reopened in stages (2014, then 2017) as a "Coastal Activity Park" for diving, snorkelling, windsurfing/kitesurfing and other non-surf water activities; by 2018 described as largely forgotten/neglected; debris from the structure was still washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R1][R3][R4][R8].

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Boscombe was a rundown 20th-century seaside suburb of Bournemouth in need of regeneration; the reef was one plank of a wider council-led seafront renewal that also refurbished Boscombe Pier and built new beachfront "pods" and flats [R1][R10]. A feasibility study was approved in 1999 and detailed plans approved in March 2003, with construction not starting until 2008 [R6][R1]. Financing was structured opportunistically around unrelated seafront property sales rather than a dedicated capital grant [R1][R4].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The reef was designed as a submerged, angled ramp of stacked geotextile sand containers that would intercept the dominant swell direction and reshape it into rideable peeling waves, rather than "creating" waves from nothing [R10]. ASR director Shaw Mead described the mechanism directly: "The reef doesn't actually create waves. It's angled to catch the mean wave direction, and it acts as a ramp which changes the way the waves break" [R10]. The design target was a "Grade 5" wave under good swell conditions, producing rides of roughly 75 m to the right and 35 m to the left, suited to bodyboarders and surfers [R10]. Eleven specific design/performance objectives were set, including materially increasing surf-day frequency (from ~77 to ~154 good surf days/yr) and beach-visit numbers (from ~5,000 to ~10,000/yr) [R1][R2].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The structure eventually installed — 55 sand-filled geotextile bags forming a ~1-hectare submerged mound ~13,000 m³ in volume — matched the general geotube concept, but construction ran roughly a decade behind the original 1999–2003 planning timeline and cost more than double the original £1.4 million estimate, landing at £3–3.2 million for the reef alone [R1][R2][R6]. Construction was repeatedly delayed and beset by "setbacks during building works" before the reef finally opened in November 2009 [R1]. Shaw Mead later blamed the outcome on "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions," distancing his own design/surf-science role from those problems [R8]. Rendle (2016): built crest about +0.5 m chart datum against a design crest of 0 m CD (Table 4.4; 0.3 m CD on the Dec 2006 drawing), so the crest is higher than planned (p. 70); not all containers were filled to capacity and some bags of the plan were missing in the final construction (p. 98, p. 122) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): the reef was built to design under a fixed-price contract and completed in late September 2009 [R18] (designers' view; the card's headline opening date is November 2009 and Rendle 2016 documents shortfalls [R17], so sources disagree). AUDIT NOTE 2026-10-10: 'submerged' holds at high water only; the built crest (+0.5 m CD, about -0.9 m MSL using the project's conversion MSL = CD - 1.40 m, NTSLF offset; Rendle uses 1.66 m, unresolved) is exposed at low tide (Rendle p.70-71) [R17][R20].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: A University of Plymouth interim evaluation (Dr Mark Davidson, published May 2010) found the reef met only 4 of its 11 original design objectives, stating: "The wave length is rather too intense and challenging [and it] is not quite as consistent as it should be" [R1][R2]. This evaluation is credited solely to Dr Mark Davidson in every source found; a claim (raised during a Gemini-survey cross-check) that the evaluation was co-authored by "Reeve" and "Medina" is not confirmed anywhere and is rejected — the only genuine Davidson co-authored paper found online is the separate, later Rendle & Davidson (2012, ICCE Proceedings) study on structural degradation, with a different co-author [R1]. In practice the reef worked best around low tide, with rides largely limited to steep, short sections, mainly ridden by bodyboarders rather than the standup surfers it was marketed to [R1]. A routine inspection in March 2011 found "substantial changes" to the reef's profile; it was closed for safety on 31 March 2011 [R1]. In April 2011 further damage was found, with one geo-container removed and another repaired, apparently after an unidentified boat's propeller struck the reef [R1][R9]. Repairs begun in August 2011 were suspended for winter and never satisfactorily completed [R1][R7]. ASR Ltd went into liquidation in September 2012 (one source: November 2012), owing the council roughly £14,800–£15,000; the council obtained a £306,531 insurance settlement in 2013 [R1][R4][R6]. A 2012 plan to repurpose the site as a dive/snorkel trail was itself abandoned [R5]. The site was rebranded in 2014 and again in 2017 as a "Coastal Activity Park," with surfing dropped as a priority [R1][R6]. Debris from the decaying structure was reported washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Rendle (2016, p. 70-71): Davidson 2010 found 4 of 11 criteria met and 2 partly; rides about 20 m left / 40 m right against 20 m / 65 m designed; surfable only 1-2 h around mid-tide because the crest is exposed at low tide and too deep at high tide; the wave model shows attenuation in the lee (p. 143-144) and the shoreline did not respond, no salient (p. 102) [R17]. SOURCES DISAGREE on the Plymouth evaluation score: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4), reporting the Plymouth University monitoring of May 2010, say the reef met 7 of 11 criteria (7 of the 9 agreed by Council and builders) and that media mis-reported '4 out of 10' [R18]; Rendle (2016, p.70-71) gives 4 of 11 met and 2 partly [R17]. The authors of [R18] designed the reef (interested party); Davidson (2010) must be checked directly. Both kept. Shoreline: Blacka et al. (2013, p.70) report no noticeable long-term change of the 0 m shoreline (Rendle & Davidson 2012); design accretion was predicted mostly near the -1 m contour (K. Black pers. comm.), which Rendle & Davidson did not report; inshore scour and steepening were well predicted; rated surfing 'partially', protection 'minor' [R19].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Shaw Mead's own later analysis concluded sand-filled geotextile bags were a structural dead end: "the sandbags were an evolutionary dead-end," and "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" — a design fundamentally vulnerable to point-impact damage [R8][R9]. The proximate damage cause was a boat-propeller strike, a mechanism Geosynthetics Magazine groups with damage at other ASR reefs elsewhere (anchor damage at Gold Coast, debris strikes at Kovalam, over-filling at Mount Maunganui) as evidence of a general geotextile-reef vulnerability pattern [R9]. Even before the propeller strike, the University of Plymouth's Davidson evaluation had already found the reef meeting only 4 of 11 design objectives, indicating the wave-shaping design itself, not only later physical damage, fell short [R1][R2]. Shaw Mead's own explanation for the broader project's failure also emphasises non-engineering causes — "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions" during a near-decade gap between 2003 planning approval and 2008 construction start [R8][R6][R1]. Rendle (2016): after winter 2009-10 sand moved inside the bags (seaward to landward, p. 94); a T4 container (746.7 m3) lost its sand in 2011 (cause contested: weak container, propeller strike or vandalism) and a second in 2012, together 1,493.4 m3 = 12.5 % of 11,900 m3 (Table 5.3, p. 98), gaps of 5 m then 8-10 m, 2 m crest dip; construction shortcuts (wrong grain size supplied, weather, end-of-summer deadline, p. 98); first inspection found poorly repaired tears (p. 120) [R17]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4-5): 17 bathymetry surveys and 3 beach-profile surveys; beach accreted up to 60 m over >500 m within 6 months; about 60 hardwood groynes in Poole Bay (roughly every 180 m) and renourishment every 10-12 years, so the beach response sits within a managed shoreline [R18].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The project drew media coverage in an estimated 60 countries around its 2009 opening, and local Boscombe hospitality businesses reported a real economic uplift regardless of the reef's technical shortcomings [R2]. Some media coverage carried headlines setting expectations the reef's actual short, steep, low-tide-only wave could not meet [R9]. The site was closed in 2011 over safety concerns involving hazardous undercurrents and gaps in the deteriorating structure, serious enough that local surfer/photographer Chris Skone-Roberts warned "it is just a question of time before someone dies" [R2]. Loose material and debris from the decaying geotextile bags continued washing ashore for years after closure, documented as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Dolphins were reported investigating the new structure shortly after construction, an unplanned/unmeasured ecological footnote [R10].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Shaw Mead (ASR co-designer) concluded the material choice itself was wrong — sand-filled geotextile bags are "an evolutionary dead-end" for a structure that must survive years of surf-zone wave energy and occasional impacts — and moved ASR's subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to rock construction instead [R8]. Geosynthetics Magazine's review implies the fix is structural redundancy: a single ruptured bag should not be able to reshape the whole reef, pointing toward either more failure-tolerant bag engineering or abandoning fabric containers for point-impact-prone sites like a boat channel [R9]. The University of Plymouth's own evaluation implies the wave-shaping geometry needed further hydrodynamic refinement even independent of material failure, since only 4 of 11 objectives were met while the structure was still intact [R1][R2]. Local critics, including councillor Ben Grower, framed the entire project as a governance and money failure rather than a fixable engineering detail [R2][R5]. Rendle's lessons (p. 121-122): compare real seabed level with the design before building, no bags missing from the final build, seal the fill ports, the +0.5 m higher crest added stress, avoid geotextile in an exposed shallow surf zone [R17].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Boscombe's tidal range is modest by UK Atlantic-coast standards (same-day check showed roughly 0.9–1.1 m high-to-low, illustrative only) [R12]; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is effectively micro-tidal, though no sourced numeric tidal-range figure for Haifa was found in this research [R14]. What transfers directly: Boscombe's central lesson is that geotextile-sandbag construction is vulnerable to point-impact damage (boat strikes, anchors, debris) and to cascading shape-change once any single bag ruptures, regardless of tidal regime [R8][R9]. Haifa's proposed reef site is assessed against real Shikmona-buoy wave data (significant wave height 0.45–0.8 m in the surfable window, occasional peaks to ~1.2 m), a much gentler wave-energy environment than the UK Channel/Atlantic-influenced south coast that shaped Boscombe's design — meaning less storm-wave loading, but underscoring that any Israeli project should still plan explicitly for boat-strike/anchor exposure in a working coastal-shipping and fishing environment [R14]. Tide levels from the design paper (Mead et al. 2010, Table 1): MHWS +0.81 m and MLWS -0.95 m relative to MSL, i.e. a spring range of 1.76 m [R20] (project conversion from chart datum; the same-day 0.9-1.1 m above is one day only). Haifa wave figures [R14] are Lior's own readings of the IsraMar Shikmona buoy, not a published source.

footprint.name: Boscombe Surf Reef
footprint.shape_type_notes: A single elongated, asymmetric angled bank/ramp ("the reef doesn't create waves...it acts as a ramp", R10) built from parallel geotextile tubes -- not a multi-armed chevron, V, or triangular delta. The already-verified aerial photo (raisedwaterresearch.com 'Boscombe-Arial') shows one coherent dark parallelogram-shaped patch with internal parallel stripes (individual container tubes), not two separate arms meeting at an apex.
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point directly onshore of the reef's photo-measured centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward east, i.e. toward Bournemouth Pier direction / away from Boscombe Pier, matching the card's '~240 m east of the pier' framing); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0.

bbox_m.note: extent of the traced outline (shape.json canonical), alongshore x offshore

crest_depth_m.datum: metres ABOVE Lowest Astronomical Tide / spring low water datum (positive = emergent, i.e. the reef's designed crest sits above this level after sand settlement, not below it). Sign convention clarified 2026-09-25 (was stored as -0.5 with an inverted-sign explanation, which was confusing to compare against Gemini's differently-signed convention); the underlying fact is unchanged.

footprint.orientation_notes: Long axis trends WSW-ENE: the deeper/offshore end sits to the WSW (photo-measured bearing of the offshore-pointing axis is roughly 245-250 deg), the shallower/nearshore end to the ENE. This is broadly consistent with the design intent stated in R10 -- 'It's angled to catch the mean wave direction' for the dominant SSW-SW Channel swell (approx. 200-230 deg per the master comparative table Gemini also uses) -- though our photo-derived bearing (~247 deg) sits a little west of that swell window's centre; no source gives an exact design bearing figure, so this is a medium/low-confidence photo estimate, not a stated design number. The reef also produces an asymmetric wave (long right / short left, R2/R10), consistent with an asymmetric plan shape, but the photo resolution was not sufficient to confirm a sharper 'peeling corner' at one end versus a simple tapered rectangle.
footprint.materials: ~55 large sand-filled geotextile containers ('geobags'), each reported as approx. 2-3 m high x 60 m long (R7); one later source instead describes '56 sandbags between 50 and 70 metres long' built 'in two layers', with 'the biggest sandbags 2.5m high and 5m wide' (R10) -- bag-count/size figures conflict across sources and are treated as approximate, not reconciled here.

footprint.confidence: The bag field is clearly visible on a geo-referenced 2011 satellite image and its outline matches an April 2011 survey and the designers' own plan, so shape and position are well supported. But its area (0.40 ha) is only 40% of the roughly 1 hectare quoted by Wikipedia, Raised Water Research and a 2017 journal paper, and the rating scale asks for agreement within about 10%, so it is rated medium; the 13,000 m3 of sand fits 0.4-0.5 ha, which suggests the 1 ha figure is a loose envelope, but no source defines it.
open_issues: No single authoritative engineering plan-view drawing or bathymetric survey of Boscombe Surf Reef could be located online (search engines used for this pass returned CAPTCHA walls; only already-cited pages and their linked images/figures were consulted, per task rules). The 'Diagram showing layout of the geotextile bags' on Wikipedia is a simplified cartoon, not a scaled drawing.
The reef's overall plan-view length (this file's 187.5 m) is a photo-based estimate, not a text-sourced figure; treat it as medium-low confidence pending a real design drawing or survey.

Container/bag count and size are inconsistent across sources: R7 says '55 containers, 2-3 m high, 60 m long, ~1,000 t total'; R10 says '56 sandbags, 50-70 m long, in two layers, biggest bags 2.5 m high x 5 m wide'. Neither this file nor the card resolves the discrepancy.

Area is reported two ways in real sources: 'one hectare / 2.5 acres' (R1, R4 -- used here) vs. 'the area of a football pitch' (R10, which at a standard pitch size, ~7,140 m2, is notably smaller). Not reconciled; the hectare figure was preferred because two independent sources agree on it and it is corroborated by our own photo measurement.

The photo-derived long-axis bearing (~245-250 deg) assumes the aerial photo is close to north-up, inferred only from the pier's visible orientation and general knowledge of the Bournemouth coastline, not from an EXIF heading or map overlay -- treat the bearing as approximate.

Individual-image measurement was done on a single relatively low-resolution, refraction-blurred aerial photo; a second/higher-resolution aerial or satellite image (e.g. Google Maps/Earth imagery of the same site) would meaningfully tighten these estimates but was not pursued here to stay within the task's 'no new photo searches' rule (Google Maps was only listed as a card image lead, not fetched as a new search).

name: Kovalam Reef (Lighthouse Beach)
year: As-built: December 2009 - February 2010 [R1][R10]; one source gives April 2010 instead [R3] - unresolved. (An earlier, differently-scoped version was proposed in 2005 but not built then [R5].)
type: Non-woven geotextile sand-filled containers ("Geotubes"/bags), built in ~30 m-long units [R1][R2][R10]
purpose: Primary: coastal-erosion protection (monsoon wave energy) [R1][R10]. Secondary: surfing/tourism amenity and ecological benefit [R1][R5][R10]
size: As-built total volume 4,800 m3, increased from an initial 3,000 m3 plan, shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand wave [R1][R10]. Crest/submergence depth: not found Sources disagree on volume: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) give 4,000 m3 [R13]; Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.4) give A$1.41 M (2013) at A$351 per m3, which implies about 4,017 m3 [R14]; the card's 4,800 m3 comes from [R1][R10]. Unresolved (3,000 initial / 4,000 [R13] / 4,300 [R15] / 4,800 [R1][R10]). Rendle (2016, PhD thesis, Table 2.1, printed p.41 = PDF p.41, held in papers/) lists "Kovalum", 2010, Kerala, India, 4,300 m3 of sand-filled containers (SFC), with 1,640,321 in the table's first cost column (currency header not checked; added 2026-10-13) [R15]. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2, report p.66) list a geotextile-container reef 65 m longshore x 85 m cross-shore, depth 1.3-3.7 m, 90 m offshore, submergence 0.2-3.4 m (a range; datum not stated; no nourishment) [R14]; site: tide range about 1.0 m, wave period 11-15 s, H 1-2.5 m (Table 4.3, p.68) [R14]. Shape model (this project's own trace, 07_scale/shapes/kovalam-reef-india/HANDOFF.md section 3, LOW confidence; Blacka et al. 2013 Fig 4.5 [R14]): the footprint was traced from one oblique, unscaled ASR aerial photo (registry img-07 = Blacka 2013 Fig 4.5) placed on the Esri 2011-02-28 frame with a fitted camera; the camera height is assumed (default 60 m; alternates 35 and 80 m). Default outline 59 x 41 m, 1,216 m2 (range 546-1,681 m2): measurements of this project's trace, shape.json canonical / HANDOFF.md section 3 (derived, not a source statement). The traced cross-shore size is 52 % below the 85 m of Blacka Table 4.2 [R14] (DERIVED: (85-41)/85); 4,000 m3 [R13] over 1,216 m2 would be a mean height of 3.3 m (DERIVED: 4,000/1,216), so the real footprint is probably larger (inference of this project, HANDOFF.md section 5). The card keeps the published text values and does not use the traced numbers. Open mismatch inside this project's own trace files (noted 2026-10-13, not resolved): the smallest-scale version (camera 35 m, area 640 m2) has bounding box 43 x 24 m in shape.json (outline_versions photo_trace_H35, HANDOFF.md 3.1; recomputed from its polygon vertices: x -77.0 to -34.3 = 42.7 m, y 58.5 to 82.6 = 24.1 m in the canonical frame, x along the swash line, bearing 196 deg) but 38 x 29 m (along_m, cross_m for H = 35) in rectify_result.json; both are max-minus-min extents (rectify_fit.py line 64, build_shape_json.py line 38) of the same shape, areas agree (640 / 641.5 m2), so the difference is most likely the axes used (the frame of the sweep script was not checked); SOURCE_AUDIT_2026-10-10.md row 10. Both are derived from this project's own trace, not source statements.
cost: As-built: Rs 75,000,000 [R1][R10] Audit 2026-10-10: the earlier cost_usd_approx of 1,100,000 was an unsourced conversion (it corresponded to about Rs 68/US$) and was CORRECTED in the citations audit of 2026-10-10 to 1,580,000 = Rs 75,000,000 / 47.44 Rs per US$, the average rupee rate for financial year 2009-10 (RBI series as republished in the MoSPI dataset, found by web search 2026-10-10: https://dataful.in/datasets/586; the RBI table itself was not opened; RBI daily reference rates of 27 Apr 2010 Rs 44.45 and 15 Jun 2010 Rs 46.73 bracket it, https://website.rbi.org.in press releases 'RBI Reference Rate for US $ and Euro'). Range with those daily rates: US$1.6-1.7 M. DERIVED value, rate secondary (unconfirmed at the RBI table); the rupee figure [R1][R10] is the sourced one.
financed_by: India's Tsunami Rehabilitation Project, under the Planning Commission, Government of India [R1][R10]. (The 2005 proposal predating this funding was to be jointly implemented by Kerala Tourism, the Centre for Earth Science Studies (CESS), and the Department of Harbour Engineering [R5].)
motivation: Kerala Tourism pushed the idea as early as 2005, citing tourist safety, boosting water-sports tourism, monsoon-season erosion prevention, beach widening, and fishing-community benefit [R5]. The project actually built several years later was funded through post-tsunami rehabilitation money and engaged international specialist firm ASR Ltd rather than the original state team [R1][R5][R10]
designer: ASR Ltd (New Zealand-based multi-purpose/surf-reef design-and-build firm), project leads Chris Jensen and Nick Behunin [R1]
contractor: Not separately named beyond ASR Ltd in the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement)
status_now: Reported non-functional: containers torn, deflated, and sunk such that "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" [R1]. No formal removal documented; reef instead degraded in place [R1]. A separate, later (2021) Rs 8.35 crore erosion-protection/walkway project addressed "recurring" erosion at Kovalam's Samudra, Sea Rock, and Lighthouse beaches, not confirmed as a direct repair/successor [R6]. Kerala tourism-marketing pages currently advertise an "Artificial Off Shore Coral Reef" attraction at Kovalam, claimed to reduce erosion and support marine life; its identity/relationship to the 2009-10 ASR structure could not be confirmed [R9] Decision: verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source, because early reports were positive (Collins 2010 [R3], SURFER 2010 [R4], reef monitoring beach-width gains [R1][R13]) while later sources report the structure non-functional [R1][R2]; Blacka et al. (2013) still rated both objectives 'Yes' but preliminary [R14]. Counter-view: if the 2010-11 failure reports [R1] are taken at face value the verdict would be 'failed'.
hover_text: A 4,800 m3 geotextile-bag reef built 2009-10 for ~Rs 75M (~US$1.6M) under India's post-tsunami rehabilitation fund; it briefly produced praised 7-10s rides and reportedly widened the beach, but containers began tearing within weeks and by 2010-11 the sunken structure no longer broke waves at all [R1][R10].
design_as_planned: Two distinct designs exist from two project phases. 2005 proposal (not built as such): a 500 m-long submerged structure ~200 m offshore at Eve's Beach, 3-7 m water depth, non-woven geotextile bags filled with sand, engineered to block waves over 1 m and include a "tranquil basin" for fishing-boat movement while preserving the ecosystem [R5]; protection-first, closer to a detached breakwater/lagoon system. As-built ASR Ltd design (2009-10): a smaller, more surf-focused structure - 30 m geotextile bag units totalling 4,800 m3 (up from an initial 3,000 m3 plan), shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand surfable wave at Lighthouse Beach, promising "lefts that provided 7-10 second rides," "fun and open faced," with "occasional head dip opportunity" [R1][R10]. Coastal protection remained the primary stated purpose, with surf/ecology secondary [R1][R10]. No EIA/SIA/FIA was required before construction of the as-built reef [R1]
as_built_vs_design: Location shifted from the 2005 plan's Eve's/Hawah Beach to Lighthouse Beach [R1][R5][R10]. Scale shrank from a 500 m/200 m-offshore/3-7 m-deep structure [R5] to 4,800 m3 of material in 30 m units producing a 100 m wave [R1][R10], though no single directly comparable dimension confirms by how much the footprint shrank. The as-built project itself grew from an initial 3,000 m3 plan to 4,800 m3 during construction, a ~60% increase with no source explaining why [R1][R10]. Cost rose from the 2005 estimate of Rs 40.5M to the as-built Rs 75M (~US$1.1M), roughly 85% higher, though the two figures describe different-scope projects years apart [R1][R5][R10]. Design authority shifted from a Kerala Tourism/CESS/Harbour-Engineering effort to international firm ASR Ltd [R1][R5][R10]
outcome: Initial surfing quality was described positively - 7-10 second-ride lefts, "fun and open faced" - per the reef's own before/after monitoring [R1]. Surf journalist Sean Collins, in a piece dated 29 April 2010 (reposted on surfingindia.net), called the wave potentially "the best wave an artificial reef has ever created," possibly able to "host an ASP World Tour event" [R3]. This sits awkwardly against the failure timeline: Raised Water Research and an industry comparison site both state containers began tearing and washing ashore "less than two weeks" after inauguration, with the reef sinking so that by 2010-11 "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" (Jelle Rigole quote) [R1][R10]. A separate, unsigned Surfer.com piece of 6 May 2010 similarly quoted ASR Ltd's Chris Jensen, India Surf Club's Daruka Dasa, and an unnamed Kovalam Surf Club member, all positive about the reef in its first months [R4]. Sources found do not resolve this contradiction between contemporaneous positive surf-media coverage and rapid-failure accounts. Coastal protection: the reef's own monitoring showed the beach "remained wider" in both monsoon and non-monsoon seasons after installation, but this appears to describe only the initial period before structural failure [R1]. Ecology/fishing: local fishermen reported recovering "damaged portions of the artificial reef rather than more fish," the opposite of the project's stated fish-attraction goal [R1][R5] Mead & Borrero (2011), the reef's designers (interested party): weekly photo monitoring from the lighthouse platform showed the beach 10-15 m wider in the monsoon and up to 30 m wider in the non-monsoon season than before the reef (p.5, Fig. 7) [R13]. They say surfing worked because the lighthouse end was already an 'almost' break, swells were clean with light winds in the non-monsoon season, and the container orientation allowed relaxed construction tolerances; completed late February 2010; adopted by the Indian Surfing Association (p.4) [R13]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.70): the only multi-purpose reef with a significant positive shoreline effect so far (under 3 years monitored); both objectives rated 'Yes' but preliminary (Table 4.1); the Centre for Earth Science Studies assessment was pending; unpublished observations (E. Rendle, pers. comm. 2013) say damage to the reef now hampers its protective effect [R14].
why_worked_or_failed: Why it failed: an industry comparison source attributes Kovalam's container failures specifically to "debris strikes" [R2]. Coastal engineer Shaw Mead explains the underlying mechanism generally: "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" [R2] - a single puncture cascading into total reshaping. Once containers deflated, the structure sank deeper into the seabed, pushing its crest below the depth needed to break waves at all [R1]. No EIA, SIA, or FIA was required before construction [R1], meaning potential fisheries/community impacts were not formally assessed in advance. The task brief's own seed facts describe the failure as caused by "debris strikes/vandalism"; sources fetched confirm "debris strikes" [R2] but did not corroborate vandalism or intentional damage - unreferenced, needs source. Why the design promised what it did: the 100 m left-hand wave and multi-second ride times reflect a deliberate ASR Ltd wave-shaping design distinct from the more general, protection-first 2005 proposal [R1]
unexpected_results: Fishermen retrieving reef wreckage instead of catching more fish, a direct reversal of the project's stated fishing-community goal [R1][R5]. As surf and coastal-protection improvements visibly disappeared through 2010-2011, "coastal communities and civil society of Kerala demanded a judicial and scientific enquiry and social audit" [R1] - sources do not confirm whether any inquiry was actually convened. The coexistence of enthusiastic international surf-media accounts (Collins, R3; the separate Surfer.com piece, R4) with rapid-failure accounts from other sources [R1][R2][R10] suggests the story reaching international surf media diverged sharply from what was reportedly happening on the ground within the same window. Separately, India's broader 2023-announced national artificial-reef rollout (3,477 target fishing villages, ~937 approved as of Sept 2024, ~US$34.5M total) has drawn criticism over net entanglement, "ghost fishing," and erosion risk from poorly sited structures - echoing some of Kovalam's own failure modes [R8]
could_be_better: Shaw Mead's general point - that geotextile-bag reefs are fragile as a system, since a single puncture cascades into total reshaping - implies the core lesson is that this material/technology is inherently high-risk for exposed, high-energy, or debris-prone sites [R2]. The absence of an EIA/SIA/FIA before construction is flagged by Raised Water Research as notable; a proper impact assessment could plausibly have surfaced fisheries and community concerns before construction rather than after failure [R1]. The scale/scope mismatch between the 2005 proposal (500 m, protection-first, 3-7 m depth) and the eventual 100 m surf-focused build is not explicitly critiqued by any source found, but a structure re-scoped from a broad coastal-defence design to a narrower, surf-tuned design may have traded protective robustness for wave-shaping performance - this is this dossier's own inference, not a sourced expert claim [R5][R1][R10]
relevance_to_israel: No verified, sourced tide-range figure for Kovalam/Kerala was found in the sources listed in References, apart from Blacka's 'about 1.0 m' [R14]; the qualitative statement that Kerala's Arabian Sea coast is a mixed, mesotidal-to-microtidal regime versus the microtidal Mediterranean at Haifa is the card author's own and is (unsourced). Kovalam faces monsoon-driven swell seasons (beach 10-15 m wider in the monsoon, up to 30 m in the non-monsoon months [R13]; H 1-2.5 m, T 11-15 s [R14]), a materially higher and more seasonal wave-energy environment than Israel's Mediterranean coast (the comparison with Israel is the card author's inference, unsourced), relevant to why a transplanted geotextile-bag design might face structural loads and debris-strike risks not directly comparable to a Haifa site. Transferable lessons: (1) geotextile-bag reefs are reported across multiple sites (Kovalam, Boscombe, Mount Reef, Opunake) as prone to single-point-of-failure cascading damage once any one container is breached [R2] - relevant to any Haifa proposal considering the same Geotube technology already used at Ashkelon (per this project's own source note, 01_source_notes/jmse2023_bar_drimer_paper.md, which does not itself cover Kovalam); (2) the value of requiring an impact assessment (EIA/SIA/FIA) before construction, which Kovalam skipped [R1]; (3) the risk of scope/design drift between an original protection-first proposal and an eventual, differently-scoped as-built structure, as documented here between the 2005 and 2009-10 Kovalam designs [R5][R1][R10]

reviews.role: Founder of a local surf club
reviews.quote_or_summary: In the beginning, it was great. But after the first monsoon season, some of the bags that composed the reef came loose. The reef sank deeper into the sand so most of the waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking.

The wave could very well be the best wave an artificial reef has ever created and on the right swell, could even possibly host an ASP World Tour event; also called large-scale coastal-defence spending a gigantic bandaid that siphons millions of dollars from the economy on a regular cycle.
As soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand.
Reported recovering damaged portions of the artificial reef rather than more fish from their nets.

reviews.who: Coastal communities and civil society of Kerala (collectively described)
reviews.quote_or_summary: Demanded a judicial and scientific enquiry and social audit as the reef's benefits visibly disappeared through 2010-2011.

Most importantly, the reef in India was designed to stabilize the beach... We then deployed monitoring instruments at the proposed site of the reef to get detailed data in order to design the reef to optimize the recreational component (surfing, fishing, diving).

We haven't visited Kovalam since they had the new reef built, but we plan to in the upcoming months (pre and post monsoon seasons)... It's also a great thing for Kovalam in helping them prevent coastal erosion. They were really starting to run out of beach.

Unfortunately, this year we had less surfable days because the reef only starts to work when the swell is above 3 feet, but when it works it throws up a sucking barrel. When it goes off Kovalam now offers a good quality reefbreak and the level of the kids grows gradually with every surf session.
