sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameKovalam Reef (Lighthouse Beach)
PlaceKovalam, Kerala
CountryIndia
YearAs-built: December 2009 - February 2010 [R1][R10]; one source gives April 2010 instead [R3] - unresolved. (An earlier, differently-scoped version was proposed in 2005 but not built then [R5].)
TypeNon-woven geotextile sand-filled containers ("Geotubes"/bags), built in ~30 m-long units [R1][R2][R10]
PurposePrimary: coastal-erosion protection (monsoon wave energy) [R1][R10]. Secondary: surfing/tourism amenity and ecological benefit [R1][R5][R10]
SizeAs-built total volume 4,800 m3, increased from an initial 3,000 m3 plan, shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand wave [R1][R10]. Crest/submergence depth: not found Sources disagree on volume: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4) give 4,000 m3 [R13]; Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.4) give A$1.41 M (2013) at A$351 per m3, which implies about 4,017 m3 [R14]; the card's 4,800 m3 comes from [R1][R10]. Unresolved (3,000 initial / 4,000 [R13] / 4,300 [R15] / 4,800 [R1][R10]). Rendle (2016, PhD thesis, Table 2.1, printed p.41 = PDF p.41, held in papers/) lists "Kovalum", 2010, Kerala, India, 4,300 m3 of sand-filled containers (SFC), with 1,640,321 in the table's first cost column (currency header not checked; added 2026-10-13) [R15]. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2, report p.66) list a geotextile-container reef 65 m longshore x 85 m cross-shore, depth 1.3-3.7 m, 90 m offshore, submergence 0.2-3.4 m (a range; datum not stated; no nourishment) [R14]; site: tide range about 1.0 m, wave period 11-15 s, H 1-2.5 m (Table 4.3, p.68) [R14]. Shape model (this project's own trace, 07_scale/shapes/kovalam-reef-india/HANDOFF.md section 3, LOW confidence; Blacka et al. 2013 Fig 4.5 [R14]): the footprint was traced from one oblique, unscaled ASR aerial photo (registry img-07 = Blacka 2013 Fig 4.5) placed on the Esri 2011-02-28 frame with a fitted camera; the camera height is assumed (default 60 m; alternates 35 and 80 m). Default outline 59 x 41 m, 1,216 m2 (range 546-1,681 m2): measurements of this project's trace, shape.json canonical / HANDOFF.md section 3 (derived, not a source statement). The traced cross-shore size is 52 % below the 85 m of Blacka Table 4.2 [R14] (DERIVED: (85-41)/85); 4,000 m3 [R13] over 1,216 m2 would be a mean height of 3.3 m (DERIVED: 4,000/1,216), so the real footprint is probably larger (inference of this project, HANDOFF.md section 5). The card keeps the published text values and does not use the traced numbers. Open mismatch inside this project's own trace files (noted 2026-10-13, not resolved): the smallest-scale version (camera 35 m, area 640 m2) has bounding box 43 x 24 m in shape.json (outline_versions photo_trace_H35, HANDOFF.md 3.1; recomputed from its polygon vertices: x -77.0 to -34.3 = 42.7 m, y 58.5 to 82.6 = 24.1 m in the canonical frame, x along the swash line, bearing 196 deg) but 38 x 29 m (along_m, cross_m for H = 35) in rectify_result.json; both are max-minus-min extents (rectify_fit.py line 64, build_shape_json.py line 38) of the same shape, areas agree (640 / 641.5 m2), so the difference is most likely the axes used (the frame of the sweep script was not checked); SOURCE_AUDIT_2026-10-10.md row 10. Both are derived from this project's own trace, not source statements.
CostAs-built: Rs 75,000,000 [R1][R10] Audit 2026-10-10: the earlier cost_usd_approx of 1,100,000 was an unsourced conversion (it corresponded to about Rs 68/US$) and was CORRECTED in the citations audit of 2026-10-10 to 1,580,000 = Rs 75,000,000 / 47.44 Rs per US$, the average rupee rate for financial year 2009-10 (RBI series as republished in the MoSPI dataset, found by web search 2026-10-10: https://dataful.in/datasets/586; the RBI table itself was not opened; RBI daily reference rates of 27 Apr 2010 Rs 44.45 and 15 Jun 2010 Rs 46.73 bracket it, https://website.rbi.org.in press releases 'RBI Reference Rate for US $ and Euro'). Range with those daily rates: US$1.6-1.7 M. DERIVED value, rate secondary (unconfirmed at the RBI table); the rupee figure [R1][R10] is the sourced one.
Cost (approx. USD)1580000
Financed byIndia's Tsunami Rehabilitation Project, under the Planning Commission, Government of India [R1][R10]. (The 2005 proposal predating this funding was to be jointly implemented by Kerala Tourism, the Centre for Earth Science Studies (CESS), and the Department of Harbour Engineering [R5].)
DesignerASR Ltd (New Zealand-based multi-purpose/surf-reef design-and-build firm), project leads Chris Jensen and Nick Behunin [R1]
ContractorNot separately named beyond ASR Ltd in the sources listed in References (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement)
Status nowReported non-functional: containers torn, deflated, and sunk such that "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" [R1]. No formal removal documented; reef instead degraded in place [R1]. A separate, later (2021) Rs 8.35 crore erosion-protection/walkway project addressed "recurring" erosion at Kovalam's Samudra, Sea Rock, and Lighthouse beaches, not confirmed as a direct repair/successor [R6]. Kerala tourism-marketing pages currently advertise an "Artificial Off Shore Coral Reef" attraction at Kovalam, claimed to reduce erosion and support marine life; its identity/relationship to the 2009-10 ASR structure could not be confirmed [R9] Decision: verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source, because early reports were positive (Collins 2010 [R3], SURFER 2010 [R4], reef monitoring beach-width gains [R1][R13]) while later sources report the structure non-functional [R1][R2]; Blacka et al. (2013) still rated both objectives 'Yes' but preliminary [R14]. Counter-view: if the 2010-11 failure reports [R1] are taken at face value the verdict would be 'failed'.
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Kerala Tourism pushed the idea as early as 2005, citing tourist safety, boosting water-sports tourism, monsoon-season erosion prevention, beach widening, and fishing-community benefit [R5]. The project actually built several years later was funded through post-tsunami rehabilitation money and engaged international specialist firm ASR Ltd rather than the original state team [R1][R5][R10]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: Two distinct designs exist from two project phases. 2005 proposal (not built as such): a 500 m-long submerged structure ~200 m offshore at Eve's Beach, 3-7 m water depth, non-woven geotextile bags filled with sand, engineered to block waves over 1 m and include a "tranquil basin" for fishing-boat movement while preserving the ecosystem [R5]; protection-first, closer to a detached breakwater/lagoon system. As-built ASR Ltd design (2009-10): a smaller, more surf-focused structure - 30 m geotextile bag units totalling 4,800 m3 (up from an initial 3,000 m3 plan), shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand surfable wave at Lighthouse Beach, promising "lefts that provided 7-10 second rides," "fun and open faced," with "occasional head dip opportunity" [R1][R10]. Coastal protection remained the primary stated purpose, with surf/ecology secondary [R1][R10]. No EIA/SIA/FIA was required before construction of the as-built reef [R1]

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Location shifted from the 2005 plan's Eve's/Hawah Beach to Lighthouse Beach [R1][R5][R10]. Scale shrank from a 500 m/200 m-offshore/3-7 m-deep structure [R5] to 4,800 m3 of material in 30 m units producing a 100 m wave [R1][R10], though no single directly comparable dimension confirms by how much the footprint shrank. The as-built project itself grew from an initial 3,000 m3 plan to 4,800 m3 during construction, a ~60% increase with no source explaining why [R1][R10]. Cost rose from the 2005 estimate of Rs 40.5M to the as-built Rs 75M (~US$1.1M), roughly 85% higher, though the two figures describe different-scope projects years apart [R1][R5][R10]. Design authority shifted from a Kerala Tourism/CESS/Harbour-Engineering effort to international firm ASR Ltd [R1][R5][R10]

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Initial surfing quality was described positively - 7-10 second-ride lefts, "fun and open faced" - per the reef's own before/after monitoring [R1]. Surf journalist Sean Collins, in a piece dated 29 April 2010 (reposted on surfingindia.net), called the wave potentially "the best wave an artificial reef has ever created," possibly able to "host an ASP World Tour event" [R3]. This sits awkwardly against the failure timeline: Raised Water Research and an industry comparison site both state containers began tearing and washing ashore "less than two weeks" after inauguration, with the reef sinking so that by 2010-11 "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" (Jelle Rigole quote) [R1][R10]. A separate, unsigned Surfer.com piece of 6 May 2010 similarly quoted ASR Ltd's Chris Jensen, India Surf Club's Daruka Dasa, and an unnamed Kovalam Surf Club member, all positive about the reef in its first months [R4]. Sources found do not resolve this contradiction between contemporaneous positive surf-media coverage and rapid-failure accounts. Coastal protection: the reef's own monitoring showed the beach "remained wider" in both monsoon and non-monsoon seasons after installation, but this appears to describe only the initial period before structural failure [R1]. Ecology/fishing: local fishermen reported recovering "damaged portions of the artificial reef rather than more fish," the opposite of the project's stated fish-attraction goal [R1][R5] Mead & Borrero (2011), the reef's designers (interested party): weekly photo monitoring from the lighthouse platform showed the beach 10-15 m wider in the monsoon and up to 30 m wider in the non-monsoon season than before the reef (p.5, Fig. 7) [R13]. They say surfing worked because the lighthouse end was already an 'almost' break, swells were clean with light winds in the non-monsoon season, and the container orientation allowed relaxed construction tolerances; completed late February 2010; adopted by the Indian Surfing Association (p.4) [R13]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.70): the only multi-purpose reef with a significant positive shoreline effect so far (under 3 years monitored); both objectives rated 'Yes' but preliminary (Table 4.1); the Centre for Earth Science Studies assessment was pending; unpublished observations (E. Rendle, pers. comm. 2013) say damage to the reef now hampers its protective effect [R14].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Why it failed: an industry comparison source attributes Kovalam's container failures specifically to "debris strikes" [R2]. Coastal engineer Shaw Mead explains the underlying mechanism generally: "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" [R2] - a single puncture cascading into total reshaping. Once containers deflated, the structure sank deeper into the seabed, pushing its crest below the depth needed to break waves at all [R1]. No EIA, SIA, or FIA was required before construction [R1], meaning potential fisheries/community impacts were not formally assessed in advance. The task brief's own seed facts describe the failure as caused by "debris strikes/vandalism"; sources fetched confirm "debris strikes" [R2] but did not corroborate vandalism or intentional damage - unreferenced, needs source. Why the design promised what it did: the 100 m left-hand wave and multi-second ride times reflect a deliberate ASR Ltd wave-shaping design distinct from the more general, protection-first 2005 proposal [R1]

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Fishermen retrieving reef wreckage instead of catching more fish, a direct reversal of the project's stated fishing-community goal [R1][R5]. As surf and coastal-protection improvements visibly disappeared through 2010-2011, "coastal communities and civil society of Kerala demanded a judicial and scientific enquiry and social audit" [R1] - sources do not confirm whether any inquiry was actually convened. The coexistence of enthusiastic international surf-media accounts (Collins, R3; the separate Surfer.com piece, R4) with rapid-failure accounts from other sources [R1][R2][R10] suggests the story reaching international surf media diverged sharply from what was reportedly happening on the ground within the same window. Separately, India's broader 2023-announced national artificial-reef rollout (3,477 target fishing villages, ~937 approved as of Sept 2024, ~US$34.5M total) has drawn criticism over net entanglement, "ghost fishing," and erosion risk from poorly sited structures - echoing some of Kovalam's own failure modes [R8]

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Shaw Mead's general point - that geotextile-bag reefs are fragile as a system, since a single puncture cascades into total reshaping - implies the core lesson is that this material/technology is inherently high-risk for exposed, high-energy, or debris-prone sites [R2]. The absence of an EIA/SIA/FIA before construction is flagged by Raised Water Research as notable; a proper impact assessment could plausibly have surfaced fisheries and community concerns before construction rather than after failure [R1]. The scale/scope mismatch between the 2005 proposal (500 m, protection-first, 3-7 m depth) and the eventual 100 m surf-focused build is not explicitly critiqued by any source found, but a structure re-scoped from a broad coastal-defence design to a narrower, surf-tuned design may have traded protective robustness for wave-shaping performance - this is this dossier's own inference, not a sourced expert claim [R5][R1][R10]

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: No verified, sourced tide-range figure for Kovalam/Kerala was found in the sources listed in References, apart from Blacka's 'about 1.0 m' [R14]; the qualitative statement that Kerala's Arabian Sea coast is a mixed, mesotidal-to-microtidal regime versus the microtidal Mediterranean at Haifa is the card author's own and is (unsourced). Kovalam faces monsoon-driven swell seasons (beach 10-15 m wider in the monsoon, up to 30 m in the non-monsoon months [R13]; H 1-2.5 m, T 11-15 s [R14]), a materially higher and more seasonal wave-energy environment than Israel's Mediterranean coast (the comparison with Israel is the card author's inference, unsourced), relevant to why a transplanted geotextile-bag design might face structural loads and debris-strike risks not directly comparable to a Haifa site. Transferable lessons: (1) geotextile-bag reefs are reported across multiple sites (Kovalam, Boscombe, Mount Reef, Opunake) as prone to single-point-of-failure cascading damage once any one container is breached [R2] - relevant to any Haifa proposal considering the same Geotube technology already used at Ashkelon (per this project's own source note, 01_source_notes/jmse2023_bar_drimer_paper.md, which does not itself cover Kovalam); (2) the value of requiring an impact assessment (EIA/SIA/FIA) before construction, which Kovalam skipped [R1]; (3) the risk of scope/design drift between an original protection-first proposal and an eventual, differently-scoped as-built structure, as documented here between the 2005 and 2009-10 Kovalam designs [R5][R1][R10]

name: Borth coastal defence reef (incl. Wallog headland)
year: Feasibility study May 2004 [R10][R4]; design from Oct 2009 [R1][R4]; construction started Jan 2011 [R1]; contractor's target completion Nov 2011 [R1][R9]; Coflein gives completion March 2012 [R3]; wider Phase-1 scheme described as 2011-2015 [R6] Blacka et al. (2013, p.70) also state completion in 2012 [R14].
type: Submerged rock (riprap) multi-purpose reef plus rock groynes, breakwaters and beach nourishment [R1][R4]. AUDIT NOTE 2026-10-10: 'submerged' holds only at high water [R16][R18][R19]. Design crest levels (drawings 9V5090/1020-1023 rev C1) are +0.50 mODN for the surf-reef arm (northern 'boot') and +1.50 mODN for the shore-parallel oval, which is a breakwater, not a surf reef [R16]; mean sea level is about +0.31 mODN (mean of the four SMP2 levels MHWS +2.56, MHWN +1.06, MLWN -0.64, MLWS -1.74 mODN; our computation, +-0.15 m) [R18], so the reef-arm crest is about 0.2 m above MSL and the rock is bare at low tide (Esri image of 2024-09-17, rock bare; 2012-10-27, awash) [R19]
purpose: Primary: flood and erosion protection for Borth village, built on a mobile shingle bank whose 1970s timber-groyne defences were failing [R1][R2][R4]. Secondary/amenity: shape the reef so breaking swell also creates a surf wave, because the community explicitly rejected a hard sea wall in favour of keeping an open beach [R1][R2][R4]
size: Reef sited c.400 m offshore per the contractor (2011) [R1] / c.300 m per local/heritage sources (2013 press, Coflein) [R2][R3]; 275,000 t total material moved (84,500 t shingle replacement, 18,500 t Type-3 rock 0.3-1t, 16,200 t Type-1 rock 3-6t, 42,000 t Type-4 rock 6-10t, 500 t Type-6 rock 5-100kg) [R1]; Coflein separately states c.300,000 t of rock for the whole works [R3] SOURCES DISAGREE on distance offshore: contractor c.400 m [R1], local/heritage c.300 m [R2][R3], but Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.66) give 110 m (north reef) and 140 m (south reef), probably measured to the undisturbed shoreline [R14]. Blacka also gives two reefs of rubble mound: north reef 72 m (longshore) x 170 m (cross-shore), south reef 85 m x 45 m (max dims), depth 4.0 m, crest at MSL [R14]. Typical tide range 6.0 m in Blacka Table 4.3 (p.68; term not defined) vs the card's spring range 4.7-4.8 m [R11]; both kept. Project-traced outline (not a published figure): northern mound 144.9 m long, 27.6 m mean width; southern oval 71.8 x 31.0 m; centroid of both mounds 330.5 m offshore (nearest edge 257 m, farthest 397 m), traced from the Esri image of 2024-09-17 [R19]; this differs from Blacka's rectangles (72 x 170 m, 85 x 45 m) [R14], which are maximum dimensions of an unspecified outline; per the shape audit they describe the SUPERSEDED two-reef design (a north truncated delta 180 x 65 m, 4.0 m high, and a south reef), not the final layout traced above (07_scale/shapes/borth-coastal-defence-reef/SOURCE_AUDIT_2026-10-10.md row 29 and HANDOFF.md item 3; the Blacka figures are therefore not comparable with the as-built mounds).
cost: Figures vary by source, not reconciled: Phase 1 funding envelope GBP 7M (FY2009/10-2010/11) [R4]; GBP 13.5M "first phase of the strategy" quoted in 2009 [R1]; BAM Nuttall's winning construction tender GBP 11.5M [R1]; full phased scheme costed at GBP 29M in 2011-2013 press [R1][R2]; Coflein gives completed reef/coastal-defence works at GBP 13M [R3]; Wikipedia gives GBP 12M for the 2011-2015 scheme [R6]
cost_usd_approx: ASSUMPTION (conversion made by this project, not by a source): at the 2013 average of about US$1.56 per GBP (0.6391 GBP per USD, CIA World Factbook via IndexMundi, 2013 value only; other years not confirmed) [R20], GBP 12-13M is about US$19-20M and GBP 29M about US$45M. Corrected 2026-10-10: the earlier text (US$15-17M and US$36M at 'rates of ~1.25-1.6') was unsourced and its low rate end (1.25) is below any 2011-2013 rate; use as order of magnitude only
financed_by: Coast Protection Grant from the Welsh Assembly Government (later Welsh Government) and Convergence funding from the Welsh European Funding Office (WEFO) / European Regional Development Fund [R4][R6]
motivation: Borth sits on a mobile shingle bank in Cardigan Bay; its 1970s timber groyne and breastwork sea defences were judged inadequate, with ordinary storms causing overtopping flooding through homes, per Borth councillor Ray Quant [R2]. A council feasibility study found existing defences within 10 years of failure with potentially catastrophic losses possible, triggering a 150-resident 2001 visioning meeting [R4]. Ceredigion County Council's coast and rivers engineer, Rhodri Llwyd, said the scheme had been 15 years in the making and that the community absolutely didn't want a wall, so the idea of a reef was born [R1][R2]
designer: Royal Haskoning (detailed design, appointed Oct 2009); specialist reef designer ASR (sub-consultant); physical modelling by HR Wallingford; environmental consultant Atkins [R1][R4]. Original feasibility study "Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity" completed May 2004 for Ceredigion County Council (authors not confirmed; ResearchGate record blocked, content corroborated via Borth Community website) [R10][R4]
contractor: BAM Nuttall (site agent Ray Jones); plant from Norton Plant Hire [R1][R4]
status_now: Built and in service; as of December 2011 residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties [R2][R3]. The wider Borth-to-Ynyslas coastal-protection programme was still being planned/phased in later business-case documents, implying more phases beyond the reef itself continued years after Phase 1 (details not found) [R4]
hover_text: A c.300-400 m offshore multi-purpose rock reef plus groynes and beach nourishment, built 2011-2012 for roughly GBP 12-13M (reported up to GBP 29M for the full phased scheme), financed by Welsh Government and EU (WEFO/ERDF) funding; it stopped flooding within months of substantial completion, but years later the surf-industry press still describes Borth only as "a proposed" reef site rather than crediting it with a reliable wave [R1][R2][R3][R7].
design_as_planned: The preferred option, chosen after comparing technical, economic, amenity, environmental and safety criteria, was "Rock Beach Control Structures with a Multi-Purpose Reef and Beach Nourishment" [R4][R10]. Phase 1 combined: a submerged multi-purpose reef near the Craig y Delyn cliffs at the beach's southern end (sited there so the community could keep an open beach and unobstructed views), two rock groynes and two rock breakwaters further along the frontage to retain shingle, and beach nourishment (originally 150,000 m3 of imported shingle) [R1][R4]. Designed to a 1-in-100-year storm standard while remaining adaptable to future climate change [R4]. The reef's role was explicitly dual: reduce wave energy to protect the beach from erosion and broaden the beach inshore, while also being shaped to help swell waves break as a secondary surfing amenity [R1][R2]. The team settled on "Option 9A" for outline design after comparing numerous layouts, with 3D physical wave-basin modelling by HR Wallingford used to size the rock armour [R1]
as_built_vs_design: Construction followed the planned reef/groynes/breakwaters/nourishment layout, but with two contractor-driven, budget-closing changes: the client's design already carried about GBP 1M of cost overrun after physical-model testing showed extra rock was needed, and BAM Nuttall's tender then came in a further GBP 1M over that inflated budget [R1]. BAM Nuttall closed the combined c.GBP 2M gap by (1) mining and reusing the beach's own existing shingle, bulked up with cheaper imported quarried material underneath and the original shingle put back on top, instead of importing the full 150,000 m3 specified, and (2) building a temporary rock causeway out to the reef site so land-based excavators and dumper trucks could be used instead of the originally tendered floating marine plant [R1]. The causeway was intended to be removed once the reef was finished [R9]. Construction ran on a tight tidal window (6am-9pm with a three-hour high-tide stoppage), with over 8,000 material deliveries made by September 2011 [R1][R2]
outcome: Coastal protection: residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties by December 2011, while the works were still substantially under construction [R2][R3]. An unplanned side effect of the earthworks was the exposure of a prehistoric submerged forest (oak, pine, birch, willow and hazel stumps dated to roughly 1500 BCE) tied to the Welsh legend of Cantre'r Gwaelod, now visible at low tide [R6]. Surfing outcome is contested: press coverage at construction time promised the reef would provide excellent surf conditions and boost the local economy [R2], but the Stormrider Surf Guide, years after completion, still describes Borth as merely "a proposed" artificial reef site rather than a functioning named surf break [R7], and Surf-Forecast.com rates Borth's surf quality only 3.0/5 with beginner difficulty and no posted first-hand surfer reviews [R8]. No wave-height, ride-length or surfable-days measurement for the reef was found [R7][R8] Blacka et al. (2013, p.70): performance 'yet to be determined' (completed 2012); protection and surfing rated 'unknown (insufficient monitoring)' (Table 4.1); Fig 4.1 (p.72) shows the reef in June 2012 [R14].
why_worked_or_failed: For coastal protection, the scheme functioned successfully in its early years, withstanding December-2011 storms without flooding the properties it protects within months of substantial completion [R2][R3]. Credited design choices: graded, multi-tonne rock armour (up to 10 t pieces) sized via HR Wallingford's 3D physical modelling before construction rather than off-the-shelf sizing [R1]; a reef+groyne+breakwater system working with beach nourishment instead of a rigid sea wall, chosen because the community rejected a wall [R1][R2]; and a construction sequencing (temporary causeway, tidal work windows) that let the contractor place rock accurately below the high-tide line [R1]. For the surfing function, no source found explains in engineering terms (crest depth, slope, wave-focusing geometry) why the wave has or hasn't performed; the continued "proposed" framing in the Stormrider guide is suggestive the amenity function has not been widely recognised as delivering a notable wave, but no direct technical post-mortem was located [R7]
unexpected_results: The exposure of the prehistoric petrified forest and its tie-in to the Cantre'r Gwaelod legend was an unplanned, publicised side effect of the earthworks [R6]. No sources found document fishing-pressure changes, ecological studies, rip-current safety incidents, litigation, or measurable tourism-economy impact specifically tied to the Borth reef (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement; treated as a genuine gap, not confirmed absence of any such effect)
could_be_better: No source located (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement) offers an explicit engineers'/authors' retrospective critique of the Borth scheme's design or execution (unlike, e.g., Boscombe's published post-mortem). The one available critical signal is indirect: the Stormrider Surf Guide's continued description of Borth as merely "a proposed artificial reef site" years after completion implies the reef has not become a recognised, reliably rideable wave in the way pre-construction press promised [R7]; Surf-Forecast's low consistency/quality scores point the same way [R8], though neither source explains which design choice is responsible. From a cost-management perspective, the construction tender came in over budget on top of a design that had already grown by about GBP 1M after physical-model testing, and the contractor had to redesign its construction method and material sourcing specifically to close that gap, implying the original budget/design had under-priced the works as first specified [R1]
relevance_to_israel: Cardigan Bay/Aberystwyth (immediately adjacent to Borth) is macrotidal: spring tidal range is roughly 4.7-4.8 m (high spring tide c.5.4 m, low tide down to c.0.6 m) [R11]. This is drastically larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast (Haifa/Ashkelon/Netanya etc.), which is effectively microtidal, with a tidal range on the order of tens of centimetres [R21] (a web tide table, not a primary source). A reef crest depth and rock-armour design tuned by HR Wallingford's physical modelling to work across a c.4.7 m tidal swing at Borth [R1] cannot be reused as-is on Israel's coast, since the same structure would sit permanently near a single water level in Israel rather than alternately surfacing and submerging by several metres, changing both wave-breaking performance and exposure/maintenance regime. What transfers conceptually: the core political lesson that a community explicitly chose a submerged multi-purpose reef over a hard sea wall specifically to keep an open, usable beach and views [R1][R2][R4], directly analogous to debates around geotubes/breakwaters at Ashkelon and Netanya. The value-engineering lesson (reusing existing shingle instead of full import, to control cost) is also directly transferable regardless of tidal regime [R1] Tidal range cross-check: the SMP2 Aberystwyth levels give a spring range (MHWS minus MLWS) of 2.56 - (-1.74) = 4.30 m [R18], versus 4.7-4.8 m from Tide-Forecast.com [R11] and 6.0 m in Blacka Table 4.3 [R14]; three different definitions/sources, none preferred here.

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameBorth coastal defence reef (incl. Wallog headland)
PlaceBorth, Ceredigion, Cardigan Bay
CountryUnited Kingdom
YearFeasibility study May 2004 [R10][R4]; design from Oct 2009 [R1][R4]; construction started Jan 2011 [R1]; contractor's target completion Nov 2011 [R1][R9]; Coflein gives completion March 2012 [R3]; wider Phase-1 scheme described as 2011-2015 [R6] Blacka et al. (2013, p.70) also state completion in 2012 [R14].
TypeSubmerged rock (riprap) multi-purpose reef plus rock groynes, breakwaters and beach nourishment [R1][R4]. AUDIT NOTE 2026-10-10: 'submerged' holds only at high water [R16][R18][R19]. Design crest levels (drawings 9V5090/1020-1023 rev C1) are +0.50 mODN for the surf-reef arm (northern 'boot') and +1.50 mODN for the shore-parallel oval, which is a breakwater, not a surf reef [R16]; mean sea level is about +0.31 mODN (mean of the four SMP2 levels MHWS +2.56, MHWN +1.06, MLWN -0.64, MLWS -1.74 mODN; our computation, +-0.15 m) [R18], so the reef-arm crest is about 0.2 m above MSL and the rock is bare at low tide (Esri image of 2024-09-17, rock bare; 2012-10-27, awash) [R19]
PurposePrimary: flood and erosion protection for Borth village, built on a mobile shingle bank whose 1970s timber-groyne defences were failing [R1][R2][R4]. Secondary/amenity: shape the reef so breaking swell also creates a surf wave, because the community explicitly rejected a hard sea wall in favour of keeping an open beach [R1][R2][R4]
SizeReef sited c.400 m offshore per the contractor (2011) [R1] / c.300 m per local/heritage sources (2013 press, Coflein) [R2][R3]; 275,000 t total material moved (84,500 t shingle replacement, 18,500 t Type-3 rock 0.3-1t, 16,200 t Type-1 rock 3-6t, 42,000 t Type-4 rock 6-10t, 500 t Type-6 rock 5-100kg) [R1]; Coflein separately states c.300,000 t of rock for the whole works [R3] SOURCES DISAGREE on distance offshore: contractor c.400 m [R1], local/heritage c.300 m [R2][R3], but Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.66) give 110 m (north reef) and 140 m (south reef), probably measured to the undisturbed shoreline [R14]. Blacka also gives two reefs of rubble mound: north reef 72 m (longshore) x 170 m (cross-shore), south reef 85 m x 45 m (max dims), depth 4.0 m, crest at MSL [R14]. Typical tide range 6.0 m in Blacka Table 4.3 (p.68; term not defined) vs the card's spring range 4.7-4.8 m [R11]; both kept. Project-traced outline (not a published figure): northern mound 144.9 m long, 27.6 m mean width; southern oval 71.8 x 31.0 m; centroid of both mounds 330.5 m offshore (nearest edge 257 m, farthest 397 m), traced from the Esri image of 2024-09-17 [R19]; this differs from Blacka's rectangles (72 x 170 m, 85 x 45 m) [R14], which are maximum dimensions of an unspecified outline; per the shape audit they describe the SUPERSEDED two-reef design (a north truncated delta 180 x 65 m, 4.0 m high, and a south reef), not the final layout traced above (07_scale/shapes/borth-coastal-defence-reef/SOURCE_AUDIT_2026-10-10.md row 29 and HANDOFF.md item 3; the Blacka figures are therefore not comparable with the as-built mounds).
CostFigures vary by source, not reconciled: Phase 1 funding envelope GBP 7M (FY2009/10-2010/11) [R4]; GBP 13.5M "first phase of the strategy" quoted in 2009 [R1]; BAM Nuttall's winning construction tender GBP 11.5M [R1]; full phased scheme costed at GBP 29M in 2011-2013 press [R1][R2]; Coflein gives completed reef/coastal-defence works at GBP 13M [R3]; Wikipedia gives GBP 12M for the 2011-2015 scheme [R6]
Cost (approx. USD)ASSUMPTION (conversion made by this project, not by a source): at the 2013 average of about US$1.56 per GBP (0.6391 GBP per USD, CIA World Factbook via IndexMundi, 2013 value only; other years not confirmed) [R20], GBP 12-13M is about US$19-20M and GBP 29M about US$45M. Corrected 2026-10-10: the earlier text (US$15-17M and US$36M at 'rates of ~1.25-1.6') was unsourced and its low rate end (1.25) is below any 2011-2013 rate; use as order of magnitude only
Financed byCoast Protection Grant from the Welsh Assembly Government (later Welsh Government) and Convergence funding from the Welsh European Funding Office (WEFO) / European Regional Development Fund [R4][R6]
DesignerRoyal Haskoning (detailed design, appointed Oct 2009); specialist reef designer ASR (sub-consultant); physical modelling by HR Wallingford; environmental consultant Atkins [R1][R4]. Original feasibility study "Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity" completed May 2004 for Ceredigion County Council (authors not confirmed; ResearchGate record blocked, content corroborated via Borth Community website) [R10][R4]
ContractorBAM Nuttall (site agent Ray Jones); plant from Norton Plant Hire [R1][R4]
Status nowBuilt and in service; as of December 2011 residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties [R2][R3]. The wider Borth-to-Ynyslas coastal-protection programme was still being planned/phased in later business-case documents, implying more phases beyond the reef itself continued years after Phase 1 (details not found) [R4]
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Borth sits on a mobile shingle bank in Cardigan Bay; its 1970s timber groyne and breastwork sea defences were judged inadequate, with ordinary storms causing overtopping flooding through homes, per Borth councillor Ray Quant [R2]. A council feasibility study found existing defences within 10 years of failure with potentially catastrophic losses possible, triggering a 150-resident 2001 visioning meeting [R4]. Ceredigion County Council's coast and rivers engineer, Rhodri Llwyd, said the scheme had been 15 years in the making and that the community absolutely didn't want a wall, so the idea of a reef was born [R1][R2]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The preferred option, chosen after comparing technical, economic, amenity, environmental and safety criteria, was "Rock Beach Control Structures with a Multi-Purpose Reef and Beach Nourishment" [R4][R10]. Phase 1 combined: a submerged multi-purpose reef near the Craig y Delyn cliffs at the beach's southern end (sited there so the community could keep an open beach and unobstructed views), two rock groynes and two rock breakwaters further along the frontage to retain shingle, and beach nourishment (originally 150,000 m3 of imported shingle) [R1][R4]. Designed to a 1-in-100-year storm standard while remaining adaptable to future climate change [R4]. The reef's role was explicitly dual: reduce wave energy to protect the beach from erosion and broaden the beach inshore, while also being shaped to help swell waves break as a secondary surfing amenity [R1][R2]. The team settled on "Option 9A" for outline design after comparing numerous layouts, with 3D physical wave-basin modelling by HR Wallingford used to size the rock armour [R1]

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction followed the planned reef/groynes/breakwaters/nourishment layout, but with two contractor-driven, budget-closing changes: the client's design already carried about GBP 1M of cost overrun after physical-model testing showed extra rock was needed, and BAM Nuttall's tender then came in a further GBP 1M over that inflated budget [R1]. BAM Nuttall closed the combined c.GBP 2M gap by (1) mining and reusing the beach's own existing shingle, bulked up with cheaper imported quarried material underneath and the original shingle put back on top, instead of importing the full 150,000 m3 specified, and (2) building a temporary rock causeway out to the reef site so land-based excavators and dumper trucks could be used instead of the originally tendered floating marine plant [R1]. The causeway was intended to be removed once the reef was finished [R9]. Construction ran on a tight tidal window (6am-9pm with a three-hour high-tide stoppage), with over 8,000 material deliveries made by September 2011 [R1][R2]

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Coastal protection: residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties by December 2011, while the works were still substantially under construction [R2][R3]. An unplanned side effect of the earthworks was the exposure of a prehistoric submerged forest (oak, pine, birch, willow and hazel stumps dated to roughly 1500 BCE) tied to the Welsh legend of Cantre'r Gwaelod, now visible at low tide [R6]. Surfing outcome is contested: press coverage at construction time promised the reef would provide excellent surf conditions and boost the local economy [R2], but the Stormrider Surf Guide, years after completion, still describes Borth as merely "a proposed" artificial reef site rather than a functioning named surf break [R7], and Surf-Forecast.com rates Borth's surf quality only 3.0/5 with beginner difficulty and no posted first-hand surfer reviews [R8]. No wave-height, ride-length or surfable-days measurement for the reef was found [R7][R8] Blacka et al. (2013, p.70): performance 'yet to be determined' (completed 2012); protection and surfing rated 'unknown (insufficient monitoring)' (Table 4.1); Fig 4.1 (p.72) shows the reef in June 2012 [R14].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: For coastal protection, the scheme functioned successfully in its early years, withstanding December-2011 storms without flooding the properties it protects within months of substantial completion [R2][R3]. Credited design choices: graded, multi-tonne rock armour (up to 10 t pieces) sized via HR Wallingford's 3D physical modelling before construction rather than off-the-shelf sizing [R1]; a reef+groyne+breakwater system working with beach nourishment instead of a rigid sea wall, chosen because the community rejected a wall [R1][R2]; and a construction sequencing (temporary causeway, tidal work windows) that let the contractor place rock accurately below the high-tide line [R1]. For the surfing function, no source found explains in engineering terms (crest depth, slope, wave-focusing geometry) why the wave has or hasn't performed; the continued "proposed" framing in the Stormrider guide is suggestive the amenity function has not been widely recognised as delivering a notable wave, but no direct technical post-mortem was located [R7]

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The exposure of the prehistoric petrified forest and its tie-in to the Cantre'r Gwaelod legend was an unplanned, publicised side effect of the earthworks [R6]. No sources found document fishing-pressure changes, ecological studies, rip-current safety incidents, litigation, or measurable tourism-economy impact specifically tied to the Borth reef (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement; treated as a genuine gap, not confirmed absence of any such effect)

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: No source located (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement) offers an explicit engineers'/authors' retrospective critique of the Borth scheme's design or execution (unlike, e.g., Boscombe's published post-mortem). The one available critical signal is indirect: the Stormrider Surf Guide's continued description of Borth as merely "a proposed artificial reef site" years after completion implies the reef has not become a recognised, reliably rideable wave in the way pre-construction press promised [R7]; Surf-Forecast's low consistency/quality scores point the same way [R8], though neither source explains which design choice is responsible. From a cost-management perspective, the construction tender came in over budget on top of a design that had already grown by about GBP 1M after physical-model testing, and the contractor had to redesign its construction method and material sourcing specifically to close that gap, implying the original budget/design had under-priced the works as first specified [R1]

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Cardigan Bay/Aberystwyth (immediately adjacent to Borth) is macrotidal: spring tidal range is roughly 4.7-4.8 m (high spring tide c.5.4 m, low tide down to c.0.6 m) [R11]. This is drastically larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast (Haifa/Ashkelon/Netanya etc.), which is effectively microtidal, with a tidal range on the order of tens of centimetres [R21] (a web tide table, not a primary source). A reef crest depth and rock-armour design tuned by HR Wallingford's physical modelling to work across a c.4.7 m tidal swing at Borth [R1] cannot be reused as-is on Israel's coast, since the same structure would sit permanently near a single water level in Israel rather than alternately surfacing and submerging by several metres, changing both wave-breaking performance and exposure/maintenance regime. What transfers conceptually: the core political lesson that a community explicitly chose a submerged multi-purpose reef over a hard sea wall specifically to keep an open, usable beach and views [R1][R2][R4], directly analogous to debates around geotubes/breakwaters at Ashkelon and Netanya. The value-engineering lesson (reusing existing shingle instead of full import, to control cost) is also directly transferable regardless of tidal regime [R1] Tidal range cross-check: the SMP2 Aberystwyth levels give a spring range (MHWS minus MLWS) of 2.56 - (-1.74) = 4.30 m [R18], versus 4.7-4.8 m from Tide-Forecast.com [R11] and 6.0 m in Blacka Table 4.3 [R14]; three different definitions/sources, none preferred here.

footprint.orientation_notes: VERIFIED 2026-09-25 (see verification array) with one important downgrade: the two-separate-mounds fact stands on independent textual corroboration — the New Civil Engineer contractor account describing 'a double reef' [R1] and BAM Nuttall's own progress-photo captions describing 'the northern and southern multi-purpose reef' (already in the card's images list, confirmed present verbatim in 03_images/web/borth-coastal-defence-reef.json) — not on the [S1] diagram's icon shapes. Direct visual inspection of the rendered [S1] page-3 diagram this verification pass found that (a) the diagram's small 'legend' icon next to the 'Multi-Purpose Reef' text label does show one oval/racetrack shape plus one separate, larger hook/L-shaped mound (this is the source of the oval+hook description), but (b) the icon actually stamped on the frontage line at the reef's real location is a DIFFERENT, symmetric 'double-hook'/bowtie shape (two mirrored hook forms joined at a point) that does not visually match the legend icon; (c) this same bowtie icon recurs identically at at least six other points on the same diagram — once more within the 'Completed Phase 1 Works' span itself (a second, previously-undisclosed icon cluster sitting between the reef's legend position and the Phase-2 boundary) and four more times within the 'Phase 2 Works' span marking generic future Beach Rock Breakwater/groyne locations — confirming it functions as a generic location-marker symbol, not a literal or scaled footprint drawing. Because of this, the specific 'oval mound = south, hook mound = north' assignment, and indeed the assumption that the two on-map icon clusters both represent parts of one single two-mound reef (rather than, e.g., one cluster being the reef and the other a separate Phase-1 rock breakwater), are NOT reliably supported and are downgraded to low confidence / unconfirmed; only the higher-level 'the structure comprises two separate, adjoining parts' fact remains at medium confidence, resting on the independent text sources, not on the icon art. No source in our reference list, including [S1], gives a compass bearing for the reef's long axis or for the incident swell; Cardigan Bay opens broadly west/south-west, so a swell approach from the SW-WSW quadrant (as Gemini asserts) is geographically plausible in general terms, but no source found this session states this figure specifically for Borth, so it is not treated as confirmed.
footprint.materials: Graded quarried rock armour, Type 1 (3–6 t), Type 3 (0.3–1 t), Type 4 (6–10 t) and Type 6 (5–100 kg), placed by land-based excavators via a temporary rock causeway; overall Phase 1 rock+shingle tonnage 275,000 t, of which roughly 77,200 t was graded rock armour (Types 1/3/4/6) shared across the reef, groynes and breakwaters together — not separable into a reef-only tonnage by any source found [R1] (reused from card)

images_relied_on.what_was_read_off_it: RE-EXAMINED 2026-09-25 by rendering page 3 to a high-resolution PNG with PyMuPDF and viewing it directly (confirms and refines the prior pass's reading). Page 3 ("What will it look like?") contains a labelled location diagram with a small 'legend' icon next to the text "Multi-Purpose Reef" — this legend icon does show one elongated oval/racetrack mound plus one separate, larger hook/L-shaped mound, matching the prior description. However, the icon actually stamped on the frontage line at the reef's own location (within "Completed Phase 1 Works") is a DIFFERENT, symmetric double-hook/'bowtie' shape (two mirrored hook forms joined at their points) that does not match the legend icon's oval+hook pairing. This same bowtie icon is stamped identically at 6+ other points on the same diagram — including a SECOND cluster still within "Completed Phase 1 Works" (not previously noted) and 4 more within "Phase 2 Works" marking generic future Beach Rock Breakwater/groyne locations described in the page's own body text — confirming this is a reused generic map-marker symbol, not a scaled or literal footprint drawing of the reef. Net effect: the 'two separate/adjoining structures' fact is unaffected (it rests on R1's text and the project's own photo captions, not on this icon), but the specific oval-vs-hook shape assignment, and the assumption that both Phase-1 icon clusters represent the one reef rather than the reef plus a separate structure, are downgraded to unconfirmed. The same page also contains a genuinely scaled "BREAKWATER STRUCTURE PLAN VIEW, SCALE 1:250" and "...TYPICAL CROSS SECTION, SCALE 1:100" drawing with real dimension callouts (arms 39.1 m / 27.1 m to centre of roundhead, 135 degree bend, crest 3.9 m wide, crest level +5.0 m Chart Datum at MHWS, 6 t primary rock armour, 2:1 side slopes, 0.4 m bedding layer) — CONFIRMED verbatim by direct visual inspection this pass — but this scaled drawing is explicitly for a different, standard Phase-2 rock breakwater unit (and is in fact the source of the 'hook' shape reused as the generic icon above), not the multi-purpose reef, so its numbers are read and understood but deliberately NOT applied to the reef's own dimensions.

disagree.why_ours: Our value comes from two directly quoted, independently locatable sources already fetched and re-verified this session: New Civil Engineer's contemporaneous 2011 contractor account, "a double reef located 400m offshore" [R1], and Coflein's heritage record, "The reef is 300m off the coast" [R3], corroborated by a Daily Post snippet giving the same ~300 m figure [R2]. Gemini's 200 m has no working citation behind it — none of its three listed sources ("Ceredigion County Council Final Review 2013", "BAM Nuttall Project Case Study 2012", "Coflein National Monuments Record 2015") could be located online this session (no URL was given for any of them, and none of the real, locatable documents from these same organisations that we found — the actual Coflein record, the actual New Civil Engineer article — contain a 200 m figure). Our own verified card had already flagged this exact discrepancy as the single biggest red flag in Gemini's file, and this session's direct source checks confirm that flag was correct.

footprint.confidence: The two mounds are clearly visible as bare rock on four dated, geo-referenced Esri images (2012-2024) and the outline agrees in position (0.3-4 m), orientation (1-3 deg) and length (-4 % north, +0.4 % south) with the georeferenced Royal Haskoning construction plan and with a 2022 Welsh Government LiDAR survey. The area is the visible rock edge only: 18 % smaller than the design armour-foot polygon and 34 % smaller than the LiDAR exposed footprint, so the true toe is larger than drawn.
open_issues: VERIFICATION 2026-09-25 finding: the [S1] location diagram's 'Multi-Purpose Reef' legend icon (oval+hook) does not match the icon actually stamped at the reef's frontage location (a symmetric double-hook/bowtie shape), and that stamped icon is reused identically 6+ times elsewhere on the same diagram as a generic structure-location marker (including a second, previously undisclosed cluster within 'Completed Phase 1 Works' itself, not only in the Phase-2 span as the prior draft stated). It is unresolved this session whether that second Phase-1 cluster is a redundant second stamp of the same reef or a separate Phase-1 structure (e.g. a rock breakwater); this does not change the 'two separate parts' conclusion (independently text-sourced) but does mean the oval/hook sub-shapes and the north/south assignment in polygons_m should be read as an illustrative placeholder, not a schematic derived from a reliable figure.

VERIFICATION 2026-09-25 finding: max_dimension_m was recomputed from the raw polygons_m coordinates and corrected from 162 m (which was the bounding-box diagonal, sqrt(145^2+73^2), not an actual distance between any two polygon vertices) to 145.1 m (the true maximum pairwise vertex distance, achieved between a Lobe-A vertex near (-77,335) and a Lobe-B vertex near (68,330)), since the two lobes do not reach opposite corners of the bounding box.

Alongshore length, cross-shore width, footprint area and crest depth of the multi-purpose reef are NOT published in any source located or made accessible this session, including a newly-found primary design document (Royal HaskoningDHV/Ceredigion CC/Atkins public exhibition poster PDF, S1). This mirrors the card's own 'gaps' list (reef crest depth/freeboard; reef footprint width and volume) and this session's research did not close those gaps, only narrowed the shape question.

The polygons_m in this file are an explicitly low-confidence, order-of-magnitude SCHEMATIC placeholder (method: analogy + rough tonnage scaling, not a measurement) — a future agent with access to the actual as-built survey, the ASR Ltd/HR Wallingford physical-model report, or a higher-resolution/CAD version of the Royal HaskoningDHV exhibition drawings would very likely be able to replace this with real numbers.

The New Civil Engineer article [R1] was blocked by WebFetch (HTTP 403) but was successfully fetched this session via a direct curl request with a browser-style User-Agent header; its full text was then read directly. This is worth noting for future agents who hit the same 403 with WebFetch on this domain.

The two-mound shape finding rests on one schematic location diagram [S1] whose icons are demonstrably reused elsewhere on the same page for generic Phase-2 structure locations; we are confident in the 'two adjoining mounds' topology (corroborated independently by R1's 'double reef' wording and by the card's own BAM Nuttall photo captions) but not in the exact proportions/curvature drawn for each mound, nor in which mound is truly 'northern' vs 'southern' in the field.

Live satellite/aerial imagery (Bing Maps) inspected this session did not show a visually distinguishable offshore structure near the expected site; this is inconclusive (submerged rock reefs often do not show in calm, true-colour aerial imagery) and should not be read as evidence against the reef's existence or location.

Gemini's three cited sources for this reef ('Ceredigion County Council Final Review 2013', 'BAM Nuttall Project Case Study 2012', 'Coflein National Monuments Record 2015') could not be located anywhere online this session — no URL, no matching document title, and the two genuinely locatable organisations' own real pages (the actual Coflein record NPRN 424699, the actual New Civil Engineer article) do not contain Gemini's specific numbers. We treat all of Gemini's Borth-specific numeric claims as unverified at the source, per project rule, rather than adopting any of them.

verification.item: Polygon geometry — bbox_m (145 x 73) and area_m2 (3,785) internally consistent with the stated polygons_m coordinates
verification.evidence: Recomputed independently in Python (shoelace formula + Shapely 2.x): combined bbox x=[-77,68] -> length_alongshore=145.0 m exactly; combined bbox y=[295,368] -> width_crossshore=73 m exactly; Lobe A area=1079.84 m2, Lobe B area=2705.00 m2, total=3784.84 m2 (rounds to the stated 3,785 m2). verification.item: max_dimension_m = 162 m
verification.evidence: The maximum distance between any two vertices across both polygons, computed exhaustively over all vertex pairs, is 145.09 m (between a Lobe-A vertex near (-77, 335) and a Lobe-B vertex near (68, 330)), not 162 m. 162 m equals sqrt(145^2 + 73^2), the diagonal of the bounding box — but no actual polygon vertex sits at the opposite corners needed to realise that diagonal, since the two lobes are offset rather than diagonally opposed. Fixed in the JSON to 145.1 m.

verification.item: Crest depth — 'not established', genuine unresolved gap
verification.evidence: This pass additionally searched for a technical paper ('Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity', ResearchGate) that might contain a design crest level; the ResearchGate page returned HTTP 403 (paywalled/blocked, consistent with the prior draft's account) and no other accessible source (R1-R4, S1, or further targeted web searches) gives a crest depth or level for the reef itself. The +5.0 m Chart Datum figure remains correctly attributed only to the unrelated Phase-2 breakwater (see above). Gap confirmed genuine, not an oversight.

verification.item: Gemini comparison table — fairness and accuracy of quoted Gemini values
verification.evidence: Read Gemini's own 02_world_reefs_data/reef_footprints.json (structures[] entry id='borth') and scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md (row 8) directly. Every value attributed to Gemini in our comparison table matches verbatim: distance_offshore_m=200, dimensions 200.0 x 65.0 m, footprint_area_m2=12500.0 (audit table separately gives 9,700 m2 net), crest_depth_m=1.2 with crest_depth_notes 'crest at -1.0m to -1.5m below Mean Low Water Springs (MLWS)', incident_swell_direction_deg '230°-260° (SW to WSW)', shape_typology 'Submerged Rock Berm with Tapered Flanks', and the three sources 'Ceredigion County Council: Borth Coastal Defense Scheme Final Review (2013)', 'BAM Nuttall Project Case Study: Borth Coastal Defense (2012)', 'Coflein National Monuments Record of Wales: Craig y Delyn Reef (2015)' — none of which resolve to any locatable document, matching our card's finding. The audit row marks Borth 'VERIFIED' with 'Discrepancy / Recommendation: None', accurately characterised as such in our file.

+ design plan (15 setting-out points in OS grid, residual 0.02 m) overlays the satellite: IoU 0.79 N / 0.86 S, centroids within 4 m
+ LiDAR (as-built, 1 m) confirms crest levels and the two-mound layout
- no published text length/width exists (only 300/400 m offshore); the 'text' check is against the design drawing
- area depends on the waterline: drawn 5,743 m2 vs design foot 6,989 m2 vs LiDAR 8,675 m2
- absolute position uncertainty about +-5 m (Esri; OSGB36->WGS84 Helmert 2-5 m)
footprint.text_confidence: low overall for dimensions and crest depth; medium specifically for the higher-level fact that the structure is two separate/adjoining parts rather than one continuous berm (independent text corroboration: R1's 'double reef', BAM Nuttall's 'northern and southern multi-purpose reef' captions); low/unconfirmed specifically for the finer claim of which part is oval-shaped vs hook-shaped and which is 'northern' vs 'southern' (this rests only on a generic, inconsistently-drawn map icon — see verification and orientation_notes)

name: Bunbury Airwave
year: Installation attempted December 2019 (failed during install) [R1][R5]; concept development began ~2008-2009 [R2]
type: Inflatable dome-shaped rubber (Hypalon) 'air bladder' artificial surf reef, anchored with sand ballast and filled with air/sand, glued (not welded) seams [R3][R9][R8] | Per the founder (interview 2026-10-10), the FINAL design is filled with sand instead of air, because the engineers found air did not respond well with the waves [R25]; this differs from the air/sand fill described above (see sources_disagree).
purpose: Create a reliable, rideable wave at a beach with swell but poor bathymetry ('closeouts'); position Bunbury as a surfing destination alternative to nearby Margaret River, attract competitions/tourism, give local surfers a place to progress [R1][R2][R6]
size: Base diameter 12 m (≈40 ft) [R1][R2][R3][R6]; height above seabed given as 2 m in most sources but 1.6 m at its highest point in one dedicated preview article [R1][R2][R3][R6][R9]; sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]; filled with washed coarse beach sand (140 tonnes) plus air [R9][R8]
cost: City of Bunbury committed A$75,000 as a council sponsorship (approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; total project cost reported as ~US$400,000 including installation by one source and ~US$350,000 by another — sources disagree on the total figure [R3][R10]
cost_usd_approx: ~350,000–400,000 (total project, disputed between sources); A$75,000 (~US$50,000) of that was the confirmed City of Bunbury contribution [R1][R2][R3][R10] ASSUMPTION: the A$75,000 = ~US$50,000 conversion uses an unsourced rate (~0.67); not confirmed against a rate table.
financed_by: City of Bunbury council sponsorship (A$75,000, approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; an August 2018 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign by Waveco failed to raise enough [R3]; remainder via Waveco/Bottegal investors [R5]
motivation: Bunbury sits near Margaret River, a premier surf destination, but Back Beach had swell without the bathymetry to shape it into rideable waves [R1][R2][R6]. Waveco founder Troy Bottegal had spent roughly a decade developing the inflatable-bladder concept and wanted a real-world test site [R2][R10]; the City of Bunbury under Mayor Gary Brennan saw it as a low-cost way to brand the town as a surfing destination and draw competitions and tourism [R2].
designer: Troy Bottegal, inventor and sole patent holder, director of Waveco Pty Ltd (Dunsborough, WA); conceived the idea after watching a dome-shaped ('oyster') light fitting create ripples in a bathtub [R6][R10]
contractor: Waveco Pty Ltd; installation used three divers and a boat [R9]; fabrication was originally overseas, later moved to a Western Australian manufacturer after the 2019 failure [R5][R8]
status_now: Torn along a glued seam during installation, ~90% complete, mid-December 2019; the partially-inflated bladder was removed from the water within about three days per most sources, though one source (Bottegal, 2020-07-09) separately says it was removed in half a day — the two figures conflict [R1][R5][R8][R18]. A second Airwave prototype install, needing a further ~A$300,000, was being planned for December 2020 [R18]; no source confirms whether it happened or succeeded. A 2022-03-22 article quotes Bottegal saying the Airwave would be 'back in the water in time for Summer, 2024' after relocating fabrication to a WA manufacturer [R8]. A Waveco Instagram post from June 2024 shows an active Bunbury Back Beach surf-cam [R11]. By September 2025, Waveco's own site/Instagram show its active Bunbury proposal has shifted to a 'granite artificial reef' (rock) design at a dedicated project site (bunburyartificialreef.info), framed around coastal-erosion protection rather than surf amenity [R20] — no source confirms the original inflatable Airwave was ever successfully reinstalled; status as of research date is unconfirmed for the inflatable Airwave specifically, and Waveco's current Bunbury-facing project appears to be a different (granite) technology [R8][R11][R18][R20] Addition 2026-10-10: per the founder (interview 8 Oct 2026), they are now going for concrete [R25]. Not independently confirmed; consistent in direction with the rock/granite proposal in [R20] but not the same material.
hover_text: A 12 m inflatable rubber 'air bladder' surf reef (A$75,000 council funding; total project ~US$350–400,000, disputed) that tore along a glued seam during its December 2019 installation off Bunbury Back Beach, WA, and was pulled from the water within days: it failed, because it was never completed and no independent source documents rideable waves on it [R1][R3][R8][R18]. The developer calls it 'not a failure' and says it 'successfully created peeling waves', but its own page misdates the install to 2018 and no independent report supports the wave claim [R21]; by 2025 its Bunbury proposal is a different (granite/rock) design [R20].
design_as_planned: A 12 m-diameter, dome-shaped inflatable rubber bladder anchored to the seabed with sand ballast, filled with air/sand/water, sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]. It was meant to 'lift, peak, and hold the swell to create a concave, tapered wall of water that retains its shape as it peels toward the beach' [R19], producing an A-frame peak with left and right breaks where there had previously only been closeouts [R3]. Bottegal modelled the intended wave on Thunderbomb, a wave in Nicaragua [R4]. It was designed to work across roughly 2–8 ft swell, with expected ride length ~40 m / 26 seconds, over an estimated 150 rideable-swell days per year [R2][R3][R9]. A hard-wired webcam and a planned 12-month University of Western Australia scientific study were part of the design [R9]. The reversibility/removability of the inflatable design (not ecological habitat creation) was the explicit environmental/cost pitch — 'if they don't do what you want them to do... they take half a day to move' [R10].
as_built_vs_design: Construction was reported 'halfway complete' in October 2019 against a November 2019 install target [R4]; installation slipped to December 2019, and divers/boat crew got the bladder to ~90% complete (deployed but not fully anchored) when an unexpectedly large, deep offshore swell drove strong undertow through the line-up during the final fill/anchoring phase, tearing a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The tear was along the seam, not the rubber itself [R1]; the underlying cause was the choice of Hypalon rubber, which could not be welded and so had to be glued — a joint that could not withstand pump pressure during the final fill [R8]. The bladder was removed within about three days (one conflicting account says half a day) [R1][R5][R8][R18]. The reef therefore was never completed to its designed, fully-anchored, surfable state (card author's inference from the ~90 % complete, not fully anchored state in [R1][R5]). Addition 2026-10-10: the founder says the final design used SAND instead of AIR as the fill, because the engineers found air did not respond well with the waves; the failure was a seam that opened up a couple of days after installation (not a tear during the fill phase), and until then it worked "amazingly" [R25, notes as reported by Lior]. Both accounts kept; see sources_disagree. [R25]
outcome: Installation was not completed: the bladder tore and was pulled from the water, unsurfable in its intended form [R1][R5][R8]. During the brief period it was partially in the water, Bottegal later reported that 'a wave did break on it... peeled nearly all the way to the beach... created a 0.75 metre wave' — the only quantified wave-performance data found, describing a small, uncontrolled result rather than a validated trial [R8]. No formal UWA study results were found; the planned 12-month study appears never to have started [R9]. A second prototype installation was being planned for December 2020 with a further A$300,000 [R18], but no source confirms it happened or succeeded. A 2022 article promised a Summer 2024 relaunch after moving fabrication to WA [R8]; a June 2024 Instagram post shows an active surf-cam [R11]; but by September 2025 Waveco's active Bunbury-facing project had shifted to a different, granite (rock) reef design aimed at coastal-erosion protection [R20]. No source listed in References confirms (negative finding of this card) the inflatable Airwave was ever successfully completed and operating as a surf reef at Bunbury. Addition 2026-10-10: founder says the structure worked perfectly until a seam opened a couple of days after installation [R25]; the card keeps the independent record (tear during installation, removal within about three days) and records the disagreement.
why_worked_or_failed: Failure mechanism (installation, Dec 2019): an unexpectedly deep offshore swell during the final anchoring/fill phase generated strong undertow that flexed the bladder, concentrating stress on a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The underlying materials cause was the use of Hypalon rubber, which cannot be welded; the glued seams used instead could not withstand pressure reached during the final pump/fill stage [R8]. This was a materials/fabrication-method failure compounded by an installation-timing/weather-window problem, rather than a wave-performance or siting failure — the reef never reached a state where its surf-shaping performance could be properly judged (the card author's synthesis of [R1][R5][R6][R8]; the classification is an inference, not a source statement). Addition 2026-10-10: founder account (personal communication): the seam opened a couple of days after installation, and the fill choice for the final design moved from air to sand because air did not respond well with the waves [R25]. This agrees that a seam was the failure point, but differs on timing and on whether the structure was complete (card author's comparison of [R25] with [R1][R5][R8]).
unexpected_results: The one recorded moment of the Airwave functioning — before the tear forced its removal — reportedly produced a wave that 'peeled nearly all the way to the beach' and reached about 0.75 m, an unplanned, brief glimpse of the concept working, per Bottegal's later account [R8]. No sources document fishing-pressure effects, ecological colonization, rip-current changes, safety incidents, or litigation connected to this installation in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card) — plausible given the structure was never operational for an extended period (card author's inference). Local news noted reputational 'deflation' for Bunbury when the trial failed on a high-profile install day [R1]. Addition 2026-10-10: the founder told Lior that until the seam opened it "worked amazingly, perfect waves" [R25, personal communication, notes as reported by Lior]. This is a self-interested, unrecorded, second-hand account; no independent report, photo or video confirms it, and it is larger than the single 0.75 m wave in [R8].
could_be_better: From Waveco/the designer's own account: the identified fix was materials and fabrication method — move away from glued Hypalon seams (relocating manufacture to a WA-based manufacturer) and secure fresh investment before re-attempting installation [R8]. Bottegal framed the setback as a timing/weather issue (an unplanned deep swell during the vulnerable, partially-anchored install phase) rather than a fundamental design flaw, maintaining '100 percent' confidence the concept would work [R6]. Detailed surfer/commentator critique was not found in the sources successfully retrieved for this research (negative finding of this card) [see dossier for blocked forum sources]. Addition 2026-10-10: the founder says the next version goes to CONCRETE (no detail on design, date or site) [R25]; the final design as described fills with sand, not air [R25].
relevance_to_israel: Bunbury sits on a microtidal WA coast (tidal range roughly ~1 m or less) [R13], broadly comparable in scale to the Mediterranean's small tidal range at Haifa — not itself a factor implicated in the Bunbury failure, but relevant to sizing an Israeli pilot in a similarly low-tide setting. Wave climate differs in kind: Bunbury/SW WA faces Southern Ocean groundswell (~150 rideable-swell days/year) [R9], far more energetic than the Eastern Mediterranean's short-period, wind-driven seas off Haifa. What transfers: (1) the low-cost [R10], rapidly-removable [R18] inflatable concept is attractive for a wave-poor, low-tidal-range coast like Israel's, avoiding large capital commitment before wave performance is proven; (2) the documented failure mode — glued (not welded) seam material failing under dynamic swell/undertow loading during the vulnerable partially-anchored installation phase — is a fabrication/installation-window risk any Israeli inflatable-reef pilot would need to solve first, independent of local wave/tide conditions (failure mode: [R1][R8]; the transfer is the card author's inference); (3) because Israel's swell energy is much lower than SW Australia's (card author's general statement, (unsourced) here), a device sized for Bunbury's 2–8 ft face range (UNSOURCED figure: no reference in this card gives it; treat as unverified) may be oversized for Haifa's smaller everyday waves and would need dedicated re-sizing/modelling, not found in any source reviewed here. Tide range check: GHD (2021) Table 1 gives Port of Bunbury HAT 0.6 and LAT -0.6 m AHD, a range of 1.2 m, MSL +0.1 m AHD [R26], consistent with the sample-day heights of [R13] (which are one day only).

developer_account.who: Waveco Pty Ltd (the developer; Troy Bottegal, CEO & founder)
developer_account.page: All About Us - The Story of Behind the Airwave (About page), section 'The Path to Discovery' > 'The Bunbury Deployment'
developer_account.page_dates: WordPress REST API (page id 53654): created 2019-08-11, last modified 2025-12-22; the Bunbury passage itself carries no date
developer_account.quote: In 2018, we deployed a 150-tonne sand-slurry bladder at Bunbury’s Back Beach. While it successfully created peeling waves, a final-day overpressure event led to a seam split. It wasn't a failure—it was the catalyst for our next breakthrough.
developer_account.quote_check: verified verbatim in the raw page HTML on 2026-10-05 (the page uses a curly apostrophe in Bunbury’s and an em dash)
developer_account.independence: self-published by the developer; promotional; not independent
developer_account.adjacent_text: 'Post-2018, we pivoted. We designed and patented a modular concrete version of the Airwave... Simultaneously, we developed a conventional Granite ASR design.' (same page) [R21]

checks.independent_record: Installation was attempted in December 2019: it began the week of 9 Dec, a diver spotted the seam tear on the afternoon of Fri 13 Dec, and it was reported on Mon 16 Dec [R1][R5][R6][R7][R15]. Before that it had not been deployed: ABC (2019-06-13) said it was set to be installed in November [R2]; Tracks (2019-08-12) described a trial planned for mid-November and a crowd-funding campaign 'last year' [R23]; Raised Water Research (2019-10-14) said construction was half-way [R4]; Tracks (2019-11-15) said the live trial was 'some time in the next couple of months' [R9]; RWR's spot page says it was installed in December 2019 [R3]; ABC listen (2022-10-07) says 'In 2019 ... attempted to install' [R24]. The only 2018 events found are Waveco's failed Aug 2018 Kickstarter [R3] and a 'may be installed' preview [R19]. One outlier: the 2022 Bunbury Mail intro says 'four years since' and captions a supplied photo 'The original Bunbury Airwave in 2018' [R8]; that conflicts with every dated 2019 report above.

Sand-slurry fill is corroborated: Tracks 2019 ('washed, coarse beach sand... for that slurry') [R9]; Bottegal in the Bunbury Mail ('irrigate the sandslurry') [R8]; RWR ('partially filling it with sand', the rest water and air) [R3]; a local observer on Swellnet saw a slurry pump and hoses on the beach on 7 Dec 2019 [R15]. ABC and SurferToday call it 'filled with air' [R1][R7]; Tracks 2019 says 'a mixture of sand and air' [R9]; the card's 'air bladder anchored with sand ballast' fits all of these. The mass has no independent source: 140 tonnes in Tracks 2021 and the Bunbury Mail 2022, both reporting Bottegal [R22][R8]; '150T' in a forum summary of his Feb 2020 conference talk [R15]. So 140-150 t, developer-sourced only; the 7% gap is inside the developer's own statements.
checks.assessment: material and bladder type consistent; mass is developer-only, 140-150 t (card keeps 140 t)

checks.claim: 'While it successfully created peeling waves' (wave performance)
checks.independent_record: No independent report, photograph or video of surfable waves on the reef was found. ABC (2019-12-16) reports only the tear; it paraphrases a tourist as 'looking forward to riding whatever wave the Airwave produced' and beach-goers were told to keep away [R1]. RWR, SurferToday and The Inertia report no wave [R5][R6][R7]. The ABC video 11804314 shows the bladder on the seabed with a diver and no wave (card video notes). Tracks 2021 says the plan to webcast 'perfectly peeling waves' 'didn't quite play that way' [R22]; the webcam was not live for the install [R15]. The wave claim comes from the developer alone: Bottegal told the Bunbury Mail in 2022 that 'a wave did break' just before the tear, a 'lone wave' that 'peeled for about thirty metres' and 'created a 0.75 metre wave' seen by onlookers [R8] (his recollection 27 months later; no footage or named witness cited). Second-hand only: a Swellnet user quoting Waveco's Dec 2019 Instagram says the redesign reflects 'small wave action' observed during install, and a forum summary of his Feb 2020 talk lists 'Small Wave Peak' among positives [R15].
checks.assessment: not independently supported: at most ONE small wave (about 0.75 m, about 30 m long) reported by the developer himself, while the bladder was about 90% installed and not anchored; no ride by anyone, no footage found

checks.claim: 'a final-day overpressure event led to a seam split' (failure mechanism)
checks.independent_record: Seam split: confirmed; the tear was along a glued seam, not through the rubber [R1][R5][R8]. 'Final-day': the tear was spotted on about the fifth day of the install week (Fri 13 Dec) when, per ABC reporting Bottegal, it was '90 per cent complete' but 'not completely anchored' [R1][R7]; a local observer saw it 'partially filled' that afternoon [R15]. It never operated as a finished reef. 'Overpressure': this is the developer's own later explanation, and it changes. Dec 2019: an unexpected deep swell and undertow flexed the airbag against the seam [R1][R5][R7]. Oct 2021 (Tracks): sand pumped too heavily into one quadrant put too much pressure on one section of the skin, and the new valves avoid 'the same over pressurization problem' [R22]. Mar 2022 (Bunbury Mail): glued overlapped Hypalon seams plus 'full pump pressure applied to a confined space in the final fill phase' caused a tear in the back quadrant [R8]. No independent engineering report exists.
checks.assessment: partly supported: seam split true; 'overpressure' matches his 2021-22 accounts but not his 2019 one; 'final-day' makes an unfinished install sound like a completed deployment

checks.independent_record: Bottegal told the Bunbury Mail in Mar 2022 the prototype installation 'certainly was not a failure' [R8]. But Tracks (2021-10-08) writes that he 'readily admits that the first trial of his Airwave was a failure' (Tracks' paraphrase, not a direct quote) [R22]. Facts on record: the bladder tore during installation and was removed within days (reports range from about 5 hours to 3 days) [R8][R18][R15]; no completed trial and the planned 12-month UWA study never started [R9]; a second prototype (planned Dec 2020, about A$300,000 more needed) is not confirmed built [R18][R8]; the redesign has only been tank-tested [R22]; by 2025 Waveco's Bunbury proposal is a granite reef [R20]; and its own page says it 'pivoted' away from the rubber Airwave after 2018 [R21].
checks.assessment: a judgement, not a checkable fact; the record supports 'learning prototype' as the developer's framing but not 'success'

developer_account.overall: Of the four factual claims, one is contradicted (2018), one is consistent but developer-only on mass (150 t vs 140 t elsewhere), one is partly supported (seam split yes; 'final-day overpressure' reframes an unfinished install), and one has no independent support (successfully created peeling waves). The card verdict stays 'failed'.

verdict_reason: The structure tore along a glued seam during installation (spotted Fri 13 Dec 2019, about 90% installed and not fully anchored), was removed within days, and never operated as a completed reef [R1][R5][R8][R18]. No independent report, photo or video documents rideable waves on it; the only wave claim is the developer's own later account of one lone 0.75 m wave seen during installation [R8][R21]. The developer's page says the trial 'wasn't a failure' [R21], but it misdates the deployment to 2018 (it was December 2019), Tracks reported in 2021 that Bottegal 'readily admits' the first trial was a failure [R22], no second install is confirmed [R18][R8], and by 2025 Waveco's Bunbury proposal is a different (granite) design [R20]. Verdict kept as 'failed' after checking the developer's account (2026-10-05). Update 2026-10-10: the verdict stays failed, because the structure failed within days (a seam opened) and was never a durable reef [R1][R5][R25]. In fairness, the founder (Troy) told Lior the reef worked amazingly, with perfect waves, until the seam opened, and that the final design uses sand instead of air and the next step is concrete [R25, personal communication, notes as reported by Lior]. That is a developer statement and independent confirmation of surfable waves is still lacking. WHO DECIDED: the research agent that wrote this card (2026-09-24, re-checked 2026-10-05 against the developer's page, again 2026-10-10 after the interview); the orchestrator brief records the verdict as FAILED 'despite the developer's claim'. Lior has not overruled it.
