sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameBunbury Airwave
PlaceBunbury Back Beach, Western Australia
CountryAustralia
YearInstallation attempted December 2019 (failed during install) [R1][R5]; concept development began ~2008-2009 [R2]
TypeInflatable dome-shaped rubber (Hypalon) 'air bladder' artificial surf reef, anchored with sand ballast and filled with air/sand, glued (not welded) seams [R3][R9][R8] | Per the founder (interview 2026-10-10), the FINAL design is filled with sand instead of air, because the engineers found air did not respond well with the waves [R25]; this differs from the air/sand fill described above (see sources_disagree).
PurposeCreate a reliable, rideable wave at a beach with swell but poor bathymetry ('closeouts'); position Bunbury as a surfing destination alternative to nearby Margaret River, attract competitions/tourism, give local surfers a place to progress [R1][R2][R6]
SizeBase diameter 12 m (≈40 ft) [R1][R2][R3][R6]; height above seabed given as 2 m in most sources but 1.6 m at its highest point in one dedicated preview article [R1][R2][R3][R6][R9]; sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]; filled with washed coarse beach sand (140 tonnes) plus air [R9][R8]
CostCity of Bunbury committed A$75,000 as a council sponsorship (approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; total project cost reported as ~US$400,000 including installation by one source and ~US$350,000 by another — sources disagree on the total figure [R3][R10]
Cost (approx. USD)~350,000–400,000 (total project, disputed between sources); A$75,000 (~US$50,000) of that was the confirmed City of Bunbury contribution [R1][R2][R3][R10] ASSUMPTION: the A$75,000 = ~US$50,000 conversion uses an unsourced rate (~0.67); not confirmed against a rate table.
Financed byCity of Bunbury council sponsorship (A$75,000, approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; an August 2018 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign by Waveco failed to raise enough [R3]; remainder via Waveco/Bottegal investors [R5]
DesignerTroy Bottegal, inventor and sole patent holder, director of Waveco Pty Ltd (Dunsborough, WA); conceived the idea after watching a dome-shaped ('oyster') light fitting create ripples in a bathtub [R6][R10]
ContractorWaveco Pty Ltd; installation used three divers and a boat [R9]; fabrication was originally overseas, later moved to a Western Australian manufacturer after the 2019 failure [R5][R8]
Status nowTorn along a glued seam during installation, ~90% complete, mid-December 2019; the partially-inflated bladder was removed from the water within about three days per most sources, though one source (Bottegal, 2020-07-09) separately says it was removed in half a day — the two figures conflict [R1][R5][R8][R18]. A second Airwave prototype install, needing a further ~A$300,000, was being planned for December 2020 [R18]; no source confirms whether it happened or succeeded. A 2022-03-22 article quotes Bottegal saying the Airwave would be 'back in the water in time for Summer, 2024' after relocating fabrication to a WA manufacturer [R8]. A Waveco Instagram post from June 2024 shows an active Bunbury Back Beach surf-cam [R11]. By September 2025, Waveco's own site/Instagram show its active Bunbury proposal has shifted to a 'granite artificial reef' (rock) design at a dedicated project site (bunburyartificialreef.info), framed around coastal-erosion protection rather than surf amenity [R20] — no source confirms the original inflatable Airwave was ever successfully reinstalled; status as of research date is unconfirmed for the inflatable Airwave specifically, and Waveco's current Bunbury-facing project appears to be a different (granite) technology [R8][R11][R18][R20] Addition 2026-10-10: per the founder (interview 8 Oct 2026), they are now going for concrete [R25]. Not independently confirmed; consistent in direction with the rock/granite proposal in [R20] but not the same material.

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Bunbury sits near Margaret River, a premier surf destination, but Back Beach had swell without the bathymetry to shape it into rideable waves [R1][R2][R6]. Waveco founder Troy Bottegal had spent roughly a decade developing the inflatable-bladder concept and wanted a real-world test site [R2][R10]; the City of Bunbury under Mayor Gary Brennan saw it as a low-cost way to brand the town as a surfing destination and draw competitions and tourism [R2].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: A 12 m-diameter, dome-shaped inflatable rubber bladder anchored to the seabed with sand ballast, filled with air/sand/water, sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]. It was meant to 'lift, peak, and hold the swell to create a concave, tapered wall of water that retains its shape as it peels toward the beach' [R19], producing an A-frame peak with left and right breaks where there had previously only been closeouts [R3]. Bottegal modelled the intended wave on Thunderbomb, a wave in Nicaragua [R4]. It was designed to work across roughly 2–8 ft swell, with expected ride length ~40 m / 26 seconds, over an estimated 150 rideable-swell days per year [R2][R3][R9]. A hard-wired webcam and a planned 12-month University of Western Australia scientific study were part of the design [R9]. The reversibility/removability of the inflatable design (not ecological habitat creation) was the explicit environmental/cost pitch — 'if they don't do what you want them to do... they take half a day to move' [R10].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction was reported 'halfway complete' in October 2019 against a November 2019 install target [R4]; installation slipped to December 2019, and divers/boat crew got the bladder to ~90% complete (deployed but not fully anchored) when an unexpectedly large, deep offshore swell drove strong undertow through the line-up during the final fill/anchoring phase, tearing a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The tear was along the seam, not the rubber itself [R1]; the underlying cause was the choice of Hypalon rubber, which could not be welded and so had to be glued — a joint that could not withstand pump pressure during the final fill [R8]. The bladder was removed within about three days (one conflicting account says half a day) [R1][R5][R8][R18]. The reef therefore was never completed to its designed, fully-anchored, surfable state (card author's inference from the ~90 % complete, not fully anchored state in [R1][R5]). Addition 2026-10-10: the founder says the final design used SAND instead of AIR as the fill, because the engineers found air did not respond well with the waves; the failure was a seam that opened up a couple of days after installation (not a tear during the fill phase), and until then it worked "amazingly" [R25, notes as reported by Lior]. Both accounts kept; see sources_disagree. [R25]

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Installation was not completed: the bladder tore and was pulled from the water, unsurfable in its intended form [R1][R5][R8]. During the brief period it was partially in the water, Bottegal later reported that 'a wave did break on it... peeled nearly all the way to the beach... created a 0.75 metre wave' — the only quantified wave-performance data found, describing a small, uncontrolled result rather than a validated trial [R8]. No formal UWA study results were found; the planned 12-month study appears never to have started [R9]. A second prototype installation was being planned for December 2020 with a further A$300,000 [R18], but no source confirms it happened or succeeded. A 2022 article promised a Summer 2024 relaunch after moving fabrication to WA [R8]; a June 2024 Instagram post shows an active surf-cam [R11]; but by September 2025 Waveco's active Bunbury-facing project had shifted to a different, granite (rock) reef design aimed at coastal-erosion protection [R20]. No source listed in References confirms (negative finding of this card) the inflatable Airwave was ever successfully completed and operating as a surf reef at Bunbury. Addition 2026-10-10: founder says the structure worked perfectly until a seam opened a couple of days after installation [R25]; the card keeps the independent record (tear during installation, removal within about three days) and records the disagreement.

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Failure mechanism (installation, Dec 2019): an unexpectedly deep offshore swell during the final anchoring/fill phase generated strong undertow that flexed the bladder, concentrating stress on a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The underlying materials cause was the use of Hypalon rubber, which cannot be welded; the glued seams used instead could not withstand pressure reached during the final pump/fill stage [R8]. This was a materials/fabrication-method failure compounded by an installation-timing/weather-window problem, rather than a wave-performance or siting failure — the reef never reached a state where its surf-shaping performance could be properly judged (the card author's synthesis of [R1][R5][R6][R8]; the classification is an inference, not a source statement). Addition 2026-10-10: founder account (personal communication): the seam opened a couple of days after installation, and the fill choice for the final design moved from air to sand because air did not respond well with the waves [R25]. This agrees that a seam was the failure point, but differs on timing and on whether the structure was complete (card author's comparison of [R25] with [R1][R5][R8]).

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The one recorded moment of the Airwave functioning — before the tear forced its removal — reportedly produced a wave that 'peeled nearly all the way to the beach' and reached about 0.75 m, an unplanned, brief glimpse of the concept working, per Bottegal's later account [R8]. No sources document fishing-pressure effects, ecological colonization, rip-current changes, safety incidents, or litigation connected to this installation in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card) — plausible given the structure was never operational for an extended period (card author's inference). Local news noted reputational 'deflation' for Bunbury when the trial failed on a high-profile install day [R1]. Addition 2026-10-10: the founder told Lior that until the seam opened it "worked amazingly, perfect waves" [R25, personal communication, notes as reported by Lior]. This is a self-interested, unrecorded, second-hand account; no independent report, photo or video confirms it, and it is larger than the single 0.75 m wave in [R8].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: From Waveco/the designer's own account: the identified fix was materials and fabrication method — move away from glued Hypalon seams (relocating manufacture to a WA-based manufacturer) and secure fresh investment before re-attempting installation [R8]. Bottegal framed the setback as a timing/weather issue (an unplanned deep swell during the vulnerable, partially-anchored install phase) rather than a fundamental design flaw, maintaining '100 percent' confidence the concept would work [R6]. Detailed surfer/commentator critique was not found in the sources successfully retrieved for this research (negative finding of this card) [see dossier for blocked forum sources]. Addition 2026-10-10: the founder says the next version goes to CONCRETE (no detail on design, date or site) [R25]; the final design as described fills with sand, not air [R25].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Bunbury sits on a microtidal WA coast (tidal range roughly ~1 m or less) [R13], broadly comparable in scale to the Mediterranean's small tidal range at Haifa — not itself a factor implicated in the Bunbury failure, but relevant to sizing an Israeli pilot in a similarly low-tide setting. Wave climate differs in kind: Bunbury/SW WA faces Southern Ocean groundswell (~150 rideable-swell days/year) [R9], far more energetic than the Eastern Mediterranean's short-period, wind-driven seas off Haifa. What transfers: (1) the low-cost [R10], rapidly-removable [R18] inflatable concept is attractive for a wave-poor, low-tidal-range coast like Israel's, avoiding large capital commitment before wave performance is proven; (2) the documented failure mode — glued (not welded) seam material failing under dynamic swell/undertow loading during the vulnerable partially-anchored installation phase — is a fabrication/installation-window risk any Israeli inflatable-reef pilot would need to solve first, independent of local wave/tide conditions (failure mode: [R1][R8]; the transfer is the card author's inference); (3) because Israel's swell energy is much lower than SW Australia's (card author's general statement, (unsourced) here), a device sized for Bunbury's 2–8 ft face range (UNSOURCED figure: no reference in this card gives it; treat as unverified) may be oversized for Haifa's smaller everyday waves and would need dedicated re-sizing/modelling, not found in any source reviewed here. Tide range check: GHD (2021) Table 1 gives Port of Bunbury HAT 0.6 and LAT -0.6 m AHD, a range of 1.2 m, MSL +0.1 m AHD [R26], consistent with the sample-day heights of [R13] (which are one day only).

disagree.why_ours: R3 (raisedwaterresearch.com, re-fetched 2026-09-25) states directly: 'at low tide, the shallow point is about 1m under the surface of the water.' No source supports 1.8 m. Traced Gemini's own working: its `reef_footprints.json` gives `coastal_context.ambient_seabed_depth_m = 3.8` and `crest_depth_m = 1.8` with the note 'Dome inflated to 2m height; crest submerged 1.8m' -- i.e. Gemini computed 3.8 - 2.0 = 1.8, but the 3.8 m 'ambient seabed depth' input is not sourced anywhere in Gemini's own files or ours; it appears to be an assumed/invented figure, not a cited one. Gemini's own two cited sources for this reef (a 2019 'project brief' and a 2020 Surfer Magazine review) do not appear anywhere in our reference list or in the pages we located, so they could not be independently checked.

R3 states a 30-45 m design-target range, not a single figure; R2 was re-checked 2026-09-25 and does not mention any offshore distance at all (an earlier draft of this file incorrectly cited R2 alongside R3 for this number). Gemini's 38 m happens to fall inside R3's range but is not itself sourced anywhere we could find (Gemini's own polygon in `reef_footprints.json` is simply centered at y=38, matching its stated value with no separate citation); we report the documented range's midpoint (37.5 m) instead of an unsourced point estimate.

footprint.confidence: The structure is clearly visible as a circle on a real near-nadir drone photo of the installed bladder (img1), and a second video frame from a different angle and the design plan graphic agree it is a circle. But no image has a scale bar or geo-reference and no satellite image can show it (it existed about a week in Dec 2019), so the 12 m size comes from news/site text rather than being measured, and the exact location is not traced.
open_issues: The reef was never completed (installation reached ~90% before a glued seam tore and the bladder was removed within days); every figure here is an as-designed value, not an as-installed/as-surveyed one.

Height above seabed is inconsistently reported: 2 m (R1,R2,R3 contemporaneous) vs 1.6 m (1 later retrospective, R8); R6's imperial 'about 7-feet' is an approximate corroboration only, not an independent precise measurement.

R3 and R9 in the verified card cite the same raisedwaterresearch.com URL under two different reference ids -- likely a minor duplication in the card, noted here but not corrected (out of scope for this footprint-only task).
No exact installed lat/lon or surveyed offshore distance exists; 30-45 m is the pre-installation design target, sourced to R3 only (R2 does not mention offshore distance).
Volume (117.3 m3) is our own geometric estimate, not a published figure; offered only as a sand-tonnage plausibility check.

Gemini's two cited sources for this reef ('Bottegal 2019 Project Brief', 'Surfer Magazine Trial Review 2020') could not be located or verified; treat Gemini's crest-depth and offshore-distance figures as unverified. Traced the specific mechanism of Gemini's 1.8 m crest-depth figure: it equals Gemini's own (unsourced) 3.8 m 'ambient seabed depth' input minus the 2.0 m height -- an internally consistent but externally unsupported calculation.

Attribution note: the earlier draft of this file's claim that Bunbury 'matches the flag already in Gemini's own suspicious notes' was imprecisely worded -- that 'suspicious' annotation ('one of the better-matched reefs') actually lives in OUR project's own intermediate extract file (07_scale/00_gemini_footprints_extract.json), not inside the Gemini folder itself. Gemini's own self-audit file (scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md, row 11) independently marks Bunbury 'VERIFIED' with no discrepancy flagged. Both statements are substantively accurate; only the attribution of which file the note lives in has been corrected here.

Three citation errors found and fixed during 2026-09-25 adversarial verification: (1) R2 (ABC 2019-06-13) was wrongly cited alongside R3 for the 12 m diameter and the 30-45 m offshore distance -- re-fetched twice with targeted prompts and confirmed R2 states ONLY the 2 m height, nothing else; (2) R1's diameter quote was wrongly given the '(40 feet)' parenthetical that actually belongs to R3 -- R1's real text is metric-only ('two-metre-high, 12-metre-wide'); (3) R6 (The Inertia) was quoted as giving a precise '6.5 feet' height when the actual (Wayback-Machine-verified, since the live URL 403s) text says 'about 7-feet high' -- a looser rounding. None of these fixes changed any headline number (12 m, 2 m, 1.0 m, 30-45 m all still hold on corrected citations), but the reference attributions have been corrected throughout. A fourth fix: the fill-material quote 'washed, coarse beach sand' was not actually found on the R3 page and has been replaced with the verbatim R3 quote (sand + water + air).

name: Palm Beach Reef
year: Concept design 2013; detailed design 2013–2014; construction Apr/May–Oct 2019; finalised and certified Sept 2019 [R1][R3][R5]
type: Submerged rock (quarried boulder) reef, 4–8 t boulders on individual sourcing (up to 8 t per most sources), NOT geotextile sand containers — a deliberate contrast with Narrowneck [R2][R4][R7][R16] Crest level in other datums: -1.5 m MSL = about -0.62 m relative to LAT, using Gold Coast Seaway MSL = LAT + 0.88 m [R23]; the concept paper gives the crest as -1.5 m AHD (Mortensen et al. 2015, p.4), and AHD is 0.12 m below MSL at the Seaway benchmark (AHD = LAT + 0.760 m, MSQ 2014), a difference inside the +-0.2 m crest uncertainty and not applied in the 3D model [R22][R23]. A charted 'FISH HAVEN 1.5MT' label (chart as read by the shape agent, not cited as a reference in this card) differs from the design by 0.88 m, which is the MSL-LAT offset of the Seaway [R23] (DERIVED, open: this project, 07_scale/shapes/palm-beach-gold-coast/HANDOFF.md section 5.2).
purpose: Multipurpose, in order of priority: (1) coastal-erosion protection for a narrow, storm-vulnerable beach; (2) surf amenity (a right-hand wave), explicit in the design brief from the start, unlike Narrowneck; (3) marine habitat, unquantified [R3][R8][R12][R13][R16]
size: 160 m long × 80 m wide "core" per most sources, vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own page giving 144 m wide (unresolved); ~270 m offshore per most sources vs Royal HaskoningDHV's 330 m (unresolved); crest 1.5 m below MSL at highest point, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide; ~25,000 m³ of rock (~60,000 tonnes of boulders) [R2][R4][R5][R6][R7][R9][R13][R15] Project-measured geometry (2026-10-10 audit; not source statements): the City of Gold Coast asset polygon (160 x 80 m nominal, area 11,941.7 m2) [R19] and the Bluecoast/Nearmap aerial with survey contours [R20] give a toe outline of 11,972 m2, oriented rectangle 162.3 x 91.3 m (mean width 73.8 m), long axis 109.6 deg true, about 45 deg to the shore; nearest toe edge 225 m, centroid 305 m and farthest 374 m from the Esri 2025-12-01 waterline (279 m from the OSM coast); the '~270 m' of the sources has no stated start point [R21]. The 144 m width on Royal HaskoningDHV's page equals the width of the unbuilt concept designs SCS A/B/C (175 x 144 m) [R22]. Rock quantities differ in kind: ~25,000 m3 quarried rock and ~60,000 t [R13]; the project's 3D envelope volume is 22,020 m3 (inferred from contours, voids included, a seabed offset of -0.5 / +0.5 m gives 28,010 / 16,537 m3, HANDOFF 3.3); the City asset register shows 33,000 (units not stated).
cost: AU$18.2 million per most sources, vs AU$18.3 million per ICM's technical comparison (both cited, unresolved) [R2][R4][R7][R8][R9][R12][R13][R16]
cost_usd_approx: ~US$12.5 million (Raised Water Research's own stated conversion, ~2019 rate) [R2]
financed_by: City of Gold Coast (local council), under its Ocean Beaches Strategy (adopted 2015); no state/federal co-funding found in any source checked [R8][R12]
motivation: Palm Beach is the Gold Coast's most erosion-prone beach, with the coastal road running close to the shore [R11][R16]. An earlier 2004 reef proposal near 21st Avenue was defeated by a community 'no reef' campaign and never built [R10][R16]. The successful 2013–2019 project is Phase 2 of the Palm Beach Shoreline Project, following a 2017 sand-nourishment Phase 1, and was pushed forward by a run of severe storms (2013 storm damage, a 2014 Climate Council sea-level-rise report, the 2015 Ocean Beaches Strategy, and Cyclone Oma battering Palm Beach in early 2019) [R5][R8][R12]. Mayor Tom Tate was the principal political champion throughout [R8][R12][R16].
designer: Disputed/multi-party, unreconciled across sources: DHI Australia (lead, principal engineer Simon Mortensen, won the Concept Design Study by open tender in 2013) [R3][R18]; Royal HaskoningDHV (design reference report, hydrodynamic modelling, environmental assessment, construction-phase QA, final engineering certification) [R5]; Bluecoast Consulting Engineers (core consultancy team, construction QA, as-built certification) [R1]. No source lays out how these three roles fit together.
contractor: HC2 joint venture — Hall Contracting Pty Ltd (AU) and Heron Construction Company (NZ); built using a backhoe dredge for precise rock placement, rock sourced from South-East Queensland quarries and barged from the Port of Brisbane [R4][R16]
status_now: Operational as of the most recent source checked (ICM article, updated Feb 2025, still describes it in the present tense); no removal, decommissioning, or major structural-damage report found for this reef specifically in any source fetched, including a targeted (unsuccessful) search for Cyclone Alfred (March 2025) impact [R13] Monitoring: the ICCE 2022 monitoring abstract (Prenzler et al.) reports a stable structure with no significant movement or settlement [R24] (abstract page only read; DOI, pages and full author list not confirmed).
hover_text: A 160×80 m submerged boulder reef built 2019 for AU$18.2M by the City of Gold Coast to fight erosion at Palm Beach, with a right-hand surf wave designed in from the start; it retained roughly 550,000 m³ of sand in its first two years and delivers a modest, workable (not world-class) wave, though a narrow shallow-to-deep tidal window draws local complaints [R2][R9][R15].
design_as_planned: DHI Australia (lead designer Simon Mortensen) combined empirical surf knowledge — Mortensen personally surfing Palm Beach and reference breaks — with numerical modelling (DHI's MIKE 21 SM shoreline module using 30 years of wave/current data, a 3D VOF model in OpenFOAM, in-house OptiSurf surf-simulation software) and physical wave-tank testing for rock sizing [R3][R18]. The reef was deliberately sited 'in the lee of a natural reef' offshore to exploit an existing natural wave-focusing zone, targeting a right-hand wave 'suitable for average [to advanced] surfers with accessible takeoffs and extended wall length,' with a secondary short, more intense left on larger swells [R3][R13][R15][R17]. Rock (not geotextile, as used at Narrowneck) was chosen for its 100+-year coastal-engineering track record, precise shape control, expected habitat value, and to avoid geotextile bags' documented tearing/removal-cost problems [R3]. Design freeboard was set at a minimum 1.5 m below mean sea level, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide, based on six years of local swell data [R2][R15]. Mortensen himself framed it as 'always a compromise... especially since the main focus was coastal protection' [R3].
as_built_vs_design: The built reef matches the planned footprint (size field [R19][R22]) and dominant right-hand wave, but execution surfaced issues not evident in the design promise (the card author's summary of the findings below [R15]). Swellnet's July 2019 first-look (at ~50% completion) reported the reef 'alarmingly shallow, with one rock even breaking the surface,' and a forum commenter described it going 'from too shallow to too deep really quickly' across the tide cycle — a narrower-than-hoped surfable tidal window [R15]. The timeline held essentially to plan rather than beating it: Swellnet's own 23 Aug 2019 update reported the reef only ~50% complete and 'still on track for an October finish,' and the project was finalised/certified in September 2019 — consistent with, not ahead of, the original target [R1][R5][R17]. Cost and dimension figures vary slightly by source (AU$18.2M vs AU$18.3M; 80 m vs 144 m width; 270 m vs 330 m offshore), plausibly rounding/measurement-basis differences between the council's headline figures and individual consultants' own project pages, though no source explains the gap [R2][R4][R5][R7][R9][R13].
outcome: Surfing: on its first meaningful swell test (July 2019, reef ~50% built) it broke 4–5 ft waves with rides up to ~30 m; at completion it produced a consistent right with a short, thick left on bigger swells, handling at least double-overhead SE swells [R6][R15][R17]. The Inertia groups Palm Beach with Cable Station and Burkitts Reef among Australian stone reefs delivering 'modest, measurable improvements in the quality of waves' without becoming world-class breaks [R18]. Coastal protection: ABC News reported approximately 550,000 m³ of sand retained over the reef's first two years of operation — the clearest quantitative protection outcome found [R9]. Coastal engineer Evan Watterson argued such structures compare favourably to plain beach nourishment 'over a 30-year period' [R9]. Ecology: marine-habitat creation is claimed by both Bluecoast and Raised Water Research but with zero ecological survey data found in any source fetched [R1][R2]. Longevity: no storm-damage, structural-failure, or removal reports were found for this reef specifically [R13][R17]. Awards: IPWEAQ 2019 Excellence Award for Innovation and a 2020 Excellence Award for Coastal Engineering [R5].
why_worked_or_failed: Sources repeatedly credit the rock-over-geotextile material choice as the key differentiator from failed reef projects elsewhere — rock's long engineering track record, precise shape-control, and habitat value versus geotextile bags' history of tearing and expensive removal [R3][R13][R18]. Siting the reef behind an existing natural reef to pre-focus wave energy is credited with helping it punch above its size for surf quality [R3][R13]. The tuned crest depth/freeboard (1.5 m below MSL / 60 cm at LAT) balanced rideable wave height against safety, but the resulting narrow, fast-changing tidal window drew user complaints [R15]. Lead designer Simon Mortensen's own stated regret was about process, not physical design: 'we would have been more realistic in our budgeting on how long it would actually take to work on this reef. The City got a good deal' [R3]. ICM's own comparison attributes Palm Beach's stronger wave outcome (versus Narrowneck) to its surf-first design brief at a materially higher unit cost (~AU$700/m³ vs ~AU$30/m³ at Narrowneck): 'when the objective is surfing, the design can be more focused and effective' [R13].
unexpected_results: Rock breaking the surface at low tide, flagged by Swellnet as a possible safety/design concern locals questioned [R15]. A single joking Swellnet forum comment about a shark sighting ('Predatory Pirate Shark circles Palmy Reef') was not corroborated by any other source and is not treated here as a real trend [R17]. Crowding complaints: because the reef breaks predominantly as a right-hander in a region already dominated by right-hand points, some surfers criticised it for adding to an existing imbalance and concentrating crowds [R17]. The pre-existing 2004 'no reef' community backlash that killed an earlier reef proposal at the same beach is itself a notable data point about local social license, given the later, larger 2019 project proceeded with comparatively less reported opposition [R10][R16].
could_be_better: Simon Mortensen's own retrospective criticism concerns process, not the built structure: the consultancy underestimated how long the multi-year design phase would take [R3]. Outside civil engineer Shane Abel (not on the design team) argued before construction that 'whatever they build in the ocean should be removable and 8 tonnes of rock isn't,' proposing a removable design instead of the fixed boulder approach [R16]. The Palm Beach Board Riders Club (Mike Gifford) felt stakeholder consultation with surfers was inadequate ahead of construction [R16]. Post-construction surfer commentary focused on the tide-sensitivity problem — the narrow window between 'too shallow' and 'too deep' — suggesting a design tweak to crest depth or profile might have produced a more forgiving tidal window [R15]. Some surfers also felt the community would have been better served by a different wave shape (e.g. a left or a peak) given the Gold Coast's existing abundance of right-hand points [R17].
relevance_to_israel: Tide range: Palm Beach is microtidal (~1.5 m illustrative weekly range per a live tide check), broadly consistent with the reef's own 1.5 m/60 cm freeboard spec; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is essentially micro-tidal to negligible-tidal, which means Palm Beach's core challenge — keeping a fixed-crest structure inside a workable 'not too shallow, not too deep' window across the tide cycle — would be more forgiving at Haifa, since Haifa's tide swing is smaller [R14][R15]. Wave climate: Palm Beach's design leaned on six years of dominant east-to-southeast Pacific ocean swell arriving at a site with an existing natural offshore reef to pre-focus it; Haifa's Mediterranean wave climate is smaller and less consistent, meaning a Haifa reef would likely need to actively increase wave height rather than merely reshape already-large incoming swell [R3][R15]. What transfers: (1) the rock-over-geotextile durability and shape-control lesson is directly transferable regardless of wave climate; (2) siting behind/near an existing natural feature to pre-focus energy is a transferable design principle, though Haifa may lack an equivalent natural offshore reef; (3) the tide-window lesson is less of a constraint for Haifa given its smaller tidal range, giving more freedom in crest-depth choice; (4) the cost lesson — Palm Beach's much higher per-m³ cost than Narrowneck reflects the premium of prioritising surf quality in the design brief — is directly relevant to budgeting a Haifa reef if surf quality is a primary goal [R13]. Tide planes (Gold Coast Seaway, MSQ 2026, above LAT): HAT 2.03, MHWS 1.53, MHWN 1.24, MSL 0.88, MLWN 0.51, MLWS 0.22 m, i.e. a spring range (MHWS - MLWS) of 1.31 m and HAT - LAT of 2.03 m [R23]; this replaces the single-week 'illustrative' 1.5 m of WillyWeather [R14]. Haifa tidal range itself is not sourced in this card.

We want Palm Beach to be enjoyed by everyone and to achieve this, we need to invest wisely in the shoreline project (2018); it is a wonderful day, finally, to be able to say we are going to commence this artificial reef (2019); the artificial reef is designed to control wave energy before it reaches the shore, resulting in a build-up of sand that will act as a buffer during storm season and swell events (post-completion).

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NamePalm Beach Reef
PlacePalm Beach, Gold Coast, Queensland
CountryAustralia
YearConcept design 2013; detailed design 2013–2014; construction Apr/May–Oct 2019; finalised and certified Sept 2019 [R1][R3][R5]
TypeSubmerged rock (quarried boulder) reef, 4–8 t boulders on individual sourcing (up to 8 t per most sources), NOT geotextile sand containers — a deliberate contrast with Narrowneck [R2][R4][R7][R16] Crest level in other datums: -1.5 m MSL = about -0.62 m relative to LAT, using Gold Coast Seaway MSL = LAT + 0.88 m [R23]; the concept paper gives the crest as -1.5 m AHD (Mortensen et al. 2015, p.4), and AHD is 0.12 m below MSL at the Seaway benchmark (AHD = LAT + 0.760 m, MSQ 2014), a difference inside the +-0.2 m crest uncertainty and not applied in the 3D model [R22][R23]. A charted 'FISH HAVEN 1.5MT' label (chart as read by the shape agent, not cited as a reference in this card) differs from the design by 0.88 m, which is the MSL-LAT offset of the Seaway [R23] (DERIVED, open: this project, 07_scale/shapes/palm-beach-gold-coast/HANDOFF.md section 5.2).
PurposeMultipurpose, in order of priority: (1) coastal-erosion protection for a narrow, storm-vulnerable beach; (2) surf amenity (a right-hand wave), explicit in the design brief from the start, unlike Narrowneck; (3) marine habitat, unquantified [R3][R8][R12][R13][R16]
Size160 m long × 80 m wide "core" per most sources, vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own page giving 144 m wide (unresolved); ~270 m offshore per most sources vs Royal HaskoningDHV's 330 m (unresolved); crest 1.5 m below MSL at highest point, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide; ~25,000 m³ of rock (~60,000 tonnes of boulders) [R2][R4][R5][R6][R7][R9][R13][R15] Project-measured geometry (2026-10-10 audit; not source statements): the City of Gold Coast asset polygon (160 x 80 m nominal, area 11,941.7 m2) [R19] and the Bluecoast/Nearmap aerial with survey contours [R20] give a toe outline of 11,972 m2, oriented rectangle 162.3 x 91.3 m (mean width 73.8 m), long axis 109.6 deg true, about 45 deg to the shore; nearest toe edge 225 m, centroid 305 m and farthest 374 m from the Esri 2025-12-01 waterline (279 m from the OSM coast); the '~270 m' of the sources has no stated start point [R21]. The 144 m width on Royal HaskoningDHV's page equals the width of the unbuilt concept designs SCS A/B/C (175 x 144 m) [R22]. Rock quantities differ in kind: ~25,000 m3 quarried rock and ~60,000 t [R13]; the project's 3D envelope volume is 22,020 m3 (inferred from contours, voids included, a seabed offset of -0.5 / +0.5 m gives 28,010 / 16,537 m3, HANDOFF 3.3); the City asset register shows 33,000 (units not stated).
CostAU$18.2 million per most sources, vs AU$18.3 million per ICM's technical comparison (both cited, unresolved) [R2][R4][R7][R8][R9][R12][R13][R16]
Cost (approx. USD)~US$12.5 million (Raised Water Research's own stated conversion, ~2019 rate) [R2]
Financed byCity of Gold Coast (local council), under its Ocean Beaches Strategy (adopted 2015); no state/federal co-funding found in any source checked [R8][R12]
DesignerDisputed/multi-party, unreconciled across sources: DHI Australia (lead, principal engineer Simon Mortensen, won the Concept Design Study by open tender in 2013) [R3][R18]; Royal HaskoningDHV (design reference report, hydrodynamic modelling, environmental assessment, construction-phase QA, final engineering certification) [R5]; Bluecoast Consulting Engineers (core consultancy team, construction QA, as-built certification) [R1]. No source lays out how these three roles fit together.
ContractorHC2 joint venture — Hall Contracting Pty Ltd (AU) and Heron Construction Company (NZ); built using a backhoe dredge for precise rock placement, rock sourced from South-East Queensland quarries and barged from the Port of Brisbane [R4][R16]
Status nowOperational as of the most recent source checked (ICM article, updated Feb 2025, still describes it in the present tense); no removal, decommissioning, or major structural-damage report found for this reef specifically in any source fetched, including a targeted (unsuccessful) search for Cyclone Alfred (March 2025) impact [R13] Monitoring: the ICCE 2022 monitoring abstract (Prenzler et al.) reports a stable structure with no significant movement or settlement [R24] (abstract page only read; DOI, pages and full author list not confirmed).
Verdictpartly worked

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Palm Beach is the Gold Coast's most erosion-prone beach, with the coastal road running close to the shore [R11][R16]. An earlier 2004 reef proposal near 21st Avenue was defeated by a community 'no reef' campaign and never built [R10][R16]. The successful 2013–2019 project is Phase 2 of the Palm Beach Shoreline Project, following a 2017 sand-nourishment Phase 1, and was pushed forward by a run of severe storms (2013 storm damage, a 2014 Climate Council sea-level-rise report, the 2015 Ocean Beaches Strategy, and Cyclone Oma battering Palm Beach in early 2019) [R5][R8][R12]. Mayor Tom Tate was the principal political champion throughout [R8][R12][R16].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: DHI Australia (lead designer Simon Mortensen) combined empirical surf knowledge — Mortensen personally surfing Palm Beach and reference breaks — with numerical modelling (DHI's MIKE 21 SM shoreline module using 30 years of wave/current data, a 3D VOF model in OpenFOAM, in-house OptiSurf surf-simulation software) and physical wave-tank testing for rock sizing [R3][R18]. The reef was deliberately sited 'in the lee of a natural reef' offshore to exploit an existing natural wave-focusing zone, targeting a right-hand wave 'suitable for average [to advanced] surfers with accessible takeoffs and extended wall length,' with a secondary short, more intense left on larger swells [R3][R13][R15][R17]. Rock (not geotextile, as used at Narrowneck) was chosen for its 100+-year coastal-engineering track record, precise shape control, expected habitat value, and to avoid geotextile bags' documented tearing/removal-cost problems [R3]. Design freeboard was set at a minimum 1.5 m below mean sea level, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide, based on six years of local swell data [R2][R15]. Mortensen himself framed it as 'always a compromise... especially since the main focus was coastal protection' [R3].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The built reef matches the planned footprint (size field [R19][R22]) and dominant right-hand wave, but execution surfaced issues not evident in the design promise (the card author's summary of the findings below [R15]). Swellnet's July 2019 first-look (at ~50% completion) reported the reef 'alarmingly shallow, with one rock even breaking the surface,' and a forum commenter described it going 'from too shallow to too deep really quickly' across the tide cycle — a narrower-than-hoped surfable tidal window [R15]. The timeline held essentially to plan rather than beating it: Swellnet's own 23 Aug 2019 update reported the reef only ~50% complete and 'still on track for an October finish,' and the project was finalised/certified in September 2019 — consistent with, not ahead of, the original target [R1][R5][R17]. Cost and dimension figures vary slightly by source (AU$18.2M vs AU$18.3M; 80 m vs 144 m width; 270 m vs 330 m offshore), plausibly rounding/measurement-basis differences between the council's headline figures and individual consultants' own project pages, though no source explains the gap [R2][R4][R5][R7][R9][R13].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Surfing: on its first meaningful swell test (July 2019, reef ~50% built) it broke 4–5 ft waves with rides up to ~30 m; at completion it produced a consistent right with a short, thick left on bigger swells, handling at least double-overhead SE swells [R6][R15][R17]. The Inertia groups Palm Beach with Cable Station and Burkitts Reef among Australian stone reefs delivering 'modest, measurable improvements in the quality of waves' without becoming world-class breaks [R18]. Coastal protection: ABC News reported approximately 550,000 m³ of sand retained over the reef's first two years of operation — the clearest quantitative protection outcome found [R9]. Coastal engineer Evan Watterson argued such structures compare favourably to plain beach nourishment 'over a 30-year period' [R9]. Ecology: marine-habitat creation is claimed by both Bluecoast and Raised Water Research but with zero ecological survey data found in any source fetched [R1][R2]. Longevity: no storm-damage, structural-failure, or removal reports were found for this reef specifically [R13][R17]. Awards: IPWEAQ 2019 Excellence Award for Innovation and a 2020 Excellence Award for Coastal Engineering [R5].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Sources repeatedly credit the rock-over-geotextile material choice as the key differentiator from failed reef projects elsewhere — rock's long engineering track record, precise shape-control, and habitat value versus geotextile bags' history of tearing and expensive removal [R3][R13][R18]. Siting the reef behind an existing natural reef to pre-focus wave energy is credited with helping it punch above its size for surf quality [R3][R13]. The tuned crest depth/freeboard (1.5 m below MSL / 60 cm at LAT) balanced rideable wave height against safety, but the resulting narrow, fast-changing tidal window drew user complaints [R15]. Lead designer Simon Mortensen's own stated regret was about process, not physical design: 'we would have been more realistic in our budgeting on how long it would actually take to work on this reef. The City got a good deal' [R3]. ICM's own comparison attributes Palm Beach's stronger wave outcome (versus Narrowneck) to its surf-first design brief at a materially higher unit cost (~AU$700/m³ vs ~AU$30/m³ at Narrowneck): 'when the objective is surfing, the design can be more focused and effective' [R13].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Rock breaking the surface at low tide, flagged by Swellnet as a possible safety/design concern locals questioned [R15]. A single joking Swellnet forum comment about a shark sighting ('Predatory Pirate Shark circles Palmy Reef') was not corroborated by any other source and is not treated here as a real trend [R17]. Crowding complaints: because the reef breaks predominantly as a right-hander in a region already dominated by right-hand points, some surfers criticised it for adding to an existing imbalance and concentrating crowds [R17]. The pre-existing 2004 'no reef' community backlash that killed an earlier reef proposal at the same beach is itself a notable data point about local social license, given the later, larger 2019 project proceeded with comparatively less reported opposition [R10][R16].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Simon Mortensen's own retrospective criticism concerns process, not the built structure: the consultancy underestimated how long the multi-year design phase would take [R3]. Outside civil engineer Shane Abel (not on the design team) argued before construction that 'whatever they build in the ocean should be removable and 8 tonnes of rock isn't,' proposing a removable design instead of the fixed boulder approach [R16]. The Palm Beach Board Riders Club (Mike Gifford) felt stakeholder consultation with surfers was inadequate ahead of construction [R16]. Post-construction surfer commentary focused on the tide-sensitivity problem — the narrow window between 'too shallow' and 'too deep' — suggesting a design tweak to crest depth or profile might have produced a more forgiving tidal window [R15]. Some surfers also felt the community would have been better served by a different wave shape (e.g. a left or a peak) given the Gold Coast's existing abundance of right-hand points [R17].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tide range: Palm Beach is microtidal (~1.5 m illustrative weekly range per a live tide check), broadly consistent with the reef's own 1.5 m/60 cm freeboard spec; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is essentially micro-tidal to negligible-tidal, which means Palm Beach's core challenge — keeping a fixed-crest structure inside a workable 'not too shallow, not too deep' window across the tide cycle — would be more forgiving at Haifa, since Haifa's tide swing is smaller [R14][R15]. Wave climate: Palm Beach's design leaned on six years of dominant east-to-southeast Pacific ocean swell arriving at a site with an existing natural offshore reef to pre-focus it; Haifa's Mediterranean wave climate is smaller and less consistent, meaning a Haifa reef would likely need to actively increase wave height rather than merely reshape already-large incoming swell [R3][R15]. What transfers: (1) the rock-over-geotextile durability and shape-control lesson is directly transferable regardless of wave climate; (2) siting behind/near an existing natural feature to pre-focus energy is a transferable design principle, though Haifa may lack an equivalent natural offshore reef; (3) the tide-window lesson is less of a constraint for Haifa given its smaller tidal range, giving more freedom in crest-depth choice; (4) the cost lesson — Palm Beach's much higher per-m³ cost than Narrowneck reflects the premium of prioritising surf quality in the design brief — is directly relevant to budgeting a Haifa reef if surf quality is a primary goal [R13]. Tide planes (Gold Coast Seaway, MSQ 2026, above LAT): HAT 2.03, MHWS 1.53, MHWN 1.24, MSL 0.88, MLWN 0.51, MLWS 0.22 m, i.e. a spring range (MHWS - MLWS) of 1.31 m and HAT - LAT of 2.03 m [R23]; this replaces the single-week 'illustrative' 1.5 m of WillyWeather [R14]. Haifa tidal range itself is not sourced in this card.

footprint.orientation_notes: Elongated, rounded, asymmetric rock mound. Read off the two available plan-view graphics (the labelled aerial/schematic diagrams on Cru Collective's site, sourced from the project team) and cross-checked against the visible rock-shadow patch in the ABC News aerial photo, the mound tapers to a narrower, rounded point on its shoreward (near-shore) side and broadens to a blunter, rounded mass on its seaward (offshore) side — the opposite taper direction from Gemini's assumed 'apex seaward' chevron (see gemini_comparison). Long axis (160 m) treated as alongshore, short axis (80 m) as cross-shore, matching the conventional reading of '160 m long × 80 m wide' in every source, though no source explicitly labels which figure is alongshore vs cross-shore (flagged in open_issues). The reef sits in the lee of Palm Beach's natural offshore reef [R3], targeting dominant east-to-southeast swell [R2][R15], with sand naturally transported north along this stretch of coast [S1] — hence x-positive is defined as north. No source gives a numeric shoreline bearing or swell-approach angle; Gemini's '345° NNW shoreline / 090–110° swell' figures are not supported by any source we found and are not reproduced here.
footprint.materials: Quarried rock boulders, up to 8 t each (max individual weight, stated directly by S1, R4, R7, R16; re-verified 2026-09-25) — R2 separately describes a design-evolution note, "The rock size was increased from 3 tons to 5 and 8 ton rocks," implying discrete size classes rather than a continuous range; no source states a minimum boulder weight or a formal "X–8 t" range. [Verification 2026-09-25: an earlier draft of this file stated "4–8 t each" and attributed the range to R16; R16 was re-fetched and found to state only "up to eight tonne," with no minimum — the "4 t" figure was unsupported and has been removed.] Total ~60,000 tonnes [R7, R9 — both state "60,000 tonnes" directly; R2/R4/R16 do not give a total-tonnage figure], ~25,000 m³ by volume [R13]; rock type (e.g. basalt/granite) is not specified in any source we found [R2][R4][R7][R9][R13][R16]

footprint.confidence: The outline is read from a vertical aerial photo with a scale bar and north arrow and matches the City of Gold Coast GIS polygon of the installed reef to 0.55 m (area 11,972 vs 11,942 m2); the same size, shape and ~45-degree skew to the shore appear in an independent drawing (ICCE 2022 Fig 1) and the rock is visible on 2025 satellite imagery inside that outline. Length (162 m) agrees with the quoted 160 m; the soft spots are the '80 m wide' label (91 m maximum, 74 m average), an undated aerial whose survey contours are not labelled as design or as-built, and only a quarter to a third of the rock being visible on satellite.
open_issues: Width (80 m vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own 144 m) and distance offshore (270 m vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own 330 m) remain unresolved across every source checked, including this one — carried forward unchanged from the card [R5].

No source explicitly states which published figure (160 m or 80 m) is the alongshore dimension vs the cross-shore dimension; we assumed 160 m = alongshore and 80 m = cross-shore, matching the conventional reading and Gemini's own assumption, but this is an inference, not a stated fact.

The point from which '270 m offshore' is measured (near edge, far edge, or centroid) is not specified by any source; we assumed centroid for simplicity, which shifts the true near/far edges by roughly ±40-45 m depending on which convention the original designers used.

Verification 2026-09-25 flags an internal tension: our own reading of the Cru Collective schematic (images_relied_on #1) concludes the '270m' arrow visually lands on the reef's near/shoreward edge, not its centroid — yet the polygon below places the centroid (not the near edge) at y=270. If the near-edge reading is right, the whole polygon should sit roughly 40m further offshore than drawn (shoreward tip near y=266 instead of y=226, centroid near y=310 instead of y=270). This was not corrected in the polygon itself (doing so would require a new speculative construction, which this adversarial-check task's scope does not extend to), but is flagged here as an unresolved self-consistency issue for a future revision.

No true as-built CAD drawing or bathymetric survey of the constructed reef was found publicly (despite Gemini's citation, which does not correspond to any real accessible document); our polygon's exact vertex geometry is a qualitative estimate from a non-scaled marketing schematic plus a real aerial photo, not a measurement, and should be treated as illustrative of shape family (elongated, rounded, shoreward-tapered mound) rather than a precise outline.
Precise lat/lon of the reef structure itself (as opposed to the 19th Avenue onshore reference point) was not found in any source.
Net footprint area (~9,678 m2 here) is a geometric consequence of our assumed polygon shape, not an independently published or measured figure; treat as low-confidence.

verification.evidence: Recomputed independently with python + shapely: bounding box exactly 160.0 m (x) x 80.0 m (y); shoelace/shapely area = 9677.65 m2, matching the stated 9677.6 m2; polygon is closed, is_valid=True, exterior.is_simple=True (no self-intersections); area-weighted centroid = (0.031, 270.005), matching the stated design target of centroid at (0.03, 270.0).

verification.item: Plan-view shape / taper direction (narrow shoreward, broad seaward)
verification.evidence: Downloaded and directly viewed all three cited images (Completion2.jpg, Completion.jpg, ABC aerial) at high zoom. Completion2.jpg does show a shape narrower/pointed at the arrow (shoreward) end and blunter/wider at the far (seaward) end, consistent with the card's claim, and the '270m' arrow visually lands on the icon's near tip, not its center -- but the icon itself is a generic stock-style 3D rock graphic, not a purpose-drawn technical plan, so this is weak evidence. Completion.jpg's icon is too small/low-res to independently confirm taper direction. The ABC aerial photo's dark patch is elongated and roughly consistent with the claimed taper, but the active dredger sits at the patch's near/broad end, so dredging turbidity may be inflating that end's apparent width -- a confound not previously flagged. Net: the taper-direction call remains the best-supported reading available (better than Gemini's citation-free opposite claim) but should be read as plausible, weakly-evidenced qualitative shape family, not a confirmed geometric fact -- consistent with (and now more explicitly caveated than) the card's existing 'High uncertainty' label.

name: Southern Ocean Surf Reef ("Midds Reef")
year: Quarry establishment from ~Oct 2024 [R17]; first rock placed on the seabed 18 Mar 2025 (planned six weeks) [R26][R30]; 'more than two-thirds complete' 16 May 2025, finish pushed to mid-June [R27]; storm of Mon 26 May 2025 moved some core rock [R25][R28]; officially opened 16 July 2025 'after four months of work' [R29][R31][R1][R2]. The City's programme 'Jan-Mar 2025, practical completion Mar 2025' [R3][R32] was a plan, not what happened.
type: Submerged rock-berm surf reef, 62,800 t of layered granite per the City's design table (belly, core, Class 1 armour) [R3] (the ~70,000 t quoted by The Inertia [R6] is kept as a rounded journalistic figure), no geotextile [R2][R3][R1] Tonnage note (audit 2026-10-10): the City design table gives 62,800 t [R3]; the ~70,000 t of The Inertia [R6] is a rounded journalistic figure; both kept, the design table is preferred.
purpose: Surfing amenity / tourism / youth retention - the reef's sole and primary stated design objective; unlike most artificial surf reefs, coastal erosion protection was not a driver [R3][R8][R9]
size: Length 165 m; width up to 110 m; crest at -1.0 m AHD; total volume 62,800 t (belly D50 0.16 m/12,400 t, core D50 0.49 m/23,600 t, armour D50 0.94 m/26,800 t); reef sits ~140 m offshore [R3] Shape model (07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/HANDOFF.md section 3; HIGH confidence for position, size, orientation): default outline = Bluecoast final-design outermost contour [R3], placed on the Esri 2026-01-20 image by a fitted wedge (IoU 0.84); area 13,104 m2; along/across the crest 164.6 / 121.2 m (the card's 'width up to 110 m' is the design crest length at -2 m AHD, not the outline width); nearest edge 66.8 m from the beach-face line (the card's '~140 m offshore' is the City's value from an undefined reference, 'landward toe'; not reconciled). Volume about 34,000 m3 (DERIVED: 62,800 t [R3] divided by an assumed rock bulk density of 1.85 t/m3, ASSUMPTION of the shape agent with no source, 07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/HANDOFF.md section 3; the ~70,000 t of [R6] would give about 37,800 m3 by the same density). Crest levels are design values in AHD [R3], not surveyed; no as-built survey was found (negative search result of this project). The City's own design table (registry img-10, read again 2026-10-10) states 'Reef volume 34,000 m3 (based on 2017 bathymetry)' [R3], so the volume above is no longer only DERIVED: the table value and the tonnage-over-density value agree to within rounding. Seabed and water depth under the reef (3D model, LOW confidence, 07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/3d/METHODS_3D.md sections 3.2 and 4): about -2.1 m AHD at the shoreward apex to -7.4 m AHD at the offshore toe, DERIVED from the depth contours of the 2015 RHDHV Option B plan [R21] (datum not printed; read as AHD, georeferenced by hand); a 2018 BMT sounding of 2.7 m below chart datum near the shore is about 1.6 m deeper than that profile if chart datum equals AHD [R20] (unresolved). Update 2026-10-13 (Lior uploads, agent Albany uploads): Rock mass: the City's table gives 62,800 t [R3]; ABC and The Inertia say 70,000 t of granite [R2][R6]; Raised Water Research says 'more than 47,000 m3 (70,000 tonnes)', footprint 1.61 ha, 'designed 140-375 m offshore' and a crest 'roughly .75 m under the surface at low tide', mixing 2015 and final-design values with no source [R10][R23]. Distance offshore: 140 m [R3][R26] (City news of 7 Mar 2025) vs 120 m (City news of 16 Jul 2025 [R31], RWR 'about 120 m'); not reconciled. None of the four new sources gives an as-built level, crest survey, section or seabed depth, so the 3D model's seabed and heights are unchanged (LOW). A 70,000 t sensitivity is in the 3D model (design outline: 37,898 m3, mean height 2.89 m) [3d/METHODS_3D.md].
cost: City of Albany 'Total Committed Funds' AUD $11.75 million; Wikipedia/ABC/Beachgrit report project cost as approximately AUD $13 million [R3][R1][R7]
cost_usd_approx: ~USD $7.6-8.5 million at an approximate, unsourced AUD->USD conversion of ~0.65-0.72 (indicative only, not independently sourced) [R3][R1][R7] ASSUMPTION A1: the AUD->USD factor 0.65-0.72 is the agent's rough recollection, no exchange-rate source consulted (replace with the RBA rate for 2024-25); effect about +-10 %.
financed_by: Commonwealth (Australian) Government $4.75M; WA State Government (DPIRD) $5M; City of Albany $1.995M; Albany Boardriders club $5,000 [R3]. CONFLICT: the City page lists Commonwealth 4.75 M and WA 5 M; the WA Government statement of 14 Jan 2025 ('Cook Government is contributing $4.75 million') and Raised Water Research give WA 4.75 M and Commonwealth 5 M [R32][R10]; not resolved (the total is the same). WA state pledge from both major parties in the 2017 election; federal pledge from both major parties in 2022 [R3][R2][R6]
motivation: Middleton Beach produced 'unreliable and unsurfable waves for much of the year' despite being closest to central Albany; ~30 years of local-surfer advocacy (led by Peter Bolt from 1990) sought a consistent, surfable wave to build youth surf access, tourism, and economic development for Albany - not a response to erosion or a port-mitigation problem [R1][R6][R3][R8]
designer: Bluecoast Consulting Engineers, lead design engineer Evan Watterson (principal engineer at Bluecoast per the firm's own bio; 'Principal Coastal Engineer / Director' per a separate CV) [R3][R16]
contractor: Heron Construction Limited (main contractor; marine personnel crew mobilised from New Zealand); Stantec (project superintendent); Spinifex Crushing & Screening Services (rock supplier, quarry at Mindijup Rd, Palmdale); marine plant (backhoe dredge, barges/tugs) mobilised via Darwin and Adelaide [R3][R2][R6][R17]
status_now: Built and operating since July 2025 [R1][R2]. About 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days in late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026) by commercial divers with a local vessel and Albany Boardriders, at 'more than $20,000' (lede) or 'about $24,000' (City estimate), in response to a spate of user injuries [R3][R11][R8] Decision: verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source: wave quality is reported as a success [R2][R8][R10], but injuries led to a proposed detuning and a rock repositioning [R7][R11], and no monitoring data exist. The repositioning cost is from one paywalled article only (two figures in it: >20,000 and about 24,000; read from the page metadata, no login, see D12).
hover_text: 165 m long, 62,800-tonne rock reef built for AUD ~$13M (opened July 2025) that delivers a widely praised, better-than-design surf break - but its shallow, permeable rock crest caused repeated surfer injuries, forcing an 18-rock, $20,000+ safety 'detuning' in March 2026 [R1][R2][R3][R11].
design_as_planned: The 2015 Feasibility Study's objective was 'the creation of a consistent, surfable wave, which maximises available swell conditions' for Albany's economic and demographic benefit [R3]. The Detailed Design (executive summary by 2020) targeted a left-hand break, rides up to 100 m, and surfable waves 41% of the year, aimed at beginner-to-intermediate surfers per EPA WA [R3][R2][R9]. Design used 'thorough numerical, physical and conceptual modelling', with a 2018 BMT Environmental Impact Assessment, read at the source in October 2026: its shoreline-modelling appendix says 'In all the simulations tested, there appeared to be a widening of the shoreline' (PDF p.151) and the report expects offshore placement to give no significant shoreline impact compared with inshore placement (PDF p.38) [R20]; these findings were earlier cited via [R3][R8]. Business-case modelling projected NPV $57.9M / BCR 6.69, driven by ~10 annual surfing events and ~3,500 extra overnight visitors/year (an earlier May-2023 interim figure gave NPV $19.4M / BCR 3.25) [R3][R15].
as_built_vs_design: The built reef matches the design specification closely on paper: 165 m long, up to 110 m wide, crest at -1.0 m AHD, 62,800 t of rock in three graded layers [R3]. Construction: quarry from ~Oct 2024 [R17]; first rock on the seabed 18 Mar 2025, planned six weeks [R26][R30]; 'more than two-thirds complete' on 16 May 2025 with finish moved to mid-June [R27]; opened 16 Jul 2025 [R29][R31] (the earlier reading 'main placement Jan-Mar 2025, practical completion Mar 2025' came from the City's programme and the WA Government statement of 14 Jan 2025, which were plans [R3][R32]). A New Zealand marine crew used precision geospatial placement equipment [R3][R2][R8]. Storm of Mon 26 May 2025 (highest waves in King George Sound since 2017) moved some of the smaller CORE rock shoreward before the armour was on top; the contractor surveyed and replaced it before opening [R25][R28]. No as-built level, crest survey, section or seabed depth has been published (checked again 2026-10-13 in four new sources). Once open, the reef performed 'far higher' than the 41% design-surfability target [R2][R6], though no source gives a precise revised percentage (Raised Water Research gives about 40 % of the year breaking on the reef proper [R10], which does not support 'far higher'; the claim rests on quotes in R2/R6 only). The most significant post-opening change came in late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026): about 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days by commercial divers with a local vessel and Albany Boardriders, after surveys in late 2025; cost 'more than $20,000' in the article lede and 'about $24,000' as the City's estimate (paywalled article, text read from the page metadata) [R11][R18]. This is a later change: the 3D model shows the 2025 design state, and this goes in as a note, not as geometry.
outcome: Widely reported as a rare unambiguous artificial-surf-reef success on wave quality: Swellnet says 'the reef performs far better than expectations' [R8]; Peter Bolt calls it 'intermediate-to-advanced on most days' as swell grows [R6][R2]; local surfer Cameron Warburton calls it 'a really high-performance wave' [R2]. Raised Water Research describes 0.8-1.3 m faces, 100-120 m rides, breaking on the reef proper ~40% of the year [R10]. But a persistent forum question (Aug-Oct 2025, user 'steveb') is whether it breaks well on the small (<1 m) everyday swells that dominate the local climate; local 'soggydog' answered 'No, but it has created reliable banks either side when it's too small for the reef proper' [R8]. No monitoring data, beach-width surveys, storm-damage, or fisheries/ecology results were found in sources fetched, beyond the single 2018 EIA citation [R8].
why_worked_or_failed: Sources attribute the reef's relative success to layered, precision-placed rock construction rather than geotextile sand bags, which 'failed due to the bags splitting, shifting, or settling' at earlier reefs worldwide [R8][R3][R6]. Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) argues rock reefs cannot match a sand-formed bank's contour accuracy because armour rock must be massive for stability, so shallow enough placement to break small swells 'compromises user safety'; rock permeability also means small swells 'surge into the reef rather than shoal and break', while larger swells ride over imperfections and shoal further up - explaining why the reef performs much better on bigger swells [R8]. He contrasts Albany's shallow crest (-1.0 m AHD, chosen partly 'to maximise wave breaking') unfavourably with Palm Beach (Gold Coast), which mitigated injury risk with a deeper crest [R8][R3]. Mayor Greg Stocks frames the injuries more as a behavioural issue: 'inexperienced surfers taking on quite elite waves...the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that' [R7].
unexpected_results: Injuries began within weeks of opening: Swellnet forum posts from Albany locals describe 'a good face injury', sharp rocks cutting feet, and (per 'Baldhead') 'a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion' [R8]. By October 2025 the reef was being considered for 'detuning' ('busting up a couple of the rocks in the shallower part of the wave') following a 'spate of injuries on beginner surfers who can't handle its juice' [R7]. In late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026) about 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days, at 'more than $20,000' (lede) / 'about $24,000' (City estimate) [R11][R18]. Earlier, the storm of 26 May 2025 had already moved some core rock shoreward during construction [R25][R28]. 'steveb' argued this represented a public-liability/facility-design failure, comparing the reef to a council-managed playground where 'public safety is the number one priority' [R8]. Positive unplanned effects include reliable secondary sand-bank breaks either side of the reef on small swells, and youth/community access described by Peter Bolt watching 'the kids come down here before school, in the dark, to get a wave before they go to school' [R8][R2]. Shark risk is raised as a live community concern (no confirmed incident found) [R8].
could_be_better: Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) proposes that rock-dumped reefs inherently trade wave-shape accuracy against user safety, and argues a fully prefabricated reef structure - built onshore, floated out, and installed by controlled submergence - could achieve 'accurate shape and level, no subsidence, no settlement, no sharp edges, no possible entrapment points', citing materials with a 'safe working life in excess of 100 years', and points to Palm Beach's deeper, safer crest as a precedent for the safety/wave-quality trade-off Albany did not take [R8][R3]. Most surfer sentiment in the sources is not calling for a safer/easier wave - several posters push back on 'detuning' as inherent to a legitimately world-class wave - but there is a recurring, unanswered request for clearer information on how reliably the reef breaks on the small, sub-1 m swells that make up most of Middleton Beach's actual wave climate [R7][R8].
relevance_to_israel: King George Sound (Albany) is micro-tidal (mean range 0.4 m, spring 1.1 m), broadly comparable to the Mediterranean at Haifa, which is also effectively micro-tidal, though no fetched source gives a numeric Haifa tidal-range figure [R5][R10]. Official Albany figures differ in form from the Wikipedia ones: the 2018 BMT assessment gives a Middleton Beach spring range of 0.9 m and a neap range of 0.3 m, largest range below 1.5 m [R20]; the WA Department of Transport / Bureau of Meteorology predictions for 2024 run from 0.12 to 1.40 m above LAT, mean 0.742 m above LAT (1,043 high and low waters) [R22]. Datums and averaging periods differ, so the figures are not reconciled. Albany's wave climate (consistent, long-period 12-16s Southern Ocean groundswell) is fundamentally more energetic than Haifa's, where Lior's own Shikmona-buoy measurements define 'minimum surfable' at only 0.45-0.6 m within a narrow WNW swell window [R10][R12]; the 6-8 s period is NOT part of his buoy-based definition: in his notes it belongs to the '4Surfers' forecast-site cross-check (page 1) [R12], while the periods he read off the buoy charts are 5.7-6.2 s (pages 3-4, 6 and 15 Aug 2025) [R12]. Albany's problem was reshaping abundant swell into a rideable, non-closeout wave; Haifa/Israel's problem is swell scarcity ('less than 1 day/week' naturally surfable per Lior's Haifa proposal) [R13]. What transfers: (1) rock-vs-geotextile construction lesson; (2) the shallow-crest/wave-quality vs deeper-crest/safety trade-off any Haifa project would also face; (3) the multi-decade, multi-level-government (federal/state/city/club) financing pattern; (4) because Haifa is swell-starved rather than closeout-prone, Albany is a better precedent for safe rock-reef engineering than for wave-energy requirements, where Lior's own Gold Coast/Narrowneck comparison may be more directly analogous [R8][R3][R13].

reviews.role: self-identified Albany local, Swellnet forum poster
reviews.quote_or_summary: Visitor had a good face injury yesterday. The rocks are sharp, feet are pretty cut up... It's not a beginner wave. There are dangers. But it's pretty fucking epic when you get a good one.

Well done Albany council! Proper tubey take-off, big open face section to carve off too... Good vibes in the line-up too (for now anyhow).
Mixed report: on a given swell 'it didn't seem to be breaking very well, quite full and inconsistent,' while nearby beach breaks were closing out well that day.

reviews.role: Swellnet forum poster, self-identified public-recreation-facility engineer
reviews.quote_or_summary: The potential for far more serious injuries seems high... can artificial surfing reefs be made safer and better?
A much-loved local asset and a source of pride for surfers, families and the wider community, crediting passion, persistence and community support.

[The surf reef] does perform very well at different times, and the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that... surfers acknowledge that there's risk, and all the surfing community that I've spoken to are delighted with the surf reef.

sections.html_or_text:

PlaceMiddleton Beach, Albany, Western Australia

YearQuarry establishment from ~Oct 2024 [R17]; first rock placed on the seabed 18 Mar 2025 (planned six weeks) [R26][R30]; 'more than two-thirds complete' 16 May 2025, finish pushed to mid-June [R27]; storm of Mon 26 May 2025 moved some core rock [R25][R28]; officially opened 16 July 2025 'after four months of work' [R29][R31][R1][R2]. The City's programme 'Jan-Mar 2025, practical completion Mar 2025' [R3][R32] was a plan, not what happened.
TypeSubmerged rock-berm surf reef, 62,800 t of layered granite per the City's design table (belly, core, Class 1 armour) [R3] (the ~70,000 t quoted by The Inertia [R6] is kept as a rounded journalistic figure), no geotextile [R2][R3][R1] Tonnage note (audit 2026-10-10): the City design table gives 62,800 t [R3]; the ~70,000 t of The Inertia [R6] is a rounded journalistic figure; both kept, the design table is preferred.
PurposeSurfing amenity / tourism / youth retention - the reef's sole and primary stated design objective; unlike most artificial surf reefs, coastal erosion protection was not a driver [R3][R8][R9]
SizeLength 165 m; width up to 110 m; crest at -1.0 m AHD; total volume 62,800 t (belly D50 0.16 m/12,400 t, core D50 0.49 m/23,600 t, armour D50 0.94 m/26,800 t); reef sits ~140 m offshore [R3] Shape model (07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/HANDOFF.md section 3; HIGH confidence for position, size, orientation): default outline = Bluecoast final-design outermost contour [R3], placed on the Esri 2026-01-20 image by a fitted wedge (IoU 0.84); area 13,104 m2; along/across the crest 164.6 / 121.2 m (the card's 'width up to 110 m' is the design crest length at -2 m AHD, not the outline width); nearest edge 66.8 m from the beach-face line (the card's '~140 m offshore' is the City's value from an undefined reference, 'landward toe'; not reconciled). Volume about 34,000 m3 (DERIVED: 62,800 t [R3] divided by an assumed rock bulk density of 1.85 t/m3, ASSUMPTION of the shape agent with no source, 07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/HANDOFF.md section 3; the ~70,000 t of [R6] would give about 37,800 m3 by the same density).
