sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Middleton Beach produced 'unreliable and unsurfable waves for much of the year' despite being closest to central Albany; ~30 years of local-surfer advocacy (led by Peter Bolt from 1990) sought a consistent, surfable wave to build youth surf access, tourism, and economic development for Albany - not a response to erosion or a port-mitigation problem [R1][R6][R3][R8]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The 2015 Feasibility Study's objective was 'the creation of a consistent, surfable wave, which maximises available swell conditions' for Albany's economic and demographic benefit [R3]. The Detailed Design (executive summary by 2020) targeted a left-hand break, rides up to 100 m, and surfable waves 41% of the year, aimed at beginner-to-intermediate surfers per EPA WA [R3][R2][R9]. Design used 'thorough numerical, physical and conceptual modelling', with a 2018 BMT Environmental Impact Assessment, read at the source in October 2026: its shoreline-modelling appendix says 'In all the simulations tested, there appeared to be a widening of the shoreline' (PDF p.151) and the report expects offshore placement to give no significant shoreline impact compared with inshore placement (PDF p.38) [R20]; these findings were earlier cited via [R3][R8]. Business-case modelling projected NPV $57.9M / BCR 6.69, driven by ~10 annual surfing events and ~3,500 extra overnight visitors/year (an earlier May-2023 interim figure gave NPV $19.4M / BCR 3.25) [R3][R15].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The built reef matches the design specification closely on paper: 165 m long, up to 110 m wide, crest at -1.0 m AHD, 62,800 t of rock in three graded layers [R3]. Construction: quarry from ~Oct 2024 [R17]; first rock on the seabed 18 Mar 2025, planned six weeks [R26][R30]; 'more than two-thirds complete' on 16 May 2025 with finish moved to mid-June [R27]; opened 16 Jul 2025 [R29][R31] (the earlier reading 'main placement Jan-Mar 2025, practical completion Mar 2025' came from the City's programme and the WA Government statement of 14 Jan 2025, which were plans [R3][R32]). A New Zealand marine crew used precision geospatial placement equipment [R3][R2][R8]. Storm of Mon 26 May 2025 (highest waves in King George Sound since 2017) moved some of the smaller CORE rock shoreward before the armour was on top; the contractor surveyed and replaced it before opening [R25][R28]. No as-built level, crest survey, section or seabed depth has been published (checked again 2026-10-13 in four new sources). Once open, the reef performed 'far higher' than the 41% design-surfability target [R2][R6], though no source gives a precise revised percentage (Raised Water Research gives about 40 % of the year breaking on the reef proper [R10], which does not support 'far higher'; the claim rests on quotes in R2/R6 only). The most significant post-opening change came in late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026): about 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days by commercial divers with a local vessel and Albany Boardriders, after surveys in late 2025; cost 'more than $20,000' in the article lede and 'about $24,000' as the City's estimate (paywalled article, text read from the page metadata) [R11][R18]. This is a later change: the 3D model shows the 2025 design state, and this goes in as a note, not as geometry.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Widely reported as a rare unambiguous artificial-surf-reef success on wave quality: Swellnet says 'the reef performs far better than expectations' [R8]; Peter Bolt calls it 'intermediate-to-advanced on most days' as swell grows [R6][R2]; local surfer Cameron Warburton calls it 'a really high-performance wave' [R2]. Raised Water Research describes 0.8-1.3 m faces, 100-120 m rides, breaking on the reef proper ~40% of the year [R10]. But a persistent forum question (Aug-Oct 2025, user 'steveb') is whether it breaks well on the small (<1 m) everyday swells that dominate the local climate; local 'soggydog' answered 'No, but it has created reliable banks either side when it's too small for the reef proper' [R8]. No monitoring data, beach-width surveys, storm-damage, or fisheries/ecology results were found in sources fetched, beyond the single 2018 EIA citation [R8].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Sources attribute the reef's relative success to layered, precision-placed rock construction rather than geotextile sand bags, which 'failed due to the bags splitting, shifting, or settling' at earlier reefs worldwide [R8][R3][R6]. Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) argues rock reefs cannot match a sand-formed bank's contour accuracy because armour rock must be massive for stability, so shallow enough placement to break small swells 'compromises user safety'; rock permeability also means small swells 'surge into the reef rather than shoal and break', while larger swells ride over imperfections and shoal further up - explaining why the reef performs much better on bigger swells [R8]. He contrasts Albany's shallow crest (-1.0 m AHD, chosen partly 'to maximise wave breaking') unfavourably with Palm Beach (Gold Coast), which mitigated injury risk with a deeper crest [R8][R3]. Mayor Greg Stocks frames the injuries more as a behavioural issue: 'inexperienced surfers taking on quite elite waves...the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that' [R7].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Injuries began within weeks of opening: Swellnet forum posts from Albany locals describe 'a good face injury', sharp rocks cutting feet, and (per 'Baldhead') 'a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion' [R8]. By October 2025 the reef was being considered for 'detuning' ('busting up a couple of the rocks in the shallower part of the wave') following a 'spate of injuries on beginner surfers who can't handle its juice' [R7]. In late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026) about 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days, at 'more than $20,000' (lede) / 'about $24,000' (City estimate) [R11][R18]. Earlier, the storm of 26 May 2025 had already moved some core rock shoreward during construction [R25][R28]. 'steveb' argued this represented a public-liability/facility-design failure, comparing the reef to a council-managed playground where 'public safety is the number one priority' [R8]. Positive unplanned effects include reliable secondary sand-bank breaks either side of the reef on small swells, and youth/community access described by Peter Bolt watching 'the kids come down here before school, in the dark, to get a wave before they go to school' [R8][R2]. Shark risk is raised as a live community concern (no confirmed incident found) [R8].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) proposes that rock-dumped reefs inherently trade wave-shape accuracy against user safety, and argues a fully prefabricated reef structure - built onshore, floated out, and installed by controlled submergence - could achieve 'accurate shape and level, no subsidence, no settlement, no sharp edges, no possible entrapment points', citing materials with a 'safe working life in excess of 100 years', and points to Palm Beach's deeper, safer crest as a precedent for the safety/wave-quality trade-off Albany did not take [R8][R3]. Most surfer sentiment in the sources is not calling for a safer/easier wave - several posters push back on 'detuning' as inherent to a legitimately world-class wave - but there is a recurring, unanswered request for clearer information on how reliably the reef breaks on the small, sub-1 m swells that make up most of Middleton Beach's actual wave climate [R7][R8].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: King George Sound (Albany) is micro-tidal (mean range 0.4 m, spring 1.1 m), broadly comparable to the Mediterranean at Haifa, which is also effectively micro-tidal, though no fetched source gives a numeric Haifa tidal-range figure [R5][R10]. Official Albany figures differ in form from the Wikipedia ones: the 2018 BMT assessment gives a Middleton Beach spring range of 0.9 m and a neap range of 0.3 m, largest range below 1.5 m [R20]; the WA Department of Transport / Bureau of Meteorology predictions for 2024 run from 0.12 to 1.40 m above LAT, mean 0.742 m above LAT (1,043 high and low waters) [R22]. Datums and averaging periods differ, so the figures are not reconciled. Albany's wave climate (consistent, long-period 12-16s Southern Ocean groundswell) is fundamentally more energetic than Haifa's, where Lior's own Shikmona-buoy measurements define 'minimum surfable' at only 0.45-0.6 m within a narrow WNW swell window [R10][R12]; the 6-8 s period is NOT part of his buoy-based definition: in his notes it belongs to the '4Surfers' forecast-site cross-check (page 1) [R12], while the periods he read off the buoy charts are 5.7-6.2 s (pages 3-4, 6 and 15 Aug 2025) [R12]. Albany's problem was reshaping abundant swell into a rideable, non-closeout wave; Haifa/Israel's problem is swell scarcity ('less than 1 day/week' naturally surfable per Lior's Haifa proposal) [R13]. What transfers: (1) rock-vs-geotextile construction lesson; (2) the shallow-crest/wave-quality vs deeper-crest/safety trade-off any Haifa project would also face; (3) the multi-decade, multi-level-government (federal/state/city/club) financing pattern; (4) because Haifa is swell-starved rather than closeout-prone, Albany is a better precedent for safe rock-reef engineering than for wave-energy requirements, where Lior's own Gold Coast/Narrowneck comparison may be more directly analogous [R8][R3][R13].

footprint.orientation_notes: The Bluecoast/ASR 'Final Reef Design' table (reproduced as a figure on R3, filename design.jpg) specifies 'Crest orientation: Curved, 270°N-305°N... Maximises breaking and creates waves that peel evenly along the reef.' This is the bearing of the reef's own curved crest/wave-break line (a ~35 degree arc), not a stated swell-approach azimuth — no source we found gives a numeric swell-approach bearing (contrary to Gemini's invented '160-190 deg SSE-S', see gemini_comparison). The design table also specifies 'Surfing direction: Left-hander' and a 'Take-off area' at the more offshore, wider end of the reef (per the same figure), with the wave peeling toward the narrower, more shoreward end, matching R3's text 'the design provides surfing rides of up to 100m'. Our polygon therefore tapers to a point at its shoreward/updrift-adjacent end and bulges to its maximum ~110 m cross-shore width at the offshore 'take-off' end, per this figure — but the figure's own two dimension-arrow annotations (110 m and 140 m) do not share a consistent pixel scale (see derivation row 8), so this reading is topological/qualitative only, not a scaled tracing.
footprint.materials: Submerged rock-berm surf reef; ~62,800 t of layered granite in three graded layers — belly (D50 0.16 m, 12,400 t, 18%), core (D50 0.49 m, 23,600 t, 36%), Class 1 armour (D50 0.94 m, 26,800 t, 46%); no geotextile [R3]

footprint.confidence: The built reef shows as a dark wedge on a geo-referenced Esri image of 2026-01-20 that is absent from the 2025-01-16 image of the same spot, and the outline agrees with the scale-barred Bluecoast design plan (outline overlap 81 %, orientation within 3 deg) and with the City's 165 m length (design plan 165 m, satellite 157 m, -5 %).
open_issues: No true as-built plan-view CAD drawing or bathymetric survey was found publicly. The only plan-view figure available (design.jpg, legend 'ASR Design') is a pre-final concept sketch whose own two printed dimension arrows (110 m and 140 m) scale inconsistently by ~37% when pixel-measured — it was therefore used only for qualitative shape/taper topology, never for scaled vertex coordinates.

The design.jpg figure combines the physical reef outline with a separate wave-refraction/peel-line fan; distinguishing the two required close visual inspection and there remains some residual uncertainty about exactly where the rock structure's own edge lies versus the illustrative wave lines.

The two real aerial construction photos (R10, R2) are both dated/captioned May 2025, i.e. mid-construction — they may show a partially-built extent rather than the completed footprint, so were used only to corroborate general taper direction, not final size.

Exact polygon vertices are a low-confidence synthetic estimate, constrained only by the sourced 165 m x 110 m bounding envelope and the qualitative crescent curvature described in the design table; treat the polygon as illustrative of shape family, not a precise outline.
area_m2 (9,720) is not a published figure — it is a geometric consequence of our assumed polygon and should be treated as low-confidence, same caveat as Gemini's own area figures.

The x-axis 'positive = north' convention is inferred from the apparent north-up orientation of the design figure (land west, water east, coast trending N-S) rather than from an explicit stated bearing or printed north arrow — flagged as an assumption.

Distance offshore has a documented range across sources (120 m per Wikipedia/R4, 140 m per the current R3 page, ~145 m per a 2023 FAQ/R15) reflecting design evolution over time; we used the current page's 140 m figure as primary, consistent with the card.

Reef volume (34,000 m3) comes from an earlier 2017-bathymetry concept-stage table on the same figure as the shape sketch and may not equal the final as-built volume; only the final tonnage (62,800 t) is well corroborated across sources.

R15 (City of Albany, May 2023 FAQ PDF), read in full during the 2026-09-25 verification pass, gives an earlier interim design of 'up to 100 metres in width' (vs the final 110 m) and an interim footprint of 'approximately 16,000m2' (vs our ~9,720 m2 estimate and Gemini's unsourced 13,500/12,363 m2) — consistent with the card's existing 'design evolution over time' framing for the offshore-distance figure, now shown to also apply to width and area. The current R3 page's 165/110/140 figures were kept as primary, per existing methodology (prefer the final/current page over superseded interim estimates).

No individual designer name could be independently confirmed for this project as of the 2026-09-25 verification pass (see gemini_comparison.disagree, 'designer names'). Only the firm, Bluecoast Consulting Engineers, is confirmed (R3, R15's consultant-team list); a prior draft's attribution of 'Evan Watterson' to this specific project did not hold up against its own cited sources and was withdrawn.

name: Xala Reef (Costalegre artificial surf reef)
place: Xala development, Costalegre coast, Jalisco (between Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo)
year: Unclear/phased: boulder surf break reported built by April 2025 [R3][R4]; Raised Water Research calls it 'newly completed' and, in its announcement of 31 March 2026, billed a reveal event for 16 April 2026 [R1]
type: Rock/boulder reef — 3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders, not geotextile sand tubes [R3][R4]
purpose: Dual: (1) private members'-only high-performance surf break for Xala's owners/guests; (2) coastal protection/beach restoration, engineered to 'restore the beach, not flatten it' [R3][R4][R5]
size: Not disclosed — no length, width, crest depth, or fill volume found in any source this sweep [R1][R3][R4][R5] Shape/3D model: none, trace not possible (07_scale/shapes/mexico-reef-2026-unnamed/HANDOFF.md): no image shows the structure and no dimensions or coordinates exist; the 160 x 80 m 'analogy envelope' in 07_scale/reefs/ and Gemini's ~140 x 75 m are unsourced and not used. The card therefore has no model numbers to match (statement about this project's own files, 07_scale/shapes/mexico-reef-2026-unnamed/HANDOFF.md).
cost: Not disclosed for the reef specifically [R3][R5]
financed_by: Xala development by Activos Turísticos de México (ACTUR), led by Ricardo Santa Cruz and Jerónimo Bremer [R3]; Richard Gere is a co-founder/backer [R3][R4]; Six Senses (IHG) will operate the resort hotel [R3][R5]. No source itemizes who specifically paid for the reef construction [R3][R4][R5]
motivation: Positioned as part of a 'regenerative,' low-density luxury development contrasted with conventional Mexican coastal resorts; developer Ricardo Santa Cruz frames the project around ecological restraint over density and a buyer base (largely Californian tech-wealth) that doesn't want a conventional resort [R3][R4]
designer: Simon Brandi Mortensen, Principal Coastal Engineer and Managing Director, DHI Seaport (MSc Coastal Engineering, TU Denmark; 19 years in coastal projects; designer of Australia's Palm Beach Reef) [R1][R6]
status_now: Described as complete ('newly completed') in Raised Water Research's announcement of 31 March 2026 [R1] (the source's framing, not a verified fact); that announcement billed a reveal at a California Surf Club event in Redondo Beach, CA, for 16 April 2026 [R1][R9]; no source seen reports that the event took place. Access is private/limited — Xala caps built units at 93 against an approved 4,500 [R1][R3][R4] Audit 2026-10-10: the earlier wording 'publicly unveiled 16 April 2026' was removed because it is not supported as a past event: R1 is an announcement posted 2026-03-31 that bills the reveal for 16 April 2026; no source seen reports that it took place, and 'complete and operational' is R1's framing, not a verified fact. (The shape HANDOFF carried the same wording; corrected in the citations audit of 2026-10-10.)
hover_text: A private, members'-only rock/boulder surf reef (3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders) built inside the Xala luxury resort development on Mexico's Costalegre coast, Jalisco; cost and exact build date undisclosed, announced 31 March 2026 with a public reveal billed for 16 April 2026 [R1] — too new for any independent outcome data to exist yet [R1][R3][R4].
design_as_planned: No detailed design brief (target wave height, period, break type, or beach-width promise) was found in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card). Documented: quarried rock/boulder construction (3,000 truckloads), not geotextile sand-filled tubes [R3][R4], consistent with designer Simon Mortensen's stated philosophy that geotextile reefs suffer from bags 'breaking, shifting or sinking' with removal costs sometimes exceeding placement costs, whereas rock is 'natural and provides many small crevasses for marine habitat' [R12]. Stated intent: coastal protection/beach nourishment combined with a 'consistently great wave,' explicitly contrasted with reef designs that would 'flatten' rather than 'restore' the beach [R3][R4][R5]. No public engineering report, EIS, or design paper was located in this card's searches (negative finding).
as_built_vs_design: Not enough independent material was found (negative finding of this card) to compare as-designed vs as-built — no construction-progress reporting, as-built drawings, or named contractor were located. The only construction detail available (3,000 truckloads of quarry boulders) is presented in press coverage as the finished description, not a revised design target [R3][R4]. A roughly one-year gap between the reef being described as part of Xala's built amenities (April 2025 [R3][R4]) and Raised Water Research's 'newly completed'/unveiling framing (March–April 2026 [R1]) is unresolved in sources found — possibly phased construction, or the reef was substantially built by 2025 and only formally unveiled in 2026.
outcome: No independent surf report, wave-height measurement, or session footage description was found; Raised Water Research withheld even the reef's exact location until the reveal event billed for 16 April 2026 and promised 'never-before-seen footage,' implying essentially no public track record as of its 31 March 2026 announcement [R1]. Coastal-protection performance (before/after beach-profile or erosion data) is not measured/reported in any source found (negative finding of this card). Ecology is not reported for the reef structure itself, though the wider Xala site includes a leatherback/Olive Ridley/green sea-turtle sanctuary and Ramsar-listed estuaries as separate conservation features [R5][R10]. Access/longevity/damage-event data does not yet exist given that the reef was only announced in March-April 2026 [R1]; no source was found stating otherwise (negative finding of this card).
why_worked_or_failed: No outcome data was found to assess this directly (negative finding of this card). The only available engineering signal is designer pedigree: Simon Mortensen led the design of Australia's Palm Beach Reef (Gold Coast; design 2013–2014, construction April–September 2019 [R6][R7]; ~$18.2M AUD/~$12.5M USD, financed by the City of Gold Coast; 4–8 tonne rock boulders plus 470,000 m³ of beach-nourishment sand), which Raised Water Research assesses as a design success — 'the reef appears to be a success,' producing a consistent ~60 m right-hander and a shorter left in bigger swell [R7]. This is background on the designer's method only, not evidence about Xala's own performance — no source directly ties Palm Beach's outcome data to the Xala build. Decision: verdict 'n-a' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24) because the reef is too new and no performance data exist [R1]; it is not a judgement of success or failure.
unexpected_results: Nothing Xala-specific was found in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card) (no litigation, safety incidents, fishing pressure, rip currents, or tourism-surge reporting). One indirect signal: an unrelated online repost of the Hollywood Reporter piece on a political/finance forum drew at least one favorable outside comment calling the whole project 'a neat idea/project,' but this concerns the development in general, not the reef, and is a single anonymous forum post [R4].
could_be_better: No source listed in References offers a critique of the Xala reef specifically (negative finding of this card) (too new; no engineering post-mortem or surfer complaint thread was found). Generic rock-reef trade-off to watch for once surf reports exist: rock-bottom reefs (versus sand-bottom breaks) have drawn 'harder surface' complaints at other sites such as Palm Beach Reef (no source for this complaint is held in the Palm Beach card either, (unsourced)) — flagged here only as a general risk category, not a documented Xala complaint. No author/expert or surfer view was found for Xala specifically (negative finding); the site's private/members-only access model [R3][R4] may itself suppress independent public reviews for some time (the card author's inference).
relevance_to_israel: Tide range and local wave climate at the Xala/Costalegre site were not found in this card's searches. What transfers conceptually, independent of Xala's own unverified outcome (all items are the card author's inferences): (1) Material choice precedent — the designer's shift toward quarried rock/boulder construction [R3][R12] (also used at Palm Beach Reef, 4–8 t boulders [R7]) rather than geotextile sand-filled tubes is directly comparable to the geotube-vs-rock materials question already live in this project's Israel dossiers (e.g. Ashkelon's 2018 geotube) — a rock-reef alternative is one materials option Israeli planners could weigh against documented geotube failure modes (undersized tubes, sand burial). (2) Governance-model contrast — Xala's reef is privately financed and privately accessed (members-only resort [R3][R4][R5]), unlike Israel's public-agency-funded structures (e.g. Ashkelon, Michmoret), a useful contrast case for 'who pays / who gets access' framing, though not a coastal-engineering transfer.

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameXala Reef (Costalegre artificial surf reef)
PlaceXala development, Costalegre coast, Jalisco (between Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo)
CountryMexico
YearUnclear/phased: boulder surf break reported built by April 2025 [R3][R4]; Raised Water Research calls it 'newly completed' and, in its announcement of 31 March 2026, billed a reveal event for 16 April 2026 [R1]
TypeRock/boulder reef — 3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders, not geotextile sand tubes [R3][R4]
PurposeDual: (1) private members'-only high-performance surf break for Xala's owners/guests; (2) coastal protection/beach restoration, engineered to 'restore the beach, not flatten it' [R3][R4][R5]
SizeNot disclosed — no length, width, crest depth, or fill volume found in any source this sweep [R1][R3][R4][R5] Shape/3D model: none, trace not possible (07_scale/shapes/mexico-reef-2026-unnamed/HANDOFF.md): no image shows the structure and no dimensions or coordinates exist; the 160 x 80 m 'analogy envelope' in 07_scale/reefs/ and Gemini's ~140 x 75 m are unsourced and not used. The card therefore has no model numbers to match (statement about this project's own files, 07_scale/shapes/mexico-reef-2026-unnamed/HANDOFF.md).
CostNot disclosed for the reef specifically [R3][R5]
Financed byXala development by Activos Turísticos de México (ACTUR), led by Ricardo Santa Cruz and Jerónimo Bremer [R3]; Richard Gere is a co-founder/backer [R3][R4]; Six Senses (IHG) will operate the resort hotel [R3][R5]. No source itemizes who specifically paid for the reef construction [R3][R4][R5]
DesignerSimon Brandi Mortensen, Principal Coastal Engineer and Managing Director, DHI Seaport (MSc Coastal Engineering, TU Denmark; 19 years in coastal projects; designer of Australia's Palm Beach Reef) [R1][R6]
ContractorNot stated in sources found
Status nowDescribed as complete ('newly completed') in Raised Water Research's announcement of 31 March 2026 [R1] (the source's framing, not a verified fact); that announcement billed a reveal at a California Surf Club event in Redondo Beach, CA, for 16 April 2026 [R1][R9]; no source seen reports that the event took place. Access is private/limited — Xala caps built units at 93 against an approved 4,500 [R1][R3][R4] Audit 2026-10-10: the earlier wording 'publicly unveiled 16 April 2026' was removed because it is not supported as a past event: R1 is an announcement posted 2026-03-31 that bills the reveal for 16 April 2026; no source seen reports that it took place, and 'complete and operational' is R1's framing, not a verified fact. (The shape HANDOFF carried the same wording; corrected in the citations audit of 2026-10-10.)

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Positioned as part of a 'regenerative,' low-density luxury development contrasted with conventional Mexican coastal resorts; developer Ricardo Santa Cruz frames the project around ecological restraint over density and a buyer base (largely Californian tech-wealth) that doesn't want a conventional resort [R3][R4]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: No detailed design brief (target wave height, period, break type, or beach-width promise) was found in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card). Documented: quarried rock/boulder construction (3,000 truckloads), not geotextile sand-filled tubes [R3][R4], consistent with designer Simon Mortensen's stated philosophy that geotextile reefs suffer from bags 'breaking, shifting or sinking' with removal costs sometimes exceeding placement costs, whereas rock is 'natural and provides many small crevasses for marine habitat' [R12]. Stated intent: coastal protection/beach nourishment combined with a 'consistently great wave,' explicitly contrasted with reef designs that would 'flatten' rather than 'restore' the beach [R3][R4][R5]. No public engineering report, EIS, or design paper was located in this card's searches (negative finding).

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Not enough independent material was found (negative finding of this card) to compare as-designed vs as-built — no construction-progress reporting, as-built drawings, or named contractor were located. The only construction detail available (3,000 truckloads of quarry boulders) is presented in press coverage as the finished description, not a revised design target [R3][R4]. A roughly one-year gap between the reef being described as part of Xala's built amenities (April 2025 [R3][R4]) and Raised Water Research's 'newly completed'/unveiling framing (March–April 2026 [R1]) is unresolved in sources found — possibly phased construction, or the reef was substantially built by 2025 and only formally unveiled in 2026.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: No independent surf report, wave-height measurement, or session footage description was found; Raised Water Research withheld even the reef's exact location until the reveal event billed for 16 April 2026 and promised 'never-before-seen footage,' implying essentially no public track record as of its 31 March 2026 announcement [R1]. Coastal-protection performance (before/after beach-profile or erosion data) is not measured/reported in any source found (negative finding of this card). Ecology is not reported for the reef structure itself, though the wider Xala site includes a leatherback/Olive Ridley/green sea-turtle sanctuary and Ramsar-listed estuaries as separate conservation features [R5][R10]. Access/longevity/damage-event data does not yet exist given that the reef was only announced in March-April 2026 [R1]; no source was found stating otherwise (negative finding of this card).

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: No outcome data was found to assess this directly (negative finding of this card). The only available engineering signal is designer pedigree: Simon Mortensen led the design of Australia's Palm Beach Reef (Gold Coast; design 2013–2014, construction April–September 2019 [R6][R7]; ~$18.2M AUD/~$12.5M USD, financed by the City of Gold Coast; 4–8 tonne rock boulders plus 470,000 m³ of beach-nourishment sand), which Raised Water Research assesses as a design success — 'the reef appears to be a success,' producing a consistent ~60 m right-hander and a shorter left in bigger swell [R7]. This is background on the designer's method only, not evidence about Xala's own performance — no source directly ties Palm Beach's outcome data to the Xala build. Decision: verdict 'n-a' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24) because the reef is too new and no performance data exist [R1]; it is not a judgement of success or failure.

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Nothing Xala-specific was found in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card) (no litigation, safety incidents, fishing pressure, rip currents, or tourism-surge reporting). One indirect signal: an unrelated online repost of the Hollywood Reporter piece on a political/finance forum drew at least one favorable outside comment calling the whole project 'a neat idea/project,' but this concerns the development in general, not the reef, and is a single anonymous forum post [R4].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: No source listed in References offers a critique of the Xala reef specifically (negative finding of this card) (too new; no engineering post-mortem or surfer complaint thread was found). Generic rock-reef trade-off to watch for once surf reports exist: rock-bottom reefs (versus sand-bottom breaks) have drawn 'harder surface' complaints at other sites such as Palm Beach Reef (no source for this complaint is held in the Palm Beach card either, (unsourced)) — flagged here only as a general risk category, not a documented Xala complaint. No author/expert or surfer view was found for Xala specifically (negative finding); the site's private/members-only access model [R3][R4] may itself suppress independent public reviews for some time (the card author's inference).

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tide range and local wave climate at the Xala/Costalegre site were not found in this card's searches. What transfers conceptually, independent of Xala's own unverified outcome (all items are the card author's inferences): (1) Material choice precedent — the designer's shift toward quarried rock/boulder construction [R3][R12] (also used at Palm Beach Reef, 4–8 t boulders [R7]) rather than geotextile sand-filled tubes is directly comparable to the geotube-vs-rock materials question already live in this project's Israel dossiers (e.g. Ashkelon's 2018 geotube) — a rock-reef alternative is one materials option Israeli planners could weigh against documented geotube failure modes (undersized tubes, sand burial). (2) Governance-model contrast — Xala's reef is privately financed and privately accessed (members-only resort [R3][R4][R5]), unlike Israel's public-agency-funded structures (e.g. Ashkelon, Michmoret), a useful contrast case for 'who pays / who gets access' framing, though not a coastal-engineering transfer.
